tool_use_result.originalFile:
An inline liquid metering valve delivers a repeatable measured volume of concentrate into a flowing carrier liquid and rinses the surfaces that contacted the concentrate after each dose, without electrical power and without any command additional to the stroke that delivers the dose.

The valve has a housing with an inlet and an outlet and a metering sleeve fixed within the housing. The metering sleeve defines a dose chamber, a concentrate port opening into the dose chamber, a carrier-liquid admission port opening into the dose chamber, and a flush bypass that opens downstream of the dose chamber. A piston slides axially in the dose chamber between a fill position and a discharge position. The piston has an upstream sealing land and a downstream sealing land axially spaced from one another and joined by a reduced-diameter waist.

Separation of the two liquids is enforced by the axial order of the land faces and the port edges rather than by the sequence in which any external command arrives. In the fill position, the waist connects the concentrate port to the dose chamber while the upstream and downstream sealing lands isolate the carrier-liquid admission port from the concentrate port. Movement of the piston toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port before the downstream sealing land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port. Carrier liquid then enters behind the measured volume of concentrate and expels that volume through a one-way outlet valve toward the outlet. Because one land face has passed the concentrate port before the other land face releases the carrier-liquid admission port, no position of the piston places the concentrate source in communication with the carrier-liquid path.

The rinse is carried out by the return of the same piston. An annular rinse channel lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve and an inner surface of the housing, and at least one rinse opening leads from that channel through the metering sleeve into the dose chamber. A follower pin carried by the piston rod opens a normally closed flush poppet connected to the flush bypass during the return stroke, so that carrier liquid sweeps the annular rinse channel, issues from the rinse opening across the surfaces wetted by the concentrate, and leaves through the flush bypass to the outlet. The flush poppet closes before the waist reconnects the concentrate port to the dose chamber, so the rinse is complete, and the rinse liquid is on its way to the outlet, before any further concentrate can enter. The rinse cannot be omitted, mistimed or deferred, because the element that opens it is the element that carries the piston.

In described embodiments, a flexible lip on the upstream sealing land wipes the wall of the dose chamber before the flush poppet opens, so that the flushing stream is presented with a film rather than with standing liquid. Two radial rinse openings are directed across the concentrate port and across the one-way outlet valve, which are the two surfaces on which residue is otherwise retained.

Dose selection is mechanical and self-indexing. An index collar surrounds the metering sleeve and has a helical cam groove engaged by the follower pin, so that each full stroke of the piston turns the index collar by one increment. Three selectable axial stop faces on the index collar limit the travel of the piston and thereby set three dose volumes, a spring-biased detent engaging one of three recesses retains the selected setting, and a transparent window in the housing shows one of three dose setting numerals carried by the index collar, so that the setting is visible without electronics.

A replaceable cartridge contains the piston, the metering sleeve, the one-way outlet valve and the flush poppet, and is retained by a threaded end cap. Removing the threaded end cap withdraws the cartridge without disturbing the connections at the inlet and the outlet.

A corresponding method admits concentrate to the dose chamber, closes the concentrate port before uncovering the carrier-liquid admission port, expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve, and then opens the flush poppet with the follower pin during the return of the piston and closes it again before the concentrate port is reconnected.

In the following description, the terms upstream and downstream refer to the direction of travel of the carrier liquid from the inlet toward the outlet, and the terms axial and radial refer to the axis along which the piston slides.

FIG. 1 shows an inline liquid metering valve 10 having a cylindrical housing 12 with an inlet 14 at one axial end and an outlet 16 at the opposite axial end, a metering sleeve 18 fixed within the housing 12, a cartridge 64 retained in the housing 12 by a threaded end cap 66, and a transparent window 52 in the housing 12.

The inline liquid metering valve 10 is connected in a line that already carries a flowing carrier liquid. Carrier liquid enters at the inlet 14, passes along the housing 12, and leaves at the outlet 16. That flow is the main flow into which each dose of concentrate is delivered, and it is also the only liquid used to rinse the valve. The metering sleeve 18 is spaced radially inward from the inner surface of the housing 12 over part of its length.

FIG. 2 shows the metering sleeve 18 defining a dose chamber 20, a concentrate port 22 opening into the dose chamber 20 and a carrier-liquid admission port 24 opening into the dose chamber 20. FIG. 2 further shows an upstream sealing land 30 and a downstream sealing land 32 joined by a reduced-diameter waist 34 in the fill position, and a one-way outlet valve 38.

The dose chamber 20 is cylindrical. The concentrate port 22 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and is connected in use to a concentrate source. The carrier-liquid admission port 24 passes through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 at an axial position downstream of the concentrate port 22, and admits carrier liquid to the dose chamber 20. The metering sleeve 18 further defines a flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20.

A piston 28 is axially slidable in the dose chamber 20 between a fill position and a discharge position. The upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 are axially spaced from one another on the piston 28 and are joined by the reduced-diameter waist 34. Each sealing land bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20, while the waist 34 stands clear of that wall and so forms an annular space that travels with the piston 28. A piston rod 36 extends from the piston 28 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 and is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke. The one-way outlet valve 38 is arranged to pass liquid from the dose chamber 20 toward the outlet 16 and to prevent flow in the opposite direction.

In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20, the extent of which is fixed by the travel then permitted to the piston 28. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 while the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.

Movement of the piston 28 toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port 22 before the downstream sealing land 32 uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port 24. The upstream sealing land 30 arrives at the concentrate port 22 and shuts it while the downstream sealing land 32 is still overlying the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Only after that has happened does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.

The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every position of the piston 28 at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18. It does not depend on the order in which external commands are given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of a separately actuated shut-off element. A slow stroke, an interrupted stroke, or a stroke reversed part way through cannot open both ports at once, because the port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens.

FIG. 4 shows an index collar 40 having a helical cam groove 42 engaged by a follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36, three selectable axial stop faces 46, a spring-biased detent 48 engaging one of three detent recesses 50, and three dose setting numerals 54.

The index collar 40 surrounds the metering sleeve 18. Each full stroke of the piston 28 draws the follower pin 44 along the helical cam groove 42 and turns the index collar 40 by one increment, so that the index collar 40 advances by itself as the valve is used and needs no separate indexing drive.

The three axial stop faces 46 are carried by the index collar 40 at different axial positions. The stop face presented by the current increment of rotation limits the travel of the piston 28 and thereby sets the dose volume, so that the three axial stop faces 46 correspond to three dose volumes. The spring-biased detent 48 engages one of the three detent recesses 50 to retain the selected setting, so that the index collar 40 is held against vibration and against the forces transmitted through the follower pin 44 until it is next indexed.

The transparent window 52 in the housing 12 shows one of the three dose setting numerals 54 carried by the index collar 40. The dose setting numeral presented at the transparent window 52 is the one associated with the axial stop face then limiting the travel of the piston 28, so that the dose setting is mechanically visible without electronics, without power at the valve and without a controller. What is seen at the transparent window 52 is the position of the mechanism itself rather than a stored value, so the displayed setting cannot disagree with the volume that the valve will deliver.

FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, the follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62 of which one is directed across the concentrate port 22, and a flush bypass 26.

The flexible lip 56 is carried on the upstream sealing land 30 and bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20. As the return stroke begins, the flexible lip 56 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20 and carries the film of concentrate remaining on that wall ahead of it, so that the rinse which follows is presented with a wetted surface rather than with standing liquid.

The annular rinse channel 60 lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve 18 and an inner surface of the housing 12, and is supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet 14. The two radial rinse openings 62 pass through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and connect the annular rinse channel 60 to the dose chamber 20. One of the two radial rinse openings 62 is directed across the concentrate port 22 and the other is directed across the one-way outlet valve 38. Those are the two surfaces on which concentrate is otherwise retained after a dose, the first because concentrate stands in the mouth of the port and the second because concentrate is the last liquid to pass the seat.

The flush poppet 58 is normally closed and is connected to the flush bypass 26. Near the end of the return stroke, the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows from the inlet 14 through the annular rinse channel 60, through the two radial rinse openings 62 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 to the outlet 16. The rinse liquid therefore leaves by the same route as the dose and is carried away in the main flow.

The flush poppet 58 closes before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. The concentrate port 22 is closed throughout the interval in which the annular rinse channel 60 communicates with the flush bypass 26, so that carrier liquid at the pressure of the main line is never presented to an open concentrate port 22 and cannot be driven back toward the concentrate source. Only when the flush poppet 58 has closed does the continuing return of the piston 28 bring the waist 34 back into register with the concentrate port 22, at which point the dose chamber 20 is charged again for the next dose.

Because the follower pin 44 that opens the flush poppet 58 is carried by the piston rod 36, the rinse occurs once for every dose and at the same point in every cycle. It is not a separate operation, it needs no command, and it cannot be omitted while the valve continues to be used. The rinse also occurs while the concentrate port 22 is shut and after the wall of the dose chamber 20 has been wiped, so that it removes a film with clean carrier liquid instead of diluting a standing charge of concentrate.

The cartridge 64 contains the piston 28, the metering sleeve 18, the one-way outlet valve 38 and the flush poppet 58, and is removable from the housing 12 as a unit. Removing the threaded end cap 66 withdraws the cartridge 64 from the housing 12 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 without disturbing the connections at the inlet 14 and the outlet 16, so that the cartridge 64 is replaced as a unit while the housing 12 remains in the line. The parts that contact the concentrate are the parts that are exchanged, so a change of concentrate or a worn sealing land is dealt with by fitting a further cartridge rather than by dismantling the installation.

In use, carrier liquid flows through the housing 12 from the inlet 14 to the outlet 16. With the piston 28 in the fill position, concentrate is admitted through the concentrate port 22 and past the waist 34 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume, the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolating the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. The piston 28 is then advanced toward the discharge position so as to close the concentrate port 22 and thereafter to uncover the carrier-liquid admission port 24 with the downstream sealing land 32. Carrier liquid is admitted through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16. The travel of the piston 28 on this stroke is limited by the selected one of the three axial stop faces 46, which sets the measured volume.

The piston 28 is then returned toward the fill position. During the return, the flexible lip 56 on the upstream sealing land 30 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20, and the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36 opens the normally closed flush poppet 58. Carrier liquid flows through the annular rinse channel 60 between the metering sleeve 18 and the housing 12, through the two radial rinse openings 62 in the metering sleeve 18 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20 to the outlet 16. The flush poppet 58 is closed before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. Over the same full stroke, the follower pin 44 travelling in the helical cam groove 42 turns the index collar 40 by one increment, the spring-biased detent 48 enters the next of the three detent recesses 50, and the dose setting numeral then presented at the transparent window 52 shows the setting that will govern the next dose. The valve is thereby left charged, rinsed and set, ready for the following cycle.

The foregoing description sets out embodiments of the invention. A skilled reader may make changes of detail to the described embodiments without departing from the scope of the claims that follow.

Each sealing land bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20, while the waist 34 stands clear of that wall. A piston rod 36 extends from the piston 28 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 and is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke. The one-way outlet valve 38 is arranged to pass liquid from the dose chamber 20 toward the outlet 16 and to prevent flow in the opposite direction.

-In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20, the extent of which is fixed by the travel then permitted to the piston 28. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 while the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.

+In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume of concentrate, the extent of which is fixed by the travel then permitted to the piston 28. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 while the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.

Movement of the piston 28 toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port 22 before the downstream sealing land 32 uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port 24. The upstream sealing land 30 arrives at the concentrate port 22 and shuts it while the downstream sealing land 32 is still overlying the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Only after that has happened does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.

# FIG. 3

View: enlarged longitudinal section of the metering portion of FIG. 1 during the return stroke, axis horizontal, with the flush poppet held open. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the sheet edges.

Geometry:

- An outer housing wall appears in section as upper and lower hatched bands at the top and bottom of the view. Inside it the sleeve wall appears as upper and lower hatched bands spaced inward from them, beginning a short way in at the left; the space between them is the bore.
- The clear gap between the sleeve bands and the outer bands, above and below, is one annular rinse channel, open at the left to the housing interior and closed at its right-hand end where the sleeve wall meets the housing wall.
- Left of that meeting, a passage leads from the bore up through the upper sleeve band and turns right, through the meeting into the housing interior beyond, which leads to the outlet: the flush bypass, with a conical seat at the turn.
- A conical head stands clear to the left of that seat, a visible gap between them, with a plain stem extending from the head leftward along the gap above the sleeve toward the piston. Head and stem are shown schematically and are the flush poppet.
- In the bore, in the left half, the piston is drawn as two hatched enlarged portions joined by a narrower middle portion. A plain shaft extends leftward on the axis past the sleeve's left end, and a short pin projects upward from it and bears on the stem of the flush poppet, holding the head clear of its seat.
- At the left edge of the left portion a thin flared projection extends up and left to the upper bore wall and a matching one down and left to the lower: the flexible lip.
- An opening through the upper sleeve band, covered by the left portion, is the concentrate port; a tube rises from it, crossing the gap and the upper outer band.
- Two openings through the lower sleeve band connect the rinse channel to the bore; they are the radial rinse openings. The left one lies beneath the concentrate port, aimed at it; the right one is aimed at a ball on a conical seat, shown schematically in a passage rising through the upper sleeve band.
- A further opening passes through the lower sleeve band at the right enlarged portion of the piston, covered by it; shown unnumbered in this view.

Numerals on this sheet: 22, 26, 28, 44, 56, 58, 60, 62.

Targets:

- 22: interior of the upper opening at the left.
- 26: interior of the flush bypass beyond the seat.
- 28: hatching of the right portion.
- 44: the short pin above the shaft.
- 56: the flared projection at the upper bore wall.
- 58: the conical head clear of its seat in the flush bypass.
- 60: the clear gap between the lower bands, left of the rinse openings.
- 62: the left lower opening.

input.summary: Fixed every finding. The description no longer locates the measured volume in the waist annulus: the dose is formed in the dose chamber and its extent is fixed by the travel then permitted to the piston, which agrees with the stop faces of claim 7. The FIG. 3 brief no longer contains an invented actuating train: the transverse boss, the opening through it and the depending flange are gone, the annular rinse channel closes where the sleeve wall meets the housing wall, and the poppet is a conical head with a plain stem on which the follower pin bears. FIG. 1 now shows the inlet and the outlet as axial stubs at opposite ends of the housing, represents the cartridge without an added flange, and keeps the piston rod inside the housing interior short of the end cap. The summary now says the element that opens the rinse is carried by the piston rod. FIGS. 2 and 3 now show the same sleeve, each adding the other view's openings unnumbered. All four briefs remain at or below 2800 characters, and the numeral lists on every sheet are unchanged and still match the drawing descriptions and the FIG. sentences in the detailed description.
reasoning: The dose locus was a drafting inference, not disclosure, and it fought the claimed stop faces. Removing it also meant removing the supporting clause earlier in the description that the waist forms an annular space travelling with the piston, so no sentence anywhere now implies a fixed dose volume set by piston geometry. The description now ties dose size to permitted travel in the same terms as claim 7 and the operation paragraph.

For FIG. 3 the poppet had to keep doing what the claims recite, gating the flush bypass and being opened by the follower pin, while shedding the invented mechanism. The head and a plain stem are all that remain, described as shown schematically, and the pin bears directly on that stem. The rinse channel now closes where the sleeve wall meets the housing wall rather than at an added boss, and the flush bypass passes through that meeting into the housing interior beyond, so the rinse still reaches the outlet without a stem penetrating a sealing member.

The FIG. 1 ports moved to the axial ends because claim 12, the description and the disclosure all recite an inlet at one axial end and an outlet at the opposite end. The claim was not touched to match the drawing; the drawing was corrected to match the claim, with the inlet stub kept below the axis and clear of the end cap so removing the cap still withdraws the cartridge without disturbing either connection.

The cartridge is now shown as the sleeve, the body in its bore and the parts they carry drawn as one removable unit standing against the inner face of the end cap, with numeral 64 targeting the broad hatched left end portion of the sleeve. That keeps a visible target for the numeral while dropping the flange and the face-to-face retention interface the source never described.

The piston rod now ends within the housing interior short of the end cap. Where the rod leaves the housing is not disclosed, and having it pass through the removable cap implied a withdrawal topology the inventor never described, so the brief simply stops short of asserting anything about it.

The summary sentence was inverted relative to the mechanism. It now matches the description: the follower pin that opens the flush poppet is carried by the piston rod, which is why the rinse happens once per cycle and cannot be deferred.

FIGS. 2 and 3 are two states of one section, so each now shows the full set of openings in that sleeve. FIG. 2 gains the two lower-band rinse openings, placed beneath the concentrate port and beneath the outlet-valve passage, and the further upper-band passage to the right of the outlet-valve passage; FIG. 3 gains the admission-port opening at the right enlarged portion of the piston. I placed the rinse openings by reference to the ports they serve rather than as a block to the right of the admission port, so the two sheets agree with each other and with the described rinse targets.

Adding those openings pushed FIG. 2 over the character limit, so I compressed wording only: no body, contact, opening or path was dropped, and the target lines still point at broad interior regions of the intended parts.

figures/fig-01.md: inlet and outlet redrawn as axial stubs, the inlet projecting leftward from the left end below the axis clear of the end cap and shaft, the outlet projecting rightward from the end wall; the cartridge bullet now describes the sleeve, the body in its bore and the parts they carry as one removable unit standing against the inner face of the end cap; the plain shaft ends within the housing interior short of the end cap; targets for 14, 16 and 64 updated.

figures/fig-02.md: added the two unnumbered lower-band openings beneath the concentrate port and beneath the outlet-valve passage and the unnumbered further upper-band passage right of the outlet-valve passage; wording compressed to stay within the character limit.

figures/fig-03.md: transverse boss, opening through it and depending flange removed; the annular rinse channel closes where the sleeve wall meets the housing wall; the flush bypass passes through that meeting into the housing interior beyond; the flush poppet is a conical head with a plain stem extending toward the piston; the follower pin bears on that stem, holding the head clear of its seat; added the unnumbered lower-band opening at the right enlarged portion of the piston; target for 26 now names the flush bypass beyond the seat.
input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md still lists no references, so the Background carries no citations and none was added. No claim was amended in this revision: every fix was to the description, the summary or a figure brief, and each moved the text or the sheet toward the claims rather than the reverse. Claim 1 continues to rest on the ordered port and land geometry that isolates the concentrate from the carrier liquid by geometry rather than by command sequence, together with the flush poppet on the flush bypass that the follower pin opens during the return stroke and that closes before the waist reconnects the concentrate port. Correcting the dose locus strengthens the internal consistency of claim 7 and its method counterpart, since dose volume is now described only as a function of permitted piston travel. Because no search was run, the claim scope should still be revisited once art is available.
input.answer:
All seven findings are resolved.

Text: the fill paragraph now says the concentrate forms a measured volume in the dose chamber whose extent is fixed by the travel then permitted to the piston, and the earlier clause about an annular space at the waist is gone, so nothing in the application locates the dose in a fixed annulus or contradicts the three stop faces. The summary now states that the element which opens the rinse is carried by the piston rod itself.

Drawings: FIG. 3 no longer specifies a transverse boss, an opening through it, or a depending flange. The annular rinse channel closes where the sleeve wall meets the housing wall, the flush bypass passes through that meeting into the housing interior leading to the outlet, and the flush poppet is a conical head with a plain stem that the follower pin bears on to hold the head clear of its seat. FIG. 1 places the inlet and outlet as axial stubs at opposite ends of the housing, represents the cartridge as the sleeve and the parts it carries standing against the inner face of the end cap with numeral 64 on the sleeve's left end portion, and stops the piston rod inside the housing short of the end cap. FIGS. 2 and 3 now depict the same sleeve: FIG. 2 adds the two rinse openings and the further upper-band passage unnumbered, and FIG. 3 adds the admission-port opening unnumbered.

Synchronization holds: the numeral table is unchanged, each sheet still carries the same eight numerals its "FIG. n shows" sentence names, the drawing descriptions match the briefs in view type and state, and every brief is at or below 2800 characters.

23	The three axial stop faces 46 are carried by the index collar 40 at different axial positions. The stop face presented by the current increment of rotation limits the travel of the piston 28 and thereby sets the dose volume, so that the three axial stop faces 46 correspond to three dose volumes. The spring-biased detent 48 engages one of the three detent recesses 50 to retain the selected setting, so that the index collar 40 is held against vibration and against the forces transmitted through the follower pin 44 until it is next indexed.
24	
25	The transparent window 52 in the housing 12 shows one of the three dose setting numerals 54 carried by the index collar 40. The dose setting numeral presented at the transparent window 52 is the one associated with the axial stop face then limiting the travel of the piston 28, so that the dose setting is mechanically visible without electronics, without power at the valve and without a controller. What is seen at the transparent window 52 is the position of the mechanism itself rather than a stored value, so the displayed setting cannot disagree with the volume that the valve will deliver.
26	
27	FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, the follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62 of which one is directed across the concentrate port 22, and a flush bypass 26.

In the following description, the terms upstream and downstream refer to the direction of travel of the carrier liquid from the inlet toward the outlet, and the terms axial and radial refer to the axis along which the piston slides.

FIG. 1 shows an inline liquid metering valve 10 having a cylindrical housing 12 with an inlet 14 at one axial end and an outlet 16 at the opposite axial end, a metering sleeve 18 fixed within the housing 12, a cartridge 64 retained in the housing 12 by a threaded end cap 66, and a transparent window 52 in the housing 12.

The inline liquid metering valve 10 is connected in a line that already carries a flowing carrier liquid. Carrier liquid enters at the inlet 14, passes along the housing 12, and leaves at the outlet 16. That flow is the main flow into which each dose of concentrate is delivered, and it is also the only liquid used to rinse the valve. The metering sleeve 18 is spaced radially inward from the inner surface of the housing 12 over part of its length.

FIG. 2 shows the metering sleeve 18 defining a dose chamber 20, a concentrate port 22 opening into the dose chamber 20 and a carrier-liquid admission port 24 opening into the dose chamber 20. FIG. 2 further shows an upstream sealing land 30 and a downstream sealing land 32 joined by a reduced-diameter waist 34 in the fill position, and a one-way outlet valve 38.

The dose chamber 20 is cylindrical. The concentrate port 22 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and is connected in use to a concentrate source. The carrier-liquid admission port 24 passes through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 at an axial position downstream of the concentrate port 22, and admits carrier liquid to the dose chamber 20. The metering sleeve 18 further defines a flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20.

A piston 28 is axially slidable in the dose chamber 20 between a fill position and a discharge position. The upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 are axially spaced from one another on the piston 28 and are joined by the reduced-diameter waist 34. Each sealing land bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20, while the waist 34 stands clear of that wall. A piston rod 36 extends from the piston 28 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 and is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke. The one-way outlet valve 38 is arranged to pass liquid from the dose chamber 20 toward the outlet 16 and to prevent flow in the opposite direction.

In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume of concentrate, the extent of which is fixed by the travel then permitted to the piston 28. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 while the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.

Movement of the piston 28 toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port 22 before the downstream sealing land 32 uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port 24. The upstream sealing land 30 arrives at the concentrate port 22 and shuts it while the downstream sealing land 32 is still overlying the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Only after that has happened does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.

The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every position of the piston 28 at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18. It does not depend on the order in which external commands are given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of a separately actuated shut-off element. A slow stroke, an interrupted stroke, or a stroke reversed part way through cannot open both ports at once, because the port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens.

FIG. 4 shows an index collar 40 having a helical cam groove 42 engaged by a follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36, three selectable axial stop faces 46, a spring-biased detent 48 engaging one of three detent recesses 50, and three dose setting numerals 54.

The index collar 40 surrounds the metering sleeve 18. Each full stroke of the piston 28 draws the follower pin 44 along the helical cam groove 42 and turns the index collar 40 by one increment, so that the index collar 40 advances by itself as the valve is used and needs no separate indexing drive.

The three axial stop faces 46 are carried by the index collar 40 at different axial positions. The stop face presented by the current increment of rotation limits the travel of the piston 28 and thereby sets the dose volume, so that the three axial stop faces 46 correspond to three dose volumes. The spring-biased detent 48 engages one of the three detent recesses 50 to retain the selected setting, so that the index collar 40 is held against vibration and against the forces transmitted through the follower pin 44 until it is next indexed.

The transparent window 52 in the housing 12 shows one of the three dose setting numerals 54 carried by the index collar 40. The dose setting numeral presented at the transparent window 52 is the one associated with the axial stop face then limiting the travel of the piston 28, so that the dose setting is mechanically visible without electronics, without power at the valve and without a controller. What is seen at the transparent window 52 is the position of the mechanism itself rather than a stored value, so the displayed setting cannot disagree with the volume that the valve will deliver.

FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, the follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62 of which one is directed across the concentrate port 22, and a flush bypass 26.

The flexible lip 56 is carried on the upstream sealing land 30 and bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20. As the return stroke begins, the flexible lip 56 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20 and carries the film of concentrate remaining on that wall ahead of it, so that the rinse which follows is presented with a wetted surface rather than with standing liquid.

The annular rinse channel 60 lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve 18 and an inner surface of the housing 12, and is supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet 14. The two radial rinse openings 62 pass through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and connect the annular rinse channel 60 to the dose chamber 20. One of the two radial rinse openings 62 is directed across the concentrate port 22 and the other is directed across the one-way outlet valve 38. Those are the two surfaces on which concentrate is otherwise retained after a dose, the first because concentrate stands in the mouth of the port and the second because concentrate is the last liquid to pass the seat.

The flush poppet 58 is normally closed and is connected to the flush bypass 26. Near the end of the return stroke, the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows from the inlet 14 through the annular rinse channel 60, through the two radial rinse openings 62 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 to the outlet 16. The rinse liquid therefore leaves by the same route as the dose and is carried away in the main flow.

The flush poppet 58 closes before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. The concentrate port 22 is closed throughout the interval in which the annular rinse channel 60 communicates with the flush bypass 26, so that carrier liquid at the pressure of the main line is never presented to an open concentrate port 22 and cannot be driven back toward the concentrate source. Only when the flush poppet 58 has closed does the continuing return of the piston 28 bring the waist 34 back into register with the concentrate port 22, at which point the dose chamber 20 is charged again for the next dose.

Because the follower pin 44 that opens the flush poppet 58 is carried by the piston rod 36, the rinse occurs once for every dose and at the same point in every cycle. It is not a separate operation, it needs no command, and it cannot be omitted while the valve continues to be used. The rinse also occurs while the concentrate port 22 is shut and after the wall of the dose chamber 20 has been wiped, so that it removes a film with clean carrier liquid instead of diluting a standing charge of concentrate.

The cartridge 64 contains the piston 28, the metering sleeve 18, the one-way outlet valve 38 and the flush poppet 58, and is removable from the housing 12 as a unit. Removing the threaded end cap 66 withdraws the cartridge 64 from the housing 12 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 without disturbing the connections at the inlet 14 and the outlet 16, so that the cartridge 64 is replaced as a unit while the housing 12 remains in the line. The parts that contact the concentrate are the parts that are exchanged, so a change of concentrate or a worn sealing land is dealt with by fitting a further cartridge rather than by dismantling the installation.

In use, carrier liquid flows through the housing 12 from the inlet 14 to the outlet 16. With the piston 28 in the fill position, concentrate is admitted through the concentrate port 22 and past the waist 34 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume, the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolating the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. The piston 28 is then advanced toward the discharge position so as to close the concentrate port 22 and thereafter to uncover the carrier-liquid admission port 24 with the downstream sealing land 32. Carrier liquid is admitted through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16. The travel of the piston 28 on this stroke is limited by the selected one of the three axial stop faces 46, which sets the measured volume.

The piston 28 is then returned toward the fill position. During the return, the flexible lip 56 on the upstream sealing land 30 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20, and the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36 opens the normally closed flush poppet 58. Carrier liquid flows through the annular rinse channel 60 between the metering sleeve 18 and the housing 12, through the two radial rinse openings 62 in the metering sleeve 18 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20 to the outlet 16. The flush poppet 58 is closed before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. Over the same full stroke, the follower pin 44 travelling in the helical cam groove 42 turns the index collar 40 by one increment, the spring-biased detent 48 enters the next of the three detent recesses 50, and the dose setting numeral then presented at the transparent window 52 shows the setting that will govern the next dose. The valve is thereby left charged, rinsed and set, ready for the following cycle.

The foregoing description sets out embodiments of the invention. A skilled reader may make changes of detail to the described embodiments without departing from the scope of the claims that follow.

An inline liquid metering valve delivers a repeatable measured volume of concentrate into a flowing carrier liquid and rinses the surfaces that contacted the concentrate after each dose, without electrical power and without any command additional to the stroke that delivers the dose.

The valve has a housing with an inlet and an outlet and a metering sleeve fixed within the housing. The metering sleeve defines a dose chamber, a concentrate port opening into the dose chamber, a carrier-liquid admission port opening into the dose chamber, and a flush bypass that opens downstream of the dose chamber. A piston slides axially in the dose chamber between a fill position and a discharge position. The piston has an upstream sealing land and a downstream sealing land axially spaced from one another and joined by a reduced-diameter waist.

Separation of the two liquids is enforced by the axial order of the land faces and the port edges rather than by the sequence in which any external command arrives. In the fill position, the waist connects the concentrate port to the dose chamber while the upstream and downstream sealing lands isolate the carrier-liquid admission port from the concentrate port. Movement of the piston toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port before the downstream sealing land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port. Carrier liquid then enters behind the measured volume of concentrate and expels that volume through a one-way outlet valve toward the outlet. Because one land face has passed the concentrate port before the other land face releases the carrier-liquid admission port, no position of the piston places the concentrate source in communication with the carrier-liquid path.

The rinse is carried out by the return of the same piston. An annular rinse channel lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve and an inner surface of the housing, and at least one rinse opening leads from that channel through the metering sleeve into the dose chamber. A follower pin carried by the piston rod opens a normally closed flush poppet connected to the flush bypass during the return stroke, so that carrier liquid sweeps the annular rinse channel, issues from the rinse opening across the surfaces wetted by the concentrate, and leaves through the flush bypass to the outlet. The flush poppet closes before the waist reconnects the concentrate port to the dose chamber, so the rinse is complete, and the rinse liquid is on its way to the outlet, before any further concentrate can enter. The rinse cannot be omitted, mistimed or deferred, because the element that opens it is carried by the piston rod itself.

In described embodiments, a flexible lip on the upstream sealing land wipes the wall of the dose chamber before the flush poppet opens, so that the flushing stream is presented with a film rather than with standing liquid. Two radial rinse openings are directed across the concentrate port and across the one-way outlet valve, which are the two surfaces on which residue is otherwise retained.

Dose selection is mechanical and self-indexing. An index collar surrounds the metering sleeve and has a helical cam groove engaged by the follower pin, so that each full stroke of the piston turns the index collar by one increment. Three selectable axial stop faces on the index collar limit the travel of the piston and thereby set three dose volumes, a spring-biased detent engaging one of three recesses retains the selected setting, and a transparent window in the housing shows one of three dose setting numerals carried by the index collar, so that the setting is visible without electronics.

A replaceable cartridge contains the piston, the metering sleeve, the one-way outlet valve and the flush poppet, and is retained by a threaded end cap. Removing the threaded end cap withdraws the cartridge without disturbing the connections at the inlet and the outlet.

A corresponding method admits concentrate to the dose chamber, closes the concentrate port before uncovering the carrier-liquid admission port, expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve, and then opens the flush poppet with the follower pin during the return of the piston and closes it again before the concentrate port is reconnected.

# FIG. 3

View: enlarged longitudinal section of the metering portion of FIG. 1 during the return stroke, axis horizontal, with the flush poppet held open. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the sheet edges.

Geometry:

- An outer housing wall appears in section as upper and lower hatched bands at the top and bottom of the view. Inside it the sleeve wall appears as upper and lower hatched bands spaced inward, beginning a short way in at the left; the space between them is the bore.
- The clear gap between the sleeve and outer bands, above and below, is one annular rinse channel, open at the left to the housing interior and closed at its right-hand end where the sleeve wall meets the housing wall.
- Left of that meeting a passage leads from the bore up through the upper sleeve band and turns right, through the meeting into the housing interior beyond, which leads to the outlet: the flush bypass, with a conical seat at the turn. A conical head stands clear to the left of that seat, a visible gap between them, with a plain stem extending leftward from the head along the gap above the sleeve toward the piston; head and stem are shown schematically and are the flush poppet.
- In the bore, in the left half, the piston is drawn as two hatched enlarged portions joined by a narrower middle portion. A plain shaft extends leftward on the axis past the sleeve's left end, and a short pin projects upward from it, bearing on the stem of the flush poppet and holding the head clear of its seat.
- At the left edge of the left portion a thin flared projection extends up and left to the upper bore wall and a matching one down and left to the lower: the flexible lip.
- An opening through the upper sleeve band, covered by the left portion, is the concentrate port; a tube rises from it across the gap and the upper outer band.
- Two openings through the lower sleeve band connect the rinse channel to the bore; they are the radial rinse openings. The left lies beneath the concentrate port, aimed at it; the right is aimed at a ball on a conical seat, shown schematically in a passage rising through the upper band.
- A further opening passes through the lower sleeve band at the right portion of the piston, covered by it; shown unnumbered in this view.

Numerals on this sheet: 22, 26, 28, 44, 56, 58, 60, 62.

Targets:

- 22: interior of the upper opening at the left.
- 26: interior of the flush bypass beyond the seat.
- 28: the piston as a whole; leader ends just outside the outline of the two-land body, clear of all hatching, with an arrowhead directed at it.
- 44: the short pin above the shaft.
- 56: the flared projection at the upper bore wall.
- 58: the conical head clear of its seat in the flush bypass.
- 60: the clear gap between the lower bands.
- 62: the left lower opening.

content.content: 41	In use, carrier liquid flows through the housing 12 from the inlet 14 to the outlet 16. With the piston 28 in the fill position, concentrate is admitted through the concentrate port 22 and past the waist 34 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume, the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolating the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. The piston 28 is then advanced toward the discharge position so as to close the concentrate port 22 and thereafter to uncover the carrier-liquid admission port 24 with the downstream sealing land 32. Carrier liquid is admitted through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16. The extent of the travel available to the piston 28, and therefore the measured volume, is fixed by the selected one of the three axial stop faces 46.

input.summary: Fixed every finding. The description now attributes the measured volume to the travel available to the piston as fixed by the selected stop face, without naming a stroke, so the fill paragraph and the operation paragraph agree. The detent sentence now says only that the setting is retained until the collar is next indexed; the summary no longer claims operation without electrical power, and the display paragraph says only "without electronics"; the reference to a seat of the one-way outlet valve now names the one-way outlet valve 38; and the FIG. 3 view sentence recites the flush bypass 26 with the definite article. On the sheets, FIG. 1 now shows the sleeve and housing gap over part of the sleeve's length with the sleeve wall meeting the housing wall at the right-hand end of that gap, matching FIG. 3 and the description; the piston rod ends within the sleeve bore short of the end cap; numeral 64 now leads to the removable unit from outside all hatching; numeral 28 in FIG. 3 does the same for the piston; and the FIG. 4 detent spring is shown broken off at its upper end instead of carried by a bracket. All four briefs remain at or below 2800 characters, and the numeral lists, the drawing descriptions and the FIG. sentences in the detailed description are unchanged and still match.
reasoning: The dose-volume conflict was resolved by making both passages speak of travel available to the piston rather than travel on a named stroke, which is as far as the disclosure goes. The fill paragraph already said the extent is fixed by the travel then permitted, so only the operation paragraph needed changing, and claim 7 and its method counterpart continue to read on both without either passage choosing a stroke the inventor never chose.

The detent claim of function shrank to what the inventor wrote. Retention until the next indexing is the disclosed effect; holding against vibration and against the pin forces was drafting embellishment and it also fought the preceding paragraph, where the pin force is exactly what indexes the collar.

The electrical statements now track the source exactly. The inventor tied the absence of electronics to the visibility of the dose setting, so that is the only place the application says it. Nothing now asserts anything about how the piston is driven, which the disclosure never characterises.

The seat reference was replaced with the one-way outlet valve 38 itself. The application text stays shape-neutral about that valve, and the ball-and-seat depiction remains confined to the figure briefs where it is marked shown schematically.

FIG. 1 and FIG. 3 now describe one topology for one annular space. FIG. 3 needs the channel closed at its right-hand end so the flush bypass is the exit for the rinse flow, and the description says the sleeve is spaced from the housing over part of its length, so FIG. 1 was corrected to that same closure rather than the claims or description being adjusted to the earlier drawing.

Numerals 64 and 28 designate assemblies, so they now use the convention FIG. 1 already used for numeral 10: the leader ends outside all hatching with an arrowhead directed at the unit. That keeps 18 the sleeve and 64 the cartridge distinguishable on one sheet, and keeps 28 the whole piston distinct from the land numerals on FIG. 2.

The FIG. 4 bracket was an added support member, not a depiction convention, so it is gone and the coil spring is simply shown broken off at its upper end, which anchors the drawing visually without asserting a part the inventor never described.

FIG. 1 no longer places the shaft's left end in a region the same brief fills with the end cap standing against the sleeve; the shaft now ends within the sleeve bore short of the cap, and the brief says nothing about whether or where the rod leaves the housing.

Both edited briefs needed compression to stay within the character limit after the longer assembly-numeral targets were added. I cut wording only: every body, opening, contact and path in those sheets is still specified, and the remaining targets sit on broad interior regions of their parts.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md still lists no references, so the Background carries no citations and none was added. No claim was amended in this revision: every fix was to the description, the summary or a figure brief. Claim 1 continues to rest on the ordered port and land geometry that isolates the concentrate from the carrier liquid by geometry rather than by command sequence, together with the flush poppet on the flush bypass that the follower pin opens during the return stroke and that closes before the waist reconnects the concentrate port. Removing the unsupported detent effects and the electrical-power assertion narrows only advocacy language, not scope, and naming the one-way outlet valve instead of its seat keeps the description shape-neutral where the claims are shape-neutral. Because no search was run, the claim scope should still be revisited once art is available.

The summary no longer says the cycle runs without electrical power, and the display paragraph says only that the setting is mechanically visible without electronics. The rinse paragraph names the one-way outlet valve 38 rather than a seat with no antecedent, and the FIG. 3 view sentence now recites the flush bypass 26.

Drawings: FIG. 1 shows the clear gap over part of the sleeve's length with the sleeve wall meeting the housing wall at the right-hand end of that gap, which is the same topology FIG. 3 and the description recite, so the rinse flow has no path to the outlet except the flush bypass. The plain shaft ends within the sleeve bore short of the end cap. Numeral 64 now leads to the removable unit from outside all hatching with an arrowhead, and numeral 28 does the same for the piston in FIG. 3, so 18, 64, 28 and 32 each designate one thing. The FIG. 4 detent is a ball and a coil spring shown broken off at its upper end, with no bracket.

Synchronization holds: the numeral table is unchanged, each sheet carries the same eight numerals its "FIG. n shows" sentence names, the drawing descriptions match the briefs in view type and state, and every brief is at or below 2800 characters.

In the following description, the terms upstream and downstream refer to the direction of travel of the carrier liquid from the inlet toward the outlet, and the terms axial and radial refer to the axis along which the piston slides.

FIG. 1 shows an inline liquid metering valve 10 having a cylindrical housing 12 with an inlet 14 at one axial end and an outlet 16 at the opposite axial end, a metering sleeve 18 fixed within the housing 12, a cartridge 64 retained in the housing 12 by a threaded end cap 66, and a transparent window 52 in the housing 12.

The inline liquid metering valve 10 is connected in a line that already carries a flowing carrier liquid. Carrier liquid enters at the inlet 14, passes along the housing 12, and leaves at the outlet 16. That flow is the main flow into which each dose of concentrate is delivered, and it is also the only liquid used to rinse the valve. The metering sleeve 18 is spaced radially inward from the inner surface of the housing 12 over part of its length.

FIG. 2 shows the metering sleeve 18 defining a dose chamber 20, a concentrate port 22 opening into the dose chamber 20 and a carrier-liquid admission port 24 opening into the dose chamber 20. FIG. 2 further shows an upstream sealing land 30 and a downstream sealing land 32 joined by a reduced-diameter waist 34 in the fill position, and a one-way outlet valve 38.

The dose chamber 20 is cylindrical. The concentrate port 22 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and is connected in use to a concentrate source. The carrier-liquid admission port 24 passes through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 at an axial position downstream of the concentrate port 22, and admits carrier liquid to the dose chamber 20. The metering sleeve 18 further defines a flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20.

A piston 28 is axially slidable in the dose chamber 20 between a fill position and a discharge position. The upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 are axially spaced from one another on the piston 28 and are joined by the reduced-diameter waist 34. Each sealing land bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20, while the waist 34 stands clear of that wall. A piston rod 36 extends from the piston 28 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 and is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke. The one-way outlet valve 38 is arranged to pass liquid from the dose chamber 20 toward the outlet 16 and to prevent flow in the opposite direction.

In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume of concentrate, the extent of which is fixed by the travel then permitted to the piston 28. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 while the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.

Movement of the piston 28 toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port 22 before the downstream sealing land 32 uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port 24. The upstream sealing land 30 arrives at the concentrate port 22 and shuts it while the downstream sealing land 32 is still overlying the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Only after that has happened does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.

The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every position of the piston 28 at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18. It does not depend on the order in which external commands are given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of a separately actuated shut-off element. A slow stroke, an interrupted stroke, or a stroke reversed part way through cannot open both ports at once, because the port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens.

FIG. 4 shows an index collar 40 having a helical cam groove 42 engaged by a follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36, three selectable axial stop faces 46, a spring-biased detent 48 engaging one of three detent recesses 50, and three dose setting numerals 54.

The index collar 40 surrounds the metering sleeve 18. Each full stroke of the piston 28 draws the follower pin 44 along the helical cam groove 42 and turns the index collar 40 by one increment, so that the index collar 40 advances by itself as the valve is used and needs no separate indexing drive.

The three axial stop faces 46 are carried by the index collar 40 at different axial positions. The stop face presented by the current increment of rotation limits the travel of the piston 28 and thereby sets the dose volume, so that the three axial stop faces 46 correspond to three dose volumes. The spring-biased detent 48 engages one of the three detent recesses 50 to retain the selected setting until the index collar 40 is next indexed.

The transparent window 52 in the housing 12 shows one of the three dose setting numerals 54 carried by the index collar 40. The dose setting numeral presented at the transparent window 52 is the one associated with the axial stop face then limiting the travel of the piston 28, so that the dose setting is mechanically visible without electronics. What is seen at the transparent window 52 is the position of the mechanism itself rather than a stored value, so the displayed setting cannot disagree with the volume that the valve will deliver.

FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, the follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62 of which one is directed across the concentrate port 22, and the flush bypass 26.

The flexible lip 56 is carried on the upstream sealing land 30 and bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20. As the return stroke begins, the flexible lip 56 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20 and carries the film of concentrate remaining on that wall ahead of it, so that the rinse which follows is presented with a wetted surface rather than with standing liquid.

The annular rinse channel 60 lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve 18 and an inner surface of the housing 12, and is supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet 14. The two radial rinse openings 62 pass through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and connect the annular rinse channel 60 to the dose chamber 20. One of the two radial rinse openings 62 is directed across the concentrate port 22 and the other is directed across the one-way outlet valve 38. Those are the two surfaces on which concentrate is otherwise retained after a dose, the first because concentrate stands in the mouth of the port and the second because concentrate is the last liquid to pass the one-way outlet valve 38.

The flush poppet 58 is normally closed and is connected to the flush bypass 26. Near the end of the return stroke, the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows from the inlet 14 through the annular rinse channel 60, through the two radial rinse openings 62 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 to the outlet 16. The rinse liquid therefore leaves by the same route as the dose and is carried away in the main flow.

The flush poppet 58 closes before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. The concentrate port 22 is closed throughout the interval in which the annular rinse channel 60 communicates with the flush bypass 26, so that carrier liquid at the pressure of the main line is never presented to an open concentrate port 22 and cannot be driven back toward the concentrate source. Only when the flush poppet 58 has closed does the continuing return of the piston 28 bring the waist 34 back into register with the concentrate port 22, at which point the dose chamber 20 is charged again for the next dose.

Because the follower pin 44 that opens the flush poppet 58 is carried by the piston rod 36, the rinse occurs once for every dose and at the same point in every cycle. It is not a separate operation, it needs no command, and it cannot be omitted while the valve continues to be used. The rinse also occurs while the concentrate port 22 is shut and after the wall of the dose chamber 20 has been wiped, so that it removes a film with clean carrier liquid instead of diluting a standing charge of concentrate.

The cartridge 64 contains the piston 28, the metering sleeve 18, the one-way outlet valve 38 and the flush poppet 58, and is removable from the housing 12 as a unit. Removing the threaded end cap 66 withdraws the cartridge 64 from the housing 12 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 without disturbing the connections at the inlet 14 and the outlet 16, so that the cartridge 64 is replaced as a unit while the housing 12 remains in the line. The parts that contact the concentrate are the parts that are exchanged, so a change of concentrate or a worn sealing land is dealt with by fitting a further cartridge rather than by dismantling the installation.

In use, carrier liquid flows through the housing 12 from the inlet 14 to the outlet 16. With the piston 28 in the fill position, concentrate is admitted through the concentrate port 22 and past the waist 34 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume, the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolating the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. The piston 28 is then advanced toward the discharge position so as to close the concentrate port 22 and thereafter to uncover the carrier-liquid admission port 24 with the downstream sealing land 32. Carrier liquid is admitted through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16. The extent of the travel available to the piston 28, and therefore the measured volume, is fixed by the selected one of the three axial stop faces 46.

The piston 28 is then returned toward the fill position. During the return, the flexible lip 56 on the upstream sealing land 30 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20, and the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36 opens the normally closed flush poppet 58. Carrier liquid flows through the annular rinse channel 60 between the metering sleeve 18 and the housing 12, through the two radial rinse openings 62 in the metering sleeve 18 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20 to the outlet 16. The flush poppet 58 is closed before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. Over the same full stroke, the follower pin 44 travelling in the helical cam groove 42 turns the index collar 40 by one increment, the spring-biased detent 48 enters the next of the three detent recesses 50, and the dose setting numeral then presented at the transparent window 52 shows the setting that will govern the next dose. The valve is thereby left charged, rinsed and set, ready for the following cycle.

The foregoing description sets out embodiments of the invention. A skilled reader may make changes of detail to the described embodiments without departing from the scope of the claims that follow.

# FIG. 1

View: longitudinal sectional view of the inline liquid metering valve, axis horizontal. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the sheet edges.

Geometry:

- The housing is an elongate cylinder cut lengthwise on its axis, appearing as upper and lower hatched wall bands that run across most of the view and are joined at the right by a hatched end wall. The interior between them is open.
- The left end of the housing is closed by a threaded end cap, drawn as a short hatched ring seated in the left mouth, its outer surface meeting the housing bore along a shallow saw-tooth interface indicating a thread. A plain shaft on the axis extends leftward within the sleeve bore and ends short of the end cap.
- A short tubular stub projects axially leftward from the left end of the housing below the axis, clear of the end cap and the shaft, and opens into the interior; it is the inlet, shown schematically. A second such stub projects axially rightward from the end wall at the right and opens into the interior; it is the outlet, shown schematically. Both stubs end clear of the drawing area.
- The metering sleeve lies inside the housing on the same axis, drawn as an upper hatched band and a lower hatched band spaced inward from the housing wall bands, so that a clear gap is visible above and below it over part of its length, from a position right of the end cap to a position short of the end wall, the sleeve wall meeting the housing wall at the right-hand end of that gap.
- The sleeve, the body in its bore and the parts they carry are drawn as one removable unit, the left end of the sleeve standing against the inner face of the end cap; this unit is the cartridge.
- Within the sleeve bore, in the left half, is a body shown schematically as two hatched enlarged portions joined by a narrower middle portion, the plain shaft running leftward from the left portion.
- A rectangular unhatched panel is set into the upper housing wall band about midway along it, the hatching stopping at its outline; it is the transparent window. Beneath it, on an unnumbered ring surrounding the sleeve in the gap, a small plain patch is visible.

Numerals on this sheet: 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 52, 64, 66.

Targets:

- 10: the complete assembly; leader ends just outside the upper housing outline.
- 12: the hatched lower housing wall band.
- 14: the wall of the left axial stub.
- 16: the wall of the right axial stub.
- 18: the hatched upper band of the sleeve, toward its right.
- 52: the interior of the unhatched rectangular panel.
- 64: the removable unit as a whole; leader ends just outside the left end of the sleeve, clear of all hatching, with an arrowhead directed at the unit.
- 66: the hatched ring in the left mouth of the housing, above the axis.
