In the following description, the terms upstream and downstream refer to the direction of travel of the carrier liquid from the inlet toward the outlet, and the terms axial and radial refer to the axis along which the piston slides.

FIG. 1 shows an inline liquid metering valve 10 having a cylindrical housing 12 with an inlet 14 at one axial end and an outlet 16 at the opposite axial end, a metering sleeve 18 fixed within the housing 12, a cartridge 64 retained in the housing 12 by a threaded end cap 66, and a transparent window 52 in the housing 12.

The inline liquid metering valve 10 is connected in a line that already carries a flowing carrier liquid. Carrier liquid enters at the inlet 14, passes along the housing 12, and leaves at the outlet 16. That flow is the main flow into which each dose of concentrate is delivered, and it is also the only liquid used to rinse the valve. The metering sleeve 18 is spaced radially inward from the inner surface of the housing 12 over part of its length.

FIG. 2 shows the metering sleeve 18 defining a dose chamber 20, a concentrate port 22 opening into the dose chamber 20 and a carrier-liquid admission port 24 opening into the dose chamber 20. FIG. 2 further shows an upstream sealing land 30 and a downstream sealing land 32 joined by a reduced-diameter waist 34 in the fill position, and a one-way outlet valve 38.

The dose chamber 20 is cylindrical. The concentrate port 22 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and is connected in use to a concentrate source. The carrier-liquid admission port 24 passes through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 at an axial position downstream of the concentrate port 22, and admits carrier liquid to the dose chamber 20. The metering sleeve 18 further defines a flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20.

A piston 28 is axially slidable in the dose chamber 20 between a fill position and a discharge position. The upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 are axially spaced from one another on the piston 28 and are joined by the reduced-diameter waist 34. Each sealing land bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20, while the waist 34 stands clear of that wall. A piston rod 36 extends from the piston 28 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 and is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke. The one-way outlet valve 38 is arranged to pass liquid from the dose chamber 20 toward the outlet 16 and to prevent flow in the opposite direction.

In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume of concentrate, the extent of which is fixed by the travel then permitted to the piston 28. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 while the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.

Movement of the piston 28 toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port 22 before the downstream sealing land 32 uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port 24. The upstream sealing land 30 arrives at the concentrate port 22 and shuts it while the downstream sealing land 32 is still overlying the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Only after that has happened does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.

The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every position of the piston 28 at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18. It does not depend on the order in which external commands are given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of a separately actuated shut-off element. A slow stroke, an interrupted stroke, or a stroke reversed part way through cannot open both ports at once, because the port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens.

FIG. 4 shows an index collar 40 having a helical cam groove 42 engaged by a follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36, three selectable axial stop faces 46, a spring-biased detent 48 engaging one of three detent recesses 50, and three dose setting numerals 54.

The index collar 40 surrounds the metering sleeve 18. Each full stroke of the piston 28 draws the follower pin 44 along the helical cam groove 42 and turns the index collar 40 by one increment, so that the index collar 40 advances by itself as the valve is used and needs no separate indexing drive.

The three axial stop faces 46 are carried by the index collar 40 at different axial positions. The stop face presented by the current increment of rotation limits the travel of the piston 28 and thereby sets the dose volume, so that the three axial stop faces 46 correspond to three dose volumes. The spring-biased detent 48 engages one of the three detent recesses 50 to retain the selected setting until the index collar 40 is next indexed.

The transparent window 52 in the housing 12 shows one of the three dose setting numerals 54 carried by the index collar 40. The dose setting numeral presented at the transparent window 52 is the one associated with the axial stop face then limiting the travel of the piston 28, so that the dose setting is mechanically visible without electronics. What is seen at the transparent window 52 is the position of the mechanism itself rather than a stored value, so the displayed setting cannot disagree with the volume that the valve will deliver.

FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, the follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62 of which one is directed across the concentrate port 22, and the flush bypass 26.

The flexible lip 56 is carried on the upstream sealing land 30 and bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20. As the return stroke begins, the flexible lip 56 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20 and carries the film of concentrate remaining on that wall ahead of it, so that the rinse which follows is presented with a wetted surface rather than with standing liquid.

The annular rinse channel 60 lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve 18 and an inner surface of the housing 12, and is supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet 14. The two radial rinse openings 62 pass through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and connect the annular rinse channel 60 to the dose chamber 20. One of the two radial rinse openings 62 is directed across the concentrate port 22 and the other is directed across the one-way outlet valve 38. Those are the two surfaces on which concentrate is otherwise retained after a dose, the first because concentrate stands in the mouth of the port and the second because concentrate is the last liquid to pass the one-way outlet valve 38.

The flush poppet 58 is normally closed and is connected to the flush bypass 26. Near the end of the return stroke, the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows from the inlet 14 through the annular rinse channel 60, through the two radial rinse openings 62 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 to the outlet 16. The rinse liquid therefore reaches the outlet 16, as the dose does, and is carried away in the main flow.

The flush poppet 58 closes before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. The concentrate port 22 is closed throughout the interval in which the annular rinse channel 60 communicates with the flush bypass 26, so that carrier liquid at the pressure of the main line is never presented to an open concentrate port 22 and cannot be driven back toward the concentrate source. Only when the flush poppet 58 has closed does the continuing return of the piston 28 bring the waist 34 back into register with the concentrate port 22, at which point the dose chamber 20 is charged again for the next dose.

Because the follower pin 44 that opens the flush poppet 58 is carried by the piston rod 36, the rinse occurs once for every dose and at the same point in every cycle. It is not a separate operation, it needs no command, and it cannot be omitted while the valve continues to be used. The rinse also occurs while the concentrate port 22 is shut and after the wall of the dose chamber 20 has been wiped, so that it removes a film with clean carrier liquid instead of diluting a standing charge of concentrate.

The cartridge 64 contains the piston 28, the metering sleeve 18, the one-way outlet valve 38 and the flush poppet 58, and is removable from the housing 12 as a unit. Removing the threaded end cap 66 withdraws the cartridge 64 from the housing 12 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 without disturbing the connections at the inlet 14 and the outlet 16, so that the cartridge 64 is replaced as a unit while the housing 12 remains in the line.
In use, carrier liquid flows through the housing 12 from the inlet 14 to the outlet 16. With the piston 28 in the fill position, concentrate is admitted through the concentrate port 22 and past the waist 34 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume, the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolating the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. The piston 28 is then advanced toward the discharge position so as to close the concentrate port 22 and thereafter to uncover the carrier-liquid admission port 24 with the downstream sealing land 32. Carrier liquid is admitted through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16. The extent of the travel available to the piston 28, and therefore the measured volume, is fixed by the selected one of the three axial stop faces 46.

The piston 28 is then returned toward the fill position. During the return, the flexible lip 56 on the upstream sealing land 30 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20, and the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36 opens the normally closed flush poppet 58. Carrier liquid flows through the annular rinse channel 60 between the metering sleeve 18 and the housing 12, through the two radial rinse openings 62 in the metering sleeve 18 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20 to the outlet 16. The flush poppet 58 is closed before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. Over the same full stroke, the follower pin 44 travelling in the helical cam groove 42 turns the index collar 40 by one increment, the spring-biased detent 48 enters the next of the three detent recesses 50, and the dose setting numeral then presented at the transparent window 52 shows the setting that will govern the next dose. The valve is thereby left charged, rinsed and set, ready for the following cycle.

The foregoing description sets out embodiments of the invention. A skilled reader may make changes of detail to the described embodiments without departing from the scope of the claims that follow.

input.summary: Fixed all three findings. The annulus between the metering sleeve and the housing is no longer closed at its downstream end in either brief: FIG. 1 now shows the clear gap running from a position right of the end cap to the right-hand end of the sleeve, which stands short of the end wall, with the gap opening at that end into the housing interior that leads to the outlet, and FIG. 3 states the annular rinse channel is open at the left to the housing interior at the inlet and open at its right-hand end, beyond the sleeve, to the housing interior that leads to the outlet, with the flush bypass opening beyond the sleeve's right-hand end into that same interior. The description now says the rinse liquid reaches the outlet 16, as the dose does, instead of saying it leaves by the same route as the dose. The cartridge paragraph no longer asserts that the exchanged parts are all the parts that contact the concentrate, and no longer names a change of concentrate or a worn sealing land as the occasion for replacement. All four briefs remain at or below 2800 characters, the numeral lists and per-figure lists are unchanged, and the drawing descriptions still match the briefs in view type and state.
reasoning: The main carrier flow needs a through path from inlet 14 to outlet 16, which the description states and which the disclosed inline dosing function requires. Both briefs now open the annular space at its downstream end into the housing interior that leads to the outlet, so nothing in the drawings fixes a flow topology the inventor never described and nothing blocks the line the valve sits in. The description was left alone: the gap still begins right of the end cap, so the sleeve is still spaced from the housing over part of its length.

Opening that end also removes the implied technical function the closure gave the flush bypass, namely being the sole exit for rinse liquid. The claims and description already say what the rinse path is, from the annular rinse channel through the rinse openings and the flush bypass to the outlet, and that wording is unchanged, so the briefs now depict the disclosed path without asserting an undisclosed seal to force it.

The rinse and the dose share only their destination. The description now says the rinse liquid reaches the outlet as the dose does, which keeps the two routes distinct and agrees with claim 1, where the rinse travels through the annular rinse channel, the rinse opening and the flush bypass, while the dose passes through the one-way outlet valve.

The cartridge paragraph now stops at the disclosed facts: what the cartridge contains, that it is removable as a unit, and that removing the threaded end cap withdraws it without disturbing the connections at the inlet and the outlet. The claim that every concentrate-wetted part is exchanged was both untraced and in tension with the concentrate tube crossing the housing wall in the briefs, and the service occasions were invented, so both are gone.

Both edited briefs needed compression to stay within the character limit once the longer open-end wording went in. I cut only wording: every body, opening, contact and path on those sheets is still specified, the assembly-numeral leaders for 64 and 28 keep the arrowhead convention the last review accepted, and the remaining targets sit on broad interior regions of their parts.

1	In the following description, the terms upstream and downstream refer to the direction of travel of the carrier liquid from the inlet toward the outlet, and the terms axial and radial refer to the axis along which the piston slides.
2	
3	FIG. 1 shows an inline liquid metering valve 10 having a cylindrical housing 12 with an inlet 14 at one axial end and an outlet 16 at the opposite axial end, a metering sleeve 18 fixed within the housing 12, a cartridge 64 retained in the housing 12 by a threaded end cap 66, and a transparent window 52 in the housing 12.
4	
5	The inline liquid metering valve 10 is connected in a line that already carries a flowing carrier liquid. Carrier liquid enters at the inlet 14, passes along the housing 12, and leaves at the outlet 16. That flow is the main flow into which each dose of concentrate is delivered, and it is also the only liquid used to rinse the valve. The metering sleeve 18 is spaced radially inward from the inner surface of the housing 12 over part of its length.
6	
7	FIG. 2 shows the metering sleeve 18 defining a dose chamber 20, a concentrate port 22 opening into the dose chamber 20 and a carrier-liquid admission port 24 opening into the dose chamber 20. FIG. 2 further shows an upstream sealing land 30 and a downstream sealing land 32 joined by a reduced-diameter waist 34 in the fill position, and a one-way outlet valve 38.
8	
9	The dose chamber 20 is cylindrical. The concentrate port 22 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and is connected in use to a concentrate source. The carrier-liquid admission port 24 passes through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 at an axial position downstream of the concentrate port 22, and admits carrier liquid to the dose chamber 20. The metering sleeve 18 further defines a flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20.
10	
11	A piston 28 is axially slidable in the dose chamber 20 between a fill position and a discharge position. The upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 are axially spaced from one another on the piston 28 and are joined by the reduced-diameter waist 34. Each sealing land bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20, while the waist 34 stands clear of that wall. A piston rod 36 extends from the piston 28 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 and is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke. The one-way outlet valve 38 is arranged to pass liquid from the dose chamber 20 toward the outlet 16 and to prevent flow in the opposite direction.
12	
13	In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume of concentrate, the extent of which is fixed by the travel then permitted to the piston 28. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 while the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.
14	
15	Movement of the piston 28 toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port 22 before the downstream sealing land 32 uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port 24. The upstream sealing land 30 arrives at the concentrate port 22 and shuts it while the downstream sealing land 32 is still overlying the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Only after that has happened does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.
16	
17	The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every position of the piston 28 at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18. It does not depend on the order in which external commands are given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of a separately actuated shut-off element. A slow stroke, an interrupted stroke, or a stroke reversed part way through cannot open both ports at once, because the port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens.
18	
19	FIG. 4 shows an index collar 40 having a helical cam groove 42 engaged by a follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36, three selectable axial stop faces 46, a spring-biased detent 48 engaging one of three detent recesses 50, and three dose setting numerals 54.
20	
21	The index collar 40 surrounds the metering sleeve 18. Each full stroke of the piston 28 draws the follower pin 44 along the helical cam groove 42 and turns the index collar 40 by one increment, so that the index collar 40 advances by itself as the valve is used and needs no separate indexing drive.
22	
23	The three axial stop faces 46 are carried by the index collar 40 at different axial positions. The stop face presented by the current increment of rotation limits the travel of the piston 28 and thereby sets the dose volume, so that the three axial stop faces 46 correspond to three dose volumes. The spring-biased detent 48 engages one of the three detent recesses 50 to retain the selected setting until the index collar 40 is next indexed.
24	
25	The transparent window 52 in the housing 12 shows one of the three dose setting numerals 54 carried by the index collar 40. The dose setting numeral presented at the transparent window 52 is the one associated with the axial stop face then limiting the travel of the piston 28, so that the dose setting is mechanically visible without electronics. What is seen at the transparent window 52 is the position of the mechanism itself rather than a stored value, so the displayed setting cannot disagree with the volume that the valve will deliver.
26	
27	FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, the follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62 of which one is directed across the concentrate port 22, and the flush bypass 26.
28	
29	The flexible lip 56 is carried on the upstream sealing land 30 and bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20. As the return stroke begins, the flexible lip 56 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20 and carries the film of concentrate remaining on that wall ahead of it, so that the rinse which follows is presented with a wetted surface rather than with standing liquid.
30

In the following description, the terms upstream and downstream refer to the direction of travel of the carrier liquid from the inlet toward the outlet, and the terms axial and radial refer to the axis along which the piston slides.

FIG. 1 shows an inline liquid metering valve 10 having a cylindrical housing 12 with an inlet 14 at one axial end and an outlet 16 at the opposite axial end, a metering sleeve 18 fixed within the housing 12, a cartridge 64 retained in the housing 12 by a threaded end cap 66, and a transparent window 52 in the housing 12.

The inline liquid metering valve 10 is connected in a line that already carries a flowing carrier liquid. Carrier liquid enters at the inlet 14, passes along the housing 12, and leaves at the outlet 16. That flow is the main flow into which each dose of concentrate is delivered, and it is also the only liquid used to rinse the valve. The metering sleeve 18 is spaced radially inward from the inner surface of the housing 12 over part of its length.

FIG. 2 shows the metering sleeve 18 defining a dose chamber 20, a concentrate port 22 opening into the dose chamber 20 and a carrier-liquid admission port 24 opening into the dose chamber 20. FIG. 2 further shows an upstream sealing land 30 and a downstream sealing land 32 joined by a reduced-diameter waist 34 in the fill position, and a one-way outlet valve 38.

The dose chamber 20 is cylindrical. The concentrate port 22 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and is connected in use to a concentrate source. The carrier-liquid admission port 24 passes through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 at an axial position downstream of the concentrate port 22, and admits carrier liquid to the dose chamber 20. The metering sleeve 18 further defines a flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20.

A piston 28 is axially slidable in the dose chamber 20 between a fill position and a discharge position. The upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 are axially spaced from one another on the piston 28 and are joined by the reduced-diameter waist 34. Each sealing land bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20, while the waist 34 stands clear of that wall. A piston rod 36 extends from the piston 28 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 and is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke. The one-way outlet valve 38 is arranged to pass liquid from the dose chamber 20 toward the outlet 16 and to prevent flow in the opposite direction.

In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume of concentrate, the extent of which is fixed by the travel then permitted to the piston 28. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 while the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.

Movement of the piston 28 toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port 22 before the downstream sealing land 32 uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port 24. The upstream sealing land 30 arrives at the concentrate port 22 and shuts it while the downstream sealing land 32 is still overlying the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Only after that has happened does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.

The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every position of the piston 28 at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18. It does not depend on the order in which external commands are given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of a separately actuated shut-off element. A slow stroke, an interrupted stroke, or a stroke reversed part way through cannot open both ports at once, because the port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens.

FIG. 4 shows an index collar 40 having a helical cam groove 42 engaged by a follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36, three selectable axial stop faces 46, a spring-biased detent 48 engaging one of three detent recesses 50, and three dose setting numerals 54.

The index collar 40 surrounds the metering sleeve 18. Each full stroke of the piston 28 draws the follower pin 44 along the helical cam groove 42 and turns the index collar 40 by one increment, so that the index collar 40 advances by itself as the valve is used and needs no separate indexing drive.

The three axial stop faces 46 are carried by the index collar 40 at different axial positions. The stop face presented by the current increment of rotation limits the travel of the piston 28 and thereby sets the dose volume, so that the three axial stop faces 46 correspond to three dose volumes. The spring-biased detent 48 engages one of the three detent recesses 50 to retain the selected setting until the index collar 40 is next indexed.

The transparent window 52 in the housing 12 shows one of the three dose setting numerals 54 carried by the index collar 40. The dose setting numeral presented at the transparent window 52 is the one associated with the axial stop face then limiting the travel of the piston 28, so that the dose setting is mechanically visible without electronics. What is seen at the transparent window 52 is the position of the mechanism itself rather than a stored value, so the displayed setting cannot disagree with the volume that the valve will deliver.

FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, the follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62 of which one is directed across the concentrate port 22, and the flush bypass 26.

The flexible lip 56 is carried on the upstream sealing land 30 and bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20. As the return stroke begins, the flexible lip 56 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20 and carries the film of concentrate remaining on that wall ahead of it, so that the rinse which follows is presented with a wetted surface rather than with standing liquid.

The annular rinse channel 60 lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve 18 and an inner surface of the housing 12, and is supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet 14. The two radial rinse openings 62 pass through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and connect the annular rinse channel 60 to the dose chamber 20. One of the two radial rinse openings 62 is directed across the concentrate port 22 and the other is directed across the one-way outlet valve 38. Those are the two surfaces on which concentrate is otherwise retained after a dose, the first because concentrate stands in the mouth of the port and the second because concentrate is the last liquid to pass the one-way outlet valve 38.

The flush poppet 58 is normally closed and is connected to the flush bypass 26. Near the end of the return stroke, the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows from the inlet 14 through the annular rinse channel 60, through the two radial rinse openings 62 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 to the outlet 16. The rinse liquid therefore reaches the outlet 16, as the dose does, and is carried away in the main flow.

The flush poppet 58 closes before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. The concentrate port 22 is closed throughout the interval in which the annular rinse channel 60 communicates with the flush bypass 26, so that carrier liquid at the pressure of the main line is never presented to an open concentrate port 22 and cannot be driven back toward the concentrate source. Only when the flush poppet 58 has closed does the continuing return of the piston 28 bring the waist 34 back into register with the concentrate port 22, at which point the dose chamber 20 is charged again for the next dose.

Because the follower pin 44 that opens the flush poppet 58 is carried by the piston rod 36, the rinse occurs once for every dose and at the same point in every cycle. It is not a separate operation, it needs no command, and it cannot be omitted while the valve continues to be used. The rinse also occurs while the concentrate port 22 is shut and after the wall of the dose chamber 20 has been wiped, so that it removes a film with clean carrier liquid instead of diluting a standing charge of concentrate.

The cartridge 64 contains the piston 28, the metering sleeve 18, the one-way outlet valve 38 and the flush poppet 58, and is removable from the housing 12 as a unit. Removing the threaded end cap 66 withdraws the cartridge 64 from the housing 12 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 without disturbing the connections at the inlet 14 and the outlet 16, so that the cartridge 64 is replaced as a unit while the housing 12 remains in the line.

In use, carrier liquid flows through the housing 12 from the inlet 14 to the outlet 16. The piston 28 is then advanced toward the discharge position so as to close the concentrate port 22 and thereafter to uncover the carrier-liquid admission port 24 with the downstream sealing land 32. Carrier liquid is admitted through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16. The extent of the travel available to the piston 28, and therefore the measured volume, is fixed by the selected one of the three axial stop faces 46.

The piston 28 is then returned toward the fill position. During the return, the flexible lip 56 on the upstream sealing land 30 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20, and the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36 opens the normally closed flush poppet 58. Carrier liquid flows through the annular rinse channel 60 between the metering sleeve 18 and the housing 12, through the two radial rinse openings 62 in the metering sleeve 18 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20 to the outlet 16. The flush poppet 58 is closed before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. Over the same full stroke, the follower pin 44 travelling in the helical cam groove 42 turns the index collar 40 by one increment, the spring-biased detent 48 enters the next of the three detent recesses 50, and the dose setting numeral then presented at the transparent window 52 shows the setting that will govern the next dose. The valve is thereby left charged, rinsed and set, ready for the following cycle.

The foregoing description sets out embodiments of the invention. A skilled reader may make changes of detail to the described embodiments without departing from the scope of the claims that follow.

The piston 28 is then returned toward the fill position. During the return, the flexible lip 56 on the upstream sealing land 30 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20, and the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36 opens the normally closed flush poppet 58. In the following description, the terms upstream and downstream refer to the direction of travel of the carrier liquid from the inlet toward the outlet, and the terms axial and radial refer to the axis along which the piston slides.

FIG. 1 shows an inline liquid metering valve 10 having a cylindrical housing 12 with an inlet 14 at one axial end and an outlet 16 at the opposite axial end, a metering sleeve 18 fixed within the housing 12, a cartridge 64 retained in the housing 12 by a threaded end cap 66, and a transparent window 52 in the housing 12.

The inline liquid metering valve 10 is connected in a line that already carries a flowing carrier liquid. Carrier liquid enters at the inlet 14, passes along the housing 12, and leaves at the outlet 16. That flow is the main flow into which each dose of concentrate is delivered, and it is also the only liquid used to rinse the valve. The metering sleeve 18 is spaced radially inward from the inner surface of the housing 12 over part of its length.

FIG. 2 shows the metering sleeve 18 defining a dose chamber 20, a concentrate port 22 opening into the dose chamber 20 and a carrier-liquid admission port 24 opening into the dose chamber 20. FIG. 2 further shows an upstream sealing land 30 and a downstream sealing land 32 joined by a reduced-diameter waist 34 in the fill position, and a one-way outlet valve 38.

The dose chamber 20 is cylindrical. The concentrate port 22 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and is connected in use to a concentrate source. The carrier-liquid admission port 24 passes through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 at an axial position downstream of the concentrate port 22, and admits carrier liquid to the dose chamber 20. The metering sleeve 18 further defines a flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20.

A piston 28 is axially slidable in the dose chamber 20 between a fill position and a discharge position. The upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 are axially spaced from one another on the piston 28 and are joined by the reduced-diameter waist 34. Each sealing land bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20, while the waist 34 stands clear of that wall. A piston rod 36 extends from the piston 28 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 and is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke. The one-way outlet valve 38 is arranged to pass liquid from the dose chamber 20 toward the outlet 16 and to prevent flow in the opposite direction.

In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume of concentrate, the extent of which is fixed by the travel then permitted to the piston 28. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 while the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.

Movement of the piston 28 toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port 22 before the downstream sealing land 32 uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port 24. The upstream sealing land 30 arrives at the concentrate port 22 and shuts it while the downstream sealing land 32 is still overlying the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Only after that has happened does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.

The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every position of the piston 28 at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18. It does not depend on the order in which external commands are given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of a separately actuated shut-off element. A slow stroke, an interrupted stroke, or a stroke reversed part way through cannot open both ports at once, because the port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens.

FIG. 4 shows an index collar 40 having a helical cam groove 42 engaged by a follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36, three selectable axial stop faces 46, a spring-biased detent 48 engaging one of three detent recesses 50, and three dose setting numerals 54.

The index collar 40 surrounds the metering sleeve 18. Each full stroke of the piston 28 draws the follower pin 44 along the helical cam groove 42 and turns the index collar 40 by one increment, so that the index collar 40 advances by itself as the valve is used and needs no separate indexing drive.

The three axial stop faces 46 are carried by the index collar 40 at different axial positions. The stop face presented by the current increment of rotation limits the travel of the piston 28 and thereby sets the dose volume, so that the three axial stop faces 46 correspond to three dose volumes. The spring-biased detent 48 engages one of the three detent recesses 50 to retain the selected setting until the index collar 40 is next indexed.

The transparent window 52 in the housing 12 shows one of the three dose setting numerals 54 carried by the index collar 40. The dose setting numeral presented at the transparent window 52 is the one associated with the axial stop face then limiting the travel of the piston 28, so that the dose setting is mechanically visible without electronics. What is seen at the transparent window 52 is the position of the mechanism itself rather than a stored value, so the displayed setting cannot disagree with the volume that the valve will deliver.

FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, the follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62 of which one is directed across the concentrate port 22, and the flush bypass 26.

The flexible lip 56 is carried on the upstream sealing land 30 and bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20. As the return stroke begins, the flexible lip 56 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20 and carries the film of concentrate remaining on that wall ahead of it, so that the rinse which follows is presented with a wetted surface rather than with standing liquid.

The annular rinse channel 60 lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve 18 and an inner surface of the housing 12, and is supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet 14. The two radial rinse openings 62 pass through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and connect the annular rinse channel 60 to the dose chamber 20. One of the two radial rinse openings 62 is directed across the concentrate port 22 and the other is directed across the one-way outlet valve 38. Those are the two surfaces on which concentrate is otherwise retained after a dose, the first because concentrate stands in the mouth of the port and the second because concentrate is the last liquid to pass the one-way outlet valve 38.

The flush poppet 58 is normally closed and is connected to the flush bypass 26. Near the end of the return stroke, the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows from the inlet 14 through the annular rinse channel 60, through the two radial rinse openings 62 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 to the outlet 16. The rinse liquid therefore reaches the outlet 16, as the dose does, and is carried away in the main flow.

The flush poppet 58 closes before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. The concentrate port 22 is closed throughout the interval in which the annular rinse channel 60 communicates with the flush bypass 26, so that carrier liquid at the pressure of the main line is never presented to an open concentrate port 22 and cannot be driven back toward the concentrate source. Only when the flush poppet 58 has closed does the continuing return of the piston 28 bring the waist 34 back into register with the concentrate port 22, at which point the dose chamber 20 is charged again for the next dose.

Because the follower pin 44 that opens the flush poppet 58 is carried by the piston rod 36, the rinse occurs once for every dose and at the same point in every cycle. It is not a separate operation, it needs no command, and it cannot be omitted while the valve continues to be used. The rinse also occurs while the concentrate port 22 is shut and after the wall of the dose chamber 20 has been wiped, so that it removes a film with clean carrier liquid instead of diluting a standing charge of concentrate.

The cartridge 64 contains the piston 28, the metering sleeve 18, the one-way outlet valve 38 and the flush poppet 58, and is removable from the housing 12 as a unit. Removing the threaded end cap 66 withdraws the cartridge 64 from the housing 12 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 without disturbing the connections at the inlet 14 and the outlet 16, so that the cartridge 64 is replaced as a unit while the housing 12 remains in the line.

In use, carrier liquid flows through the housing 12 from the inlet 14 to the outlet 16. With the piston 28 in the fill position, concentrate is admitted through the concentrate port 22 and past the waist 34 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume, the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolating the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. The piston 28 is then advanced toward the discharge position so as to close the concentrate port 22 and thereafter to uncover the carrier-liquid admission port 24 with the downstream sealing land 32. Carrier liquid is admitted through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16. The extent of the travel available to the piston 28, and therefore the measured volume, is fixed by the selected one of the three axial stop faces 46.

The piston 28 is then returned toward the fill position. During the return, the flexible lip 56 on the upstream sealing land 30 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20, and the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36 opens the normally closed flush poppet 58. Carrier liquid flows through the annular rinse channel 60 between the metering sleeve 18 and the housing 12, through the two radial rinse openings 62 in the metering sleeve 18 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20 to the outlet 16. The flush poppet 58 is closed before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. Over the same full stroke, the follower pin 44 travelling in the helical cam groove 42 turns the index collar 40 by one increment, the spring-biased detent 48 enters the next of the three detent recesses 50, and the dose setting numeral then presented at the transparent window 52 shows the setting that will govern the next dose. The valve is thereby left charged, rinsed and set, ready for the following cycle.

An inline liquid metering valve delivers a repeatable measured volume of concentrate into a flowing carrier liquid and rinses the surfaces that contacted the concentrate after each dose, without any command additional to the stroke that delivers the dose.

The valve has a housing with an inlet and an outlet and a metering sleeve fixed within the housing. The metering sleeve defines a dose chamber, a concentrate port opening into the dose chamber, a carrier-liquid admission port opening into the dose chamber, and a flush bypass that opens downstream of the dose chamber. A piston slides axially in the dose chamber between a fill position and a discharge position. The piston has an upstream sealing land and a downstream sealing land axially spaced from one another and joined by a reduced-diameter waist.

Separation of the two liquids is enforced by the axial order of the land faces and the port edges rather than by the sequence in which any external command arrives. In the fill position, the waist connects the concentrate port to the dose chamber while the upstream and downstream sealing lands isolate the carrier-liquid admission port from the concentrate port. Movement of the piston toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port before the downstream sealing land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port. Carrier liquid then enters behind the measured volume of concentrate and expels that volume through a one-way outlet valve toward the outlet. Because one land face has passed the concentrate port before the other land face releases the carrier-liquid admission port, no position of the piston places the concentrate source in communication with the carrier-liquid path.

The rinse is carried out by the return of the same piston. An annular rinse channel lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve and an inner surface of the housing, and at least one rinse opening leads from that channel through the metering sleeve into the dose chamber. A follower pin carried by the piston rod opens a normally closed flush poppet connected to the flush bypass during the return stroke, so that carrier liquid sweeps the annular rinse channel, issues from the rinse opening across the surfaces wetted by the concentrate, and leaves through the flush bypass to the outlet. The flush poppet closes before the waist reconnects the concentrate port to the dose chamber, so the rinse is complete, and the rinse liquid is on its way to the outlet, before any further concentrate can enter. The rinse cannot be omitted, mistimed or deferred, because the element that opens it is carried by the piston rod itself.

In described embodiments, a flexible lip on the upstream sealing land wipes the wall of the dose chamber before the flush poppet opens, so that the flushing stream is presented with a film rather than with standing liquid. Two radial rinse openings are directed across the concentrate port and across the one-way outlet valve, which are the two surfaces on which residue is otherwise retained.

Dose selection is mechanical and self-indexing. An index collar surrounds the metering sleeve and has a helical cam groove engaged by the follower pin, so that each full stroke of the piston turns the index collar by one increment. Three selectable axial stop faces on the index collar limit the travel of the piston and thereby set three dose volumes, a spring-biased detent engaging one of three recesses retains the selected setting, and a transparent window in the housing shows one of three dose setting numerals carried by the index collar, so that the setting is visible without electronics.

A replaceable cartridge contains the piston, the metering sleeve, the one-way outlet valve and the flush poppet, and is retained by a threaded end cap. Removing the threaded end cap withdraws the cartridge without disturbing the connections at the inlet and the outlet.

A corresponding method admits concentrate to the dose chamber, closes the concentrate port before uncovering the carrier-liquid admission port, expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve, and then opens the flush poppet with the follower pin during the return of the piston and closes it again before the concentrate port is reconnected.

input.summary: Fixed all seven findings. FIG. 1 now takes the plain shaft out of the left end of the sleeve bore and stands the sleeve's left end within the left mouth of the housing short of the end cap, so the piston rod 36 and follower pin 44 have the same route in FIG. 1, FIG. 3 and FIG. 4. The detailed description now takes the views in the order set by the Brief Description, FIG. 1, FIG. 2, FIG. 3, FIG. 4, with no wording changes made in moving the FIG. 3 block. Five untraced result statements are deleted or reduced: the carrier liquid is now the flow that rinses the valve rather than the only liquid used; the flexible lip simply wipes the wall of the dose chamber; the sentence explaining which surfaces retain residue and why is gone from both the description and the summary; the back-flow clause attached to the closed concentrate port during the rinse interval is gone; and the window paragraph ends by saying what is seen there is the position of the index collar 40 itself. All four briefs are at or below 2800 characters, the numeral table and the per-figure numeral lists are unchanged, and the drawing descriptions still match the briefs in view type and state.
reasoning: The rod route was the only structural conflict, and the disclosure settles it: the index collar surrounds the metering sleeve and its cam groove is engaged by a follower pin carried by the piston rod, so the pin must act outside the sleeve. FIG. 1 was therefore the sheet to change. The shaft now leaves the left end of the sleeve bore and the sleeve's left end stands short of the end cap, which also drops the end-face contact the brief had asserted while keeping the cartridge retained by the threaded end cap as disclosed. FIG. 3 and FIG. 4 needed no change, so the three sheets now give the rod and the pin one consistent route.

Moving the FIG. 3 paragraphs ahead of the FIG. 4 paragraphs was a pure reordering. The view sentences, the numerals they name and every other sentence are unchanged, so the per-figure lists still match the briefs exactly and the drawing descriptions still list the views in the same order the description now discusses them.

The five deletions all removed asserted results rather than disclosed structure. Exclusivity about the rinsing liquid, the film carried ahead of the lip, the identification of the port mouth and the valve as the residue-retaining surfaces with reasons, the main-line pressure and back-flow consequence during the rinse interval, and the guarantee that the display can never disagree with the delivered volume were each a conclusion the inventor never stated. What remains is the disclosed sequence: the lip wipes the wall, the rinse openings are directed across the concentrate port and the one-way outlet valve, the concentrate port is closed throughout the interval in which the rinse channel communicates with the flush bypass, and the window shows the collar's position.

Removing those sentences costs nothing in support, because no claim recites any of them. Claim 3 recites the wiping, claim 2 the directed rinse openings, claims 4 and 16 the closed concentrate port during the rinse interval, and claim 9 the window and the numerals, and each of those limitations still appears in the description in the same words.

The summary edit matched the description edits so the two sections describe the lip and the rinse openings the same way, which was part of the finding: the earlier text stated the same asserted result three different ways across the summary and two description paragraphs.

FIG. 1 and FIG. 3 needed light compression to stay within the character limit after the longer rod and cartridge wording went in. I cut only wording: every body, opening, contact and path on those sheets is still specified, the assembly-numeral leaders for 64 and 28 keep the arrowhead convention, and the remaining targets sit on broad interior regions of their parts.

draft/06-summary.md: the flexible lip sentence ends after the flush poppet opens, and the rinse-opening sentence ends after the one-way outlet valve.
figures/fig-03.md: wording compressed to stay within the character limit, with no change to any body, opening, path or numeral target.

Claim 1 continues to rest on the ordered port and land geometry that isolates the concentrate from the carrier liquid by geometry rather than by command sequence, together with the flush poppet on the flush bypass that the follower pin opens during the return stroke and that closes before the waist reconnects the concentrate port. The piston rod 36 and the follower pin 44 therefore have one route across all three sheets: the shaft passes beyond the sleeve's left end in FIG. 3 so the pin can lift the poppet stem, and the pin can reach the cam groove of the collar that surrounds the sleeve in FIG. 4.

Text: the description now takes FIG. 1, FIG. 2, FIG. 3 and FIG. 4 in the order the Brief Description lists them, the FIG. 3 paragraphs having been moved ahead of the FIG. 4 paragraphs with their wording untouched. The carrier flow is described as the flow that rinses the valve rather than the only liquid that can. The flexible lip paragraph ends after the lip wipes the wall of the dose chamber. The sentence naming the port mouth and the one-way outlet valve as the surfaces that retain residue, and the reasons given for it, is gone from the description and the summary. The rinse-interval sentence ends after stating that the concentrate port is closed while the rinse channel communicates with the flush bypass. The window paragraph ends by saying that what is seen at the transparent window 52 is the position of the index collar 40 itself.

Synchronization holds: the numeral table is unchanged, each sheet carries the same eight numerals its "FIG. n shows" sentence names, the drawing descriptions match the briefs in view type and state, and every brief is at or below 2800 characters.

1	# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)
2	
3	This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.
4	
5	A reusable inline liquid metering valve delivers a repeatable dose of concentrate into a flowing carrier liquid and automatically rinses the surfaces that contacted the concentrate after each dose. The valve has a cylindrical housing with an inlet at one axial end and an outlet at the opposite axial end. A metering sleeve is fixed inside the housing. The sleeve defines a cylindrical dose chamber, a radial concentrate port, a carrier-liquid admission port, and a flush bypass that opens downstream of the dose chamber.
6	
7	A piston slides axially in the dose chamber between a fill position and a discharge position. The piston has two axially spaced sealing lands joined by a reduced-diameter waist. In the fill position, the waist connects the concentrate port to the dose chamber while both lands isolate the carrier-liquid path. 1	In the following description, the terms upstream and downstream refer to the direction of travel of the carrier liquid from the inlet toward the outlet, and the terms axial and radial refer to the axis along which the piston slides.
2	
3	FIG. 1 shows an inline liquid metering valve 10 having a cylindrical housing 12 with an inlet 14 at one axial end and an outlet 16 at the opposite axial end, a metering sleeve 18 fixed within the housing 12, a cartridge 64 retained in the housing 12 by a threaded end cap 66, and a transparent window 52 in the housing 12.
4	
5	The inline liquid metering valve 10 is connected in a line that already carries a flowing carrier liquid. Carrier liquid enters at the inlet 14, passes along the housing 12, and leaves at the outlet 16. That flow is the main flow into which each dose of concentrate is delivered, and it is also the flow that rinses the valve. The metering sleeve 18 is spaced radially inward from the inner surface of the housing 12 over part of its length.
6	
7	FIG. 2 shows the metering sleeve 18 defining a dose chamber 20, a concentrate port 22 opening into the dose chamber 20 and a carrier-liquid admission port 24 opening into the dose chamber 20. FIG. 2 further shows an upstream sealing land 30 and a downstream sealing land 32 joined by a reduced-diameter waist 34 in the fill position, and a one-way outlet valve 38.
8	
9	The dose chamber 20 is cylindrical. The concentrate port 22 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and is connected in use to a concentrate source. The carrier-liquid admission port 24 passes through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 at an axial position downstream of the concentrate port 22, and admits carrier liquid to the dose chamber 20. The metering sleeve 18 further defines a flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20.
10	
11	A piston 28 is axially slidable in the dose chamber 20 between a fill position and a discharge position. The upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 are axially spaced from one another on the piston 28 and are joined by the reduced-diameter waist 34. Each sealing land bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20, while the waist 34 stands clear of that wall. A piston rod 36 extends from the piston 28 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 and is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke. The one-way outlet valve 38 is arranged to pass liquid from the dose chamber 20 toward the outlet 16 and to prevent flow in the opposite direction.
12	
13	In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume of concentrate, the extent of which is fixed by the travel then permitted to the piston 28. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 while the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.
14	
15	Movement of the piston 28 toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port 22 before the downstream sealing land 32 uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port 24. The upstream sealing land 30 arrives at the concentrate port 22 and shuts it while the downstream sealing land 32 is still overlying the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Only after that has happened does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.
16	
17	The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every position of the piston 28 at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18. It does not depend on the order in which external commands are given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of a separately actuated shut-off element. A slow stroke, an interrupted stroke, or a stroke reversed part way through cannot open both ports at once, because the port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens.
18	
19	FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, the follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62 of which one is directed across the concentrate port 22, and the flush bypass 26.
20	
21	The flexible lip 56 is carried on the upstream sealing land 30 and bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20. As the return stroke begins, the flexible lip 56 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20.
22	
23	The annular rinse channel 60 lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve 18 and an inner surface of the housing 12, and is supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet 14. The two radial rinse openings 62 pass through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and connect the annular rinse channel 60 to the dose chamber 20. One of the two radial rinse openings 62 is directed across the concentrate port 22 and the other is directed across the one-way outlet valve 38.
24	
25	The flush poppet 58 is normally closed and is connected to the flush bypass 26. Near the end of the return stroke, the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows from the inlet 14 through the annular rinse channel 60, through the two radial rinse openings 62 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 to the outlet 16. The rinse liquid therefore reaches the outlet 16, as the dose does, and is carried away in the main flow.
26	
27	The flush poppet 58 closes before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. The concentrate port 22 is closed throughout the interval in which the annular rinse channel 60 communicates with the flush bypass 26. Only when the flush poppet 58 has closed does the continuing return of the piston 28 bring the waist 34 back into register with the concentrate port 22, at which point the dose chamber 20 is charged again for the next dose.
28	
29	Because the follower pin 44 that opens the flush poppet 58 is carried by the piston rod 36, the rinse occurs once for every dose and at the same point in every cycle. It is not a separate operation, it needs no command, and it cannot be omitted while the valve continues to be used. The rinse also occurs while the concentrate port 22 is shut and after the wall of the dose chamber 20 has been wiped.
30	
31	FIG. 4 shows an index collar 40 having a helical cam groove 42 engaged by a follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36, three selectable axial stop faces 46, a spring-biased detent 48 engaging one of three detent recesses 50, and three dose setting numerals 54.
32	
33	The index collar 40 surrounds the metering sleeve 18. Each full stroke of the piston 28 draws the follower pin 44 along the helical cam groove 42 and turns the index collar 40 by one increment, so that the index collar 40 advances by itself as the valve is used and needs no separate indexing drive.
34	
35	The three axial stop faces 46 are carried by the index collar 40 at different axial positions. The stop face presented by the current increment of rotation limits the travel of the piston 28 and thereby sets the dose volume, so that the three axial stop faces 46 correspond to three dose volumes. The spring-biased detent 48 engages one of the three detent recesses 50 to retain the selected setting until the index collar 40 is next indexed.
36	
37	The transparent window 52 in the housing 12 shows one of the three dose setting numerals 54 carried by the index collar 40. The dose setting numeral presented at the transparent window 52 is the one associated with the axial stop face then limiting the travel of the piston 28, so that the dose setting is mechanically visible without electronics. What is seen at the transparent window 52 is the position of the index collar 40 itself.
38	
39	The cartridge 64 contains the piston 28, the metering sleeve 18, the one-way outlet valve 38 and the flush poppet 58, and is removable from the housing 12 as a unit. Removing the threaded end cap 66 withdraws the cartridge 64 from the housing 12 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 without disturbing the connections at the inlet 14 and the outlet 16, so that the cartridge 64 is replaced as a unit while the housing 12 remains in the line.
40	
41	In use, carrier liquid flows through the housing 12 from the inlet 14 to the outlet 16. With the piston 28 in the fill position, concentrate is admitted through the concentrate port 22 and past the waist 34 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume, the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolating the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. The piston 28 is then advanced toward the discharge position so as to close the concentrate port 22 and thereafter to uncover the carrier-liquid admission port 24 with the downstream sealing land 32. Carrier liquid is admitted through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16. The extent of the travel available to the piston 28, and therefore the measured volume, is fixed by the selected one of the three axial stop faces 46.
42	
43	The piston 28 is then returned toward the fill position. During the return, the flexible lip 56 on the upstream sealing land 30 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20, and the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36 opens the normally closed flush poppet 58. Carrier liquid flows through the annular rinse channel 60 between the metering sleeve 18 and the housing 12, through the two radial rinse openings 62 in the metering sleeve 18 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20 to the outlet 16. The flush poppet 58 is closed before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. Over the same full stroke, the follower pin 44 travelling in the helical cam groove 42 turns the index collar 40 by one increment, the spring-biased detent 48 enters the next of the three detent recesses 50, and the dose setting numeral then presented at the transparent window 52 shows the setting that will govern the next dose. The valve is thereby left charged, rinsed and set, ready for the following cycle.
44

1	Many liquid handling installations add a small, accurately measured quantity of a concentrate to a much larger stream of a carrier liquid that is already flowing in a pipe. The concentrate may be aggressive, staining, strongly coloured, biologically active, or simply expensive, and the quantity that must be added is small in comparison with the carrier flow. The addition therefore has to be made repeatably, without measuring the concentrate by eye, and without allowing the concentrate to reach any part of the installation other than the carrier stream itself.
2	
3	Two practical difficulties dominate this kind of dosing. The first is separation of the two liquids upstream of the point of addition. A dosing device sits between a concentrate source and a pressurised carrier line, and any path that momentarily connects the two allows carrier liquid to be forced back into the concentrate source or allows concentrate to migrate into the carrier line at a time when no dose is called for. Devices that rely on separately actuated shut-off elements to keep the two sides apart depend on those elements being commanded in the correct order, so a control fault, a lost signal, or a slow-acting element can open both sides at once.
4	
5	The second difficulty is residue. The surfaces that the concentrate touches, in particular the port through which it enters the metering volume and the seat of the check element through which the dose leaves, retain a film of concentrate after the dose has been delivered. That film drips into the carrier stream between doses, so the quantity actually added is not the quantity that was measured. It also dries, crystallises, or reacts on the wetted surfaces, so that a valve which was accurate when new drifts, sticks, or seizes in service. The usual remedy is to break the valve out of the line and clean it by hand, which takes the installation out of service and exposes the person doing the work to the concentrate. Where a rinse is provided at all, it is commonly a separate operation that has to be commanded after the dose, and it therefore depends on an operator or a controller performing an extra step at the right moment.
6	
7	Dose selection presents a further difficulty. Adjustable dosing devices are often set by a screw or by an electronically stored value. A screw setting can be lost during cleaning and gives no indication of what was set. An electronic setting requires power, a sensor and a display at the valve, which is unwelcome in wet, washdown or hazardous locations, and it tells the operator only what the controller believes rather than what the mechanism will actually deliver.
8	
9	There remains a need for an inline metering valve in which the separation of the concentrate from the carrier liquid is enforced by the geometry of the moving parts rather than by the order in which external commands arrive, in which the surfaces wetted by the concentrate are rinsed by the carrier liquid as an unavoidable part of the return of the metering element, and in which the selected dose is both retained and displayed mechanically.
10

Many liquid handling installations add a small, accurately measured quantity of a concentrate to a much larger stream of a carrier liquid that is already flowing in a pipe. The concentrate may be aggressive, staining, strongly coloured, biologically active, or simply expensive, and the quantity that must be added is small in comparison with the carrier flow. The addition therefore has to be made repeatably, without measuring the concentrate by eye, and without allowing the concentrate to reach any part of the installation other than the carrier stream itself.

Two practical difficulties dominate this kind of dosing. The first is separation of the two liquids upstream of the point of addition. A dosing device sits between a concentrate source and a pressurised carrier line, and any path that momentarily connects the two allows carrier liquid to be forced back into the concentrate source or allows concentrate to migrate into the carrier line at a time when no dose is called for. Devices that rely on separately actuated shut-off elements to keep the two sides apart depend on those elements being commanded in the correct order, so a control fault, a lost signal, or a slow-acting element can open both sides at once.

The second difficulty is residue. The surfaces that the concentrate touches, in particular the port through which it enters the metering volume and the seat of the check element through which the dose leaves, retain a film of concentrate after the dose has been delivered. That film drips into the carrier stream between doses, so the quantity actually added is not the quantity that was measured. It also dries, crystallises, or reacts on the wetted surfaces, so that a valve which was accurate when new drifts, sticks, or seizes in service. The usual remedy is to break the valve out of the line and clean it by hand, which takes the installation out of service and exposes the person doing the work to the concentrate. Where a rinse is provided at all, it is commonly a separate operation that has to be commanded after the dose, and it therefore depends on an operator or a controller performing an extra step at the right moment.

Dose selection presents a further difficulty. Adjustable dosing devices are often set by a screw or by an electronically stored value. A screw setting can be lost during cleaning and gives no indication of what was set. An electronic setting requires power, a sensor and a display at the valve, which is unwelcome in wet, washdown or hazardous locations, and it tells the operator only what the controller believes rather than what the mechanism will actually deliver.

There remains a need for an inline metering valve in which the separation of the concentrate from the carrier liquid is enforced by the geometry of the moving parts rather than by the order in which external commands arrive, in which the surfaces wetted by the concentrate are rinsed by the carrier liquid as an unavoidable part of the return of the metering element, and in which the selected dose is both retained and displayed mechanically.

The metering sleeve defines a dose chamber, a concentrate port opening into the dose chamber, a carrier-liquid admission port opening into the dose chamber, and a flush bypass that opens downstream of the dose chamber. A piston slides axially in the dose chamber between a fill position and a discharge position. The piston has an upstream sealing land and a downstream sealing land axially spaced from one another and joined by a reduced-diameter waist.
4	
5	Separation of the two liquids is enforced by the axial order of the land faces and the port edges rather than by the sequence in which any external command arrives. In the fill position, the waist connects the concentrate port to the dose chamber while the upstream and downstream sealing lands isolate the carrier-liquid admission port from the concentrate port. Movement of the piston toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port before the downstream sealing land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port. Carrier liquid then enters behind the measured volume of concentrate and expels that volume through a one-way outlet valve toward the outlet. Because one land face has passed the concentrate port before the other land face releases the carrier-liquid admission port, no position of the piston places the concentrate source in communication with the carrier-liquid path.

An annular rinse channel lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve and an inner surface of the housing, and at least one rinse opening leads from that channel through the metering sleeve into the dose chamber.
