In the following description, the terms upstream and downstream refer to the direction of travel of the carrier liquid from the inlet toward the outlet, and the terms axial and radial refer to the axis along which the piston slides.

FIG. 1 shows an inline liquid metering valve 10 having a cylindrical housing 12 with an inlet 14 at one axial end and an outlet 16 at the opposite axial end, a metering sleeve 18 fixed within the housing 12, a cartridge 64 retained in the housing 12 by a threaded end cap 66, and a transparent window 52 in the housing 12.

The inline liquid metering valve 10 is connected in a line that already carries a flowing carrier liquid. Carrier liquid enters at the inlet 14, passes along the housing 12, and leaves at the outlet 16. That flow is the main flow into which each dose of concentrate is delivered, and it is also the flow that rinses the valve. The metering sleeve 18 is spaced radially inward from the inner surface of the housing 12 over part of its length.

FIG. 2 shows the metering sleeve 18 defining a dose chamber 20, a concentrate port 22 opening into the dose chamber 20 and a carrier-liquid admission port 24 opening into the dose chamber 20. FIG. 2 further shows an upstream sealing land 30 and a downstream sealing land 32 joined by a reduced-diameter waist 34 in the fill position, and a one-way outlet valve 38.

The dose chamber 20 is cylindrical. The concentrate port 22 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and is connected in use to a concentrate source. The carrier-liquid admission port 24 passes through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 at an axial position downstream of the concentrate port 22, and admits carrier liquid to the dose chamber 20. The metering sleeve 18 further defines a flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20.

A piston 28 is axially slidable in the dose chamber 20 between a fill position and a discharge position. The upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 are axially spaced from one another on the piston 28 and are joined by the reduced-diameter waist 34. Each sealing land bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20, while the waist 34 stands clear of that wall. A piston rod 36 extends from the piston 28 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 and is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke. The one-way outlet valve 38 is arranged to pass liquid from the dose chamber 20 toward the outlet 16 and to prevent flow in the opposite direction.

In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume of concentrate, the extent of which is fixed by the travel then permitted to the piston 28. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 while the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.

Movement of the piston 28 toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port 22 before the downstream sealing land 32 uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port 24. The upstream sealing land 30 arrives at the concentrate port 22 and shuts it while the downstream sealing land 32 is still overlying the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Only after that has happened does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.

The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every position of the piston 28 at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18. It does not depend on the order in which external commands are given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of a separately actuated shut-off element. A slow stroke, an interrupted stroke, or a stroke reversed part way through cannot open both ports at once, because the port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens.

FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, a follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62 of which one is directed across the concentrate port 22, and the flush bypass 26. The follower pin 44 is carried by the piston rod 36.

The flexible lip 56 is carried on the upstream sealing land 30 and bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20. As the return stroke begins, the flexible lip 56 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20.

The annular rinse channel 60 lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve 18 and an inner surface of the housing 12, and is supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet 14. The two radial rinse openings 62 pass through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and connect the annular rinse channel 60 to the dose chamber 20. One of the two radial rinse openings 62 is directed across the concentrate port 22 and the other is directed across the one-way outlet valve 38.

The flush poppet 58 is normally closed and is connected to the flush bypass 26. Near the end of the return stroke, the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows from the inlet 14 through the annular rinse channel 60, through the two radial rinse openings 62 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 to the outlet 16. The rinse liquid therefore reaches the outlet 16, as the dose does, and is carried away in the main flow.

The flush poppet 58 closes before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. The concentrate port 22 is closed throughout the interval in which the annular rinse channel 60 communicates with the flush bypass 26. Only when the flush poppet 58 has closed does the continuing return of the piston 28 bring the waist 34 back into register with the concentrate port 22, at which point the dose chamber 20 is charged again for the next dose.

Because the follower pin 44 that opens the flush poppet 58 is carried by the piston rod 36, the rinse occurs once for every dose and at the same point in every cycle. It is not a separate operation, it needs no command, and it cannot be omitted while the valve continues to be used. The rinse also occurs while the concentrate port 22 is shut and after the wall of the dose chamber 20 has been wiped.

FIG. 4 shows an index collar 40 having a helical cam groove 42 engaged by the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36, three selectable axial stop faces 46, a spring-biased detent 48 engaging one of three detent recesses 50, and three dose setting numerals 54.

The index collar 40 surrounds the metering sleeve 18. Each full stroke of the piston 28 draws the follower pin 44 along the helical cam groove 42 and turns the index collar 40 by one increment, so that the index collar 40 advances by itself as the valve is used and needs no separate indexing drive.

The three axial stop faces 46 are carried by the index collar 40 at different axial positions. The stop face presented by the current increment of rotation limits the travel of the piston 28 and thereby sets the dose volume, so that the three axial stop faces 46 correspond to three dose volumes. The spring-biased detent 48 engages one of the three detent recesses 50 to retain the selected setting until the index collar 40 is next indexed.

The transparent window 52 in the housing 12 shows one of the three dose setting numerals 54 carried by the index collar 40. The dose setting numeral presented at the transparent window 52 is the one associated with the axial stop face then limiting the travel of the piston 28, so that the dose setting is mechanically visible without electronics. What is seen at the transparent window 52 is the position of the index collar 40 itself.

The cartridge 64 contains the piston 28, the metering sleeve 18, the one-way outlet valve 38 and the flush poppet 58, and is removable from the housing 12 as a unit. Removing the threaded end cap 66 withdraws the cartridge 64 from the housing 12 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 without disturbing the connections at the inlet 14 and the outlet 16, so that the cartridge 64 is replaced as a unit while the housing 12 remains in the line.

In use, carrier liquid flows through the housing 12 from the inlet 14 to the outlet 16. With the piston 28 in the fill position, concentrate is admitted through the concentrate port 22 and past the waist 34 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume, the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolating the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. The piston 28 is then advanced toward the discharge position so as to close the concentrate port 22 and thereafter to uncover the carrier-liquid admission port 24 with the downstream sealing land 32. Carrier liquid is admitted through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16. The extent of the travel available to the piston 28, and therefore the measured volume, is fixed by the selected one of the three axial stop faces 46.

The piston 28 is then returned toward the fill position. During the return, the flexible lip 56 on the upstream sealing land 30 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20, and the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36 opens the normally closed flush poppet 58. Carrier liquid flows through the annular rinse channel 60 between the metering sleeve 18 and the housing 12, through the two radial rinse openings 62 in the metering sleeve 18 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20 to the outlet 16. The flush poppet 58 is closed before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. Over the same full stroke, the follower pin 44 travelling in the helical cam groove 42 turns the index collar 40 by one increment, the spring-biased detent 48 enters the next of the three detent recesses 50, and the dose setting numeral then presented at the transparent window 52 shows the setting that will govern the next dose. The valve is thereby left charged, rinsed and set, ready for the following cycle.

The foregoing description sets out embodiments of the invention. A skilled reader may make changes of detail to the described embodiments without departing from the scope of the claims that follow.

# FIG. 2

View: enlarged longitudinal sectional view of the metering portion of FIG. 1, axis horizontal, with the piston in the fill position. All line work lies well inside the drawing area.

Geometry:

- The metering sleeve is cut lengthwise on its axis and appears as upper and lower hatched wall bands running across the width of the view. The open space between them is the cylindrical dose chamber.
- An outer housing wall appears in section as hatched bands above and below the sleeve bands, each spaced outward so that a clear gap runs above and below the sleeve.
- In the left portion of the dose chamber, an upstream sealing land is drawn as a hatched block whose upper and lower edges meet the bore walls, a downstream sealing land as a second such block spaced to its right, and a waist joining them as a hatched bar of smaller height on the axis, so that open space is visible between the waist and each bore wall.
- A plain shaft on the axis extends leftward from the upstream sealing land and is broken off within the view.
- A radial opening passes through the upper sleeve band between the two sealing lands, its inner mouth opening into the space above the waist; this is the concentrate port. A short stub rises from it and is broken off at a conventional break line within the view, shown schematically as the connection to a concentrate source.
- A second opening passes through the lower sleeve band at the downstream sealing land, its inner mouth covered by that land and its outer mouth opening into the clear gap below the sleeve. This is the carrier-liquid admission port, right of the concentrate port.
- Right of the downstream sealing land, a passage leads from the dose chamber up through the upper sleeve band toward the outlet. A plain closure element drawn across the passage, shown schematically without seat or contact detail, is the one-way outlet valve.
- Further openings pass through the lower sleeve band right of the downstream sealing land and beneath the outlet-valve passage, connecting the clear gap below the sleeve to the dose chamber, and a further passage leads up through the upper sleeve band right of that passage. These are unnumbered here.

Numerals on this sheet: 18, 20, 22, 24, 30, 32, 34, 38.

Targets:

- 18: the hatched lower sleeve band.
- 20: the open space of the dose chamber above the waist.
- 22: interior of the opening in the upper sleeve band above the waist.
- 24: interior of the opening in the lower sleeve band at the downstream sealing land.
- 30: hatching of the left sealing land block.
- 32: hatching of the right sealing land block.
- 34: hatching of the narrower bar joining the two blocks.
- 38: the plain closure element in the passage.

# FIG. 3

View: enlarged longitudinal section of the metering portion of FIG. 1 during the return stroke, axis horizontal, with the flush poppet held open. All line work lies well inside the drawing area.

Geometry:

- An outer housing wall appears in section as upper and lower hatched bands. Inside it the sleeve wall appears as upper and lower hatched bands spaced inward; between them is the bore.
- The clear gap between the sleeve and outer bands, above and below, is the annular rinse channel, supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet end; its ends are not shown open to the housing interior.
- Toward the right a passage leads from the bore up through the upper sleeve band toward the outlet: the flush bypass. A plain closure element stands clear of the mouth of that passage and is connected by a plain stem to the follower pin; both are shown schematically without seat or contact detail and are the flush poppet.
- In the bore, in the left half, the piston is drawn as two hatched enlarged portions joined by a narrower middle portion. A plain shaft extends leftward on the axis past the sleeve's left end, and a short pin projects from it to the stem, holding the closure element clear of the passage mouth.
- A thin flexible projection extends from the left portion into contact with the upper bore wall and a matching one into contact with the lower bore wall: the flexible lip, shown schematically without flare direction.
- An opening through the upper sleeve band, covered by the left portion, is the concentrate port, with a short stub rising from it, broken off in the view.
- Between the piston and the flush bypass a further passage leads from the bore up through the upper sleeve band, with a plain closure element drawn across it, shown schematically: the one-way outlet valve, unnumbered.
- Two openings through the lower sleeve band connect the rinse channel to the bore: the radial rinse openings. The left one faces the concentrate port and is shown directed across it; the right one faces the one-way outlet valve passage and is shown directed across it. Their positions relative to the piston are not otherwise indicated.
- A further opening through the lower sleeve band at the right portion of the piston is covered by it; unnumbered.

Numerals on this sheet: 22, 26, 28, 44, 56, 58, 60, 62.

Targets:

- 22: interior of the upper opening at the left.
- 26: interior of the bypass passage.
- 28: the hatching of the left enlarged portion of the piston.
- 44: the short pin on the shaft.
- 56: the flexible projection at the upper bore wall.
- 58: the plain closure element clear of the passage mouth.
- 60: the clear gap between the lower bands.
- 62: the left lower opening.

input.summary: All eight findings are fixed, seven inside figures/ and one in the description. The two critical disclosure-fidelity items: the carrier-liquid admission port no longer opens into the annulus that FIG. 3 designates the annular rinse channel, its outer mouth being broken off at a conventional break line within the lower sleeve band in FIG. 2, with the matching break added to the covered lower opening in FIG. 3, so no feed connection between the admission path and the rinse channel is asserted; and the flush poppet no longer has a permanent linkage to the follower pin, the closure element now carrying a plain stem whose free end is abutted by the pin in this view, which matches the description's statement that the pin reaches the poppet and opens it near the end of the return stroke. The four major items: FIG. 1 numeral 10 now reaches the assembly by an arrowed lead line touching the outer contour of the housing at the upper right while 12 takes the upper housing wall band and the lower band is left unnumbered; numeral 64 now touches the left end face of the sleeve where it stands in the left mouth of the housing, clear of the bands targeted by 18; the annular rinse channel in FIG. 3 is open at the left toward the inlet end of the housing with its right end closed by the sleeve meeting the housing wall, so the supply path recited in the description, the summary and claim 1 is traceable in the figure; and "over part of its length" is deleted from the sleeve spacing sentence in the detailed description. The two minor items: the left radial rinse opening in FIG. 3 now lies immediately right of the left enlarged portion with its inner mouth open to the bore and directed toward the concentrate port, so nothing covers it; and numeral 28 reaches the piston as a whole by an arrowed lead line touching its lower outline where the middle portion meets the right enlarged portion, instead of landing on the block that FIG. 2 numbers 30. FIG. 2's unnumbered lower openings moved to the same axial station the FIG. 3 fix uses, so one opening is not drawn at two stations across the two sections. All four briefs were retrimmed to stay under the 2800 character cap; the space came from redundant phrasing such as a repeated statement that the stubs end inside the drawing area, not from geometry or relationships.
reasoning: The two critical items were both flow-topology assertions, and each was cured by removing the assertion rather than by adding structure. Showing the admission port's outer mouth broken off leaves the figure silent on where the port draws from, which is where the disclosure is silent, and it prevents the drawing from implying that the rinse channel feeds the metering charge, a path that would sit under the control of the flush poppet and would change what the valve does.

The poppet stem was the more consequential of the two. A permanent stem linkage would mean the follower pin governs the poppet throughout every stroke, which contradicts the disclosed timing that the poppet is normally closed and is opened near the end of the return stroke, and that timing is what claim 1 rests on. Making the stem a member of the poppet that the pin merely abuts in this one view keeps the depicted contact without asserting a permanent connection.

The rinse channel had to be opened at the inlet end rather than left closed at both ends, because the description, the summary and claim 1 all recite carrier liquid flowing through the channel, and the inlet is the only carrier-liquid source the disclosure gives. Closing the right end at the sleeve-to-housing junction keeps the single ordered route of channel, rinse openings, flush bypass, outlet, and does not reopen the permanent bypass that an earlier pass removed.

For numerals 10 and 12 and for 18 and 64, the problem was that a whole-assembly numeral and a component numeral were landing on two mirror halves of one sectioned part. Arrowed lead lines touching the outer contour of the housing and the left end face of the sleeve identify the assembly and the removable unit as units, and leaving the lower housing band unnumbered removes the mirror-image pairing that made 10 read as a second housing part.

Numeral 28 moved off the left enlarged portion for the same reason: that block is what FIG. 2 designates 30, so 28 had to reach the piston as a body. An arrowed lead line on the lower outline at the junction of the middle and right portions touches the body rather than any one land, and it stays clear of the features FIG. 2 numbers.

The left rinse opening moved off the concentrate port station because a land that covers the port also spans the bore at that station, which blocked the rinse path the description and claim 15 require. Placing the opening immediately right of the left enlarged portion gives its inner mouth an open path into the bore while keeping the disclosed direction toward the concentrate port.

I also moved FIG. 2's unnumbered lower openings to that same station, which the review did not raise. The two sections show the piston at nearly the same place, so leaving FIG. 2's opening at the old station would have put one physical opening at two axial stations across the sheets, which is the class of defect an earlier pass had already been asked to cure.

The description edit was a straight deletion. Nothing in the disclosure limits the axial extent of the sleeve-to-housing spacing, and claim 1 and the surrounding text already recite the annular rinse channel between the sleeve outer surface and the housing inner surface, so the qualifier carried no work and no support.

Nothing in this turn changed the claimed combination. Claim 1 still rests on the axial ordering of the land faces and the port edges, which closes the concentrate port before the downstream land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port so that separation is enforced by the moving geometry rather than by command sequencing, and on the flush poppet opened by the follower pin carried by the piston rod during the return stroke and closed before the waist reconnects the concentrate port. Two of this turn's fixes protect that ground rather than disturb it: reopening the rinse channel at the inlet end keeps the claimed rinse flow traceable in the drawings, and replacing the permanent poppet linkage with an abutment in one view keeps the drawings consistent with the claimed timing, in which the poppet is normally closed and is opened only near the end of the return stroke. The Background continues to state the problems those features answer, namely shut-off elements that depend on being commanded in the right order and rinses that are separate commanded operations.

The rinse channel in FIG. 3 is open at the left toward the inlet end with its right end closed at the sleeve-to-housing junction, so the supply path recited in the description, the summary and claim 1 is traceable. The left rinse opening lies immediately right of the left enlarged portion with its inner mouth open to the bore, so the land no longer blocks it, and FIG. 2's unnumbered lower openings moved to the same station so one opening is not shown at two stations. In the description, the qualifier limiting the sleeve-to-housing spacing to part of the sleeve's length is deleted. structured_output.summary: All eight findings are fixed, seven inside figures/ and one in the description. The two critical disclosure-fidelity items: the carrier-liquid admission port no longer opens into the annulus that FIG. 3 designates the annular rinse channel, its outer mouth being broken off at a conventional break line within the lower sleeve band in FIG. 2, with the matching break added to the covered lower opening in FIG. 3, so no feed connection between the admission path and the rinse channel is asserted; and the flush poppet no longer has a permanent linkage to the follower pin, the closure element now carrying a plain stem whose free end is abutted by the pin in this view, which matches the description's statement that the pin reaches the poppet and opens it near the end of the return stroke. The four major items: FIG. 1 numeral 10 now reaches the assembly by an arrowed lead line touching the outer contour of the housing at the upper right while 12 takes the upper housing wall band and the lower band is left unnumbered; numeral 64 now touches the left end face of the sleeve where it stands in the left mouth of the housing, clear of the bands targeted by 18; the annular rinse channel in FIG. 3 is open at the left toward the inlet end of the housing with its right end closed by the sleeve meeting the housing wall, so the supply path recited in the description, the summary and claim 1 is traceable in the figure; and "over part of its length" is deleted from the sleeve spacing sentence in the detailed description. The two minor items: the left radial rinse opening in FIG. 3 now lies immediately right of the left enlarged portion with its inner mouth open to the bore and directed toward the concentrate port, so nothing covers it; and numeral 28 reaches the piston as a whole by an arrowed lead line touching its lower outline where the middle portion meets the right enlarged portion, instead of landing on the block that FIG. 2 numbers 30. FIG. 2's unnumbered lower openings moved to the same axial station the FIG. 3 fix uses, so one opening is not drawn at two stations across the two sections. All four briefs were retrimmed to stay under the 2800 character cap; the space came from redundant phrasing such as a repeated statement that the stubs end inside the drawing area, not from geometry or relationships.
reasoning: The two critical items were both flow-topology assertions, and each was cured by removing the assertion rather than by adding structure. Showing the admission port's outer mouth broken off leaves the figure silent on where the port draws from, which is where the disclosure is silent, and it prevents the drawing from implying that the rinse channel feeds the metering charge, a path that would sit under the control of the flush poppet and would change what the valve does.

The poppet stem was the more consequential of the two. A permanent stem linkage would mean the follower pin governs the poppet throughout every stroke, which contradicts the disclosed timing that the poppet is normally closed and is opened near the end of the return stroke, and that timing is what claim 1 rests on. Making the stem a member of the poppet that the pin merely abuts in this one view keeps the depicted contact without asserting a permanent connection.

The rinse channel had to be opened at the inlet end rather than left closed at both ends, because the description, the summary and claim 1 all recite carrier liquid flowing through the channel, and the inlet is the only carrier-liquid source the disclosure gives. Closing the right end at the sleeve-to-housing junction keeps the single ordered route of channel, rinse openings, flush bypass, outlet, and does not reopen the permanent bypass that an earlier pass removed.

For numerals 10 and 12 and for 18 and 64, the problem was that a whole-assembly numeral and a component numeral were landing on two mirror halves of one sectioned part. Arrowed lead lines touching the outer contour of the housing and the left end face of the sleeve identify the assembly and the removable unit as units, and leaving the lower housing band unnumbered removes the mirror-image pairing that made 10 read as a second housing part.

Numeral 28 moved off the left enlarged portion for the same reason: that block is what FIG. 2 designates 30, so 28 had to reach the piston as a body. An arrowed lead line on the lower outline at the junction of the middle and right portions touches the body rather than any one land, and it stays clear of the features FIG. 2 numbers.

The left rinse opening moved off the concentrate port station because a land that covers the port also spans the bore at that station, which blocked the rinse path the description and claim 15 require. Placing the opening immediately right of the left enlarged portion gives its inner mouth an open path into the bore while keeping the disclosed direction toward the concentrate port.

I also moved FIG. 2's unnumbered lower openings to that same station, which the review did not raise. The two sections show the piston at nearly the same place, so leaving FIG. 2's opening at the old station would have put one physical opening at two axial stations across the sheets, which is the class of defect an earlier pass had already been asked to cure.

The description edit was a straight deletion. Nothing in the disclosure limits the axial extent of the sleeve-to-housing spacing, and claim 1 and the surrounding text already recite the annular rinse channel between the sleeve outer surface and the housing inner surface, so the qualifier carried no work and no support.

- **Source fidelity is clean before rendering** (fail): Scope: I traced every claim limitation, every numeral, and every structural, positional, flow-path and result statement in draft/01–10, numerals.md and the four figure briefs to the single inventor passage (identical in input/disclosure.md and the one USER turn of input/conversation.md). input/brief.md was used only for title, applicant/inventor, priority and government-support formalities.

Clean areas. The application text itself traces cleanly. Claims 1–20 map limitation-by-limitation onto disclosed matter (ordered port/land isolation, one-way outlet valve, annular rinse channel and rinse openings, follower-pin-opened normally closed flush poppet closing before the waist reconnects the concentrate port, index collar with helical cam groove, three axial stop faces, spring-biased detent and three recesses, transparent window with three numerals, cartridge and threaded end cap, cylindrical housing with axial-end inlet/outlet). The generalization to "at least one rinse opening" is a permissible narrowing-to-broadening of the disclosed pair, with the pair recited in claims 2 and 15. The detailed description adds no structure beyond the source: the entailed items I checked and accepted are that the admission port lies axially downstream of the concentrate port, that the upstream land is the land that shuts the concentrate port on the discharge stroke, that lands bear on the bore while the waist stands clear, and that the rinse channel is fed from the inlet. Numeral bookkeeping is consistent: all 29 numerals in numerals.md appear in a figure; each figure's "Numerals on this sheet" list, targets list and the corresponding description paragraph agree exactly; no numeral carries two meanings; there are no named section lines to cross-check; the Brief Description matches the four briefs; the abstract is 145 words; no drafting note, placeholder, open question or unresolved alternative remains; no "by way of example" or "any closed outline" style shape-justifying language app
  - FIG. 3 invents a poppet stem linking the flush poppet to the follower pin across the sealed bore
  - FIG. 3 asserts an undisclosed closed downstream end of the annular rinse channel
  - FIG. 3 fixes an undisclosed axial station and jet direction for the left rinse opening, and the stated path is blocked by the land
  - The index collar as drawn in FIG. 1 occupies the annulus that FIG. 3 and the description require as the rinse channel
  - FIG. 3 draws the flush bypass leading from the dose chamber, not opening downstream of it
  - FIG. 4 does not identify which end of the index collar carries the stepped stop faces
  - FIG. 1's rectangular transparent-window panel is an unmarked generic outline

## Reviewer findings

- **[critical] FIG. 3 invents a poppet stem linking the flush poppet to the follower pin across the sealed bore** (figures/FIG-3.md, Geometry bullets 3 and 4; Targets entry for 58) - The brief gives the flush poppet an actuating member and a contact topology that the inventor never disclosed, and the asserted linkage is geometrically impossible in the same view. The follower pin is placed on the shaft 'past the sleeve's left end' (as FIG. 4 requires, so it can sit in the collar's cam groove), while the poppet is placed at the bypass passage toward the right of the sleeve. A stem bridging them would have to pass the length of the dose chamber and through the two-land piston that seals that bore. The source states only that the pin opens the poppet and that the poppet is connected to the flush bypass; it says nothing about a stem, about the poppet's axial station, or about how the pin reaches it.
  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-3.md, delete the words "and carries a plain stem extending leftward, its free end abutted by the follower pin in this view" and "and abuts that stem end". Replace the poppet bullet with: "Adjacent the left end of the sleeve, at the position reached by the follower pin at the end of the return stroke, a plain closure element is shown schematically as the flush poppet, held clear of its seat by the follower pin, and connected to the flush bypass passage by a plain passage shown schematically." Change the target for 58 to "the plain closure element held open by the follower pin". No change to the description, claims or Brief Description is required.
- **[critical] FIG. 3 asserts an undisclosed closed downstream end of the annular rinse channel** (figures/FIG-3.md, Geometry bullet 2) - The brief states a flow boundary for the annular rinse channel - that its downstream end is sealed by contact between the sleeve and the housing wall. This is a contact-topology and flow-boundary statement about a functional flow passage, which is substantive even in a schematic view. The source discloses only that the channel lies between the sleeve and the housing and that carrier liquid flows through it to the rinse openings and then out through the flush bypass; it never says either end of the channel is closed, nor that the sleeve contacts the housing bore anywhere.
  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-3.md, replace that bullet with: "The clear gap between the sleeve bands and the outer housing bands is the annular rinse channel, supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet end of the housing at the left; no closure of either end of the gap is indicated."
- **[critical] FIG. 3 fixes an undisclosed axial station and jet direction for the left rinse opening, and the stated path is blocked by the land** (figures/FIG-3.md, Geometry bullets 5 and 7) - The brief assigns the left rinse opening an exact axial position relative to the upstream sealing land and a direction of discharge toward the concentrate port. Both are substantive statements about a functional port, and neither is disclosed: the source gives the number of rinse openings and the surfaces they are directed across, but no axial station relative to the lands. The chosen station also contradicts the same brief, which shows the concentrate port covered by the upstream land in this view, so the depicted opening discharges into the waist region on the far side of that land from the port it is said to rinse.
  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-3.md, replace the rinse-opening bullet with: "Two openings through the lower sleeve band connect the rinse channel to the bore, shown schematically: one at the axial station of the concentrate port and one at the axial station of the outlet-valve passage. Their axial relationship to the sealing lands and any direction of discharge are not indicated." Keep the target for 62 as "the left lower opening". The disclosed function remains stated in the description and in claims 2 and 15.
- **[major] The index collar as drawn in FIG. 1 occupies the annulus that FIG. 3 and the description require as the rinse channel** (figures/FIG-1.md, Geometry bullets 4 and 6; figures/FIG-3.md, Geometry bullet 2; draft/08-detailed-description.md paragr) - FIG. 1 places the index collar ring inside the annulus between the sleeve and the housing over the left portion of the sleeve, and states that the clear gap exists only right of the ring. FIG. 3 and the description require that same annulus to be an open rinse channel supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet, which FIG. 1 places at the left end. Taken together with the asserted closed right end, the rinse channel has no inlet and no outlet, so the disclosed rinse flow path cannot exist in the drawn structure. The source affirms both features simultaneously - the collar surrounds the sleeve inside the housing (it is read through a window in the housing) and the rinse channel lies between the sleeve and the housing - so the drawing must show the collar clear of the housing bore.
  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-1.md, change the sleeve bullet to read "...spaced inward from the housing wall bands, so that a clear gap is visible above and below it along its length", and change the ring bullet to "An unnumbered ring surrounds the sleeve over the left portion of its length, standing clear of the housing wall so that the gap continues past it, its left part standing beyond the sleeve's left end." Combined with the fix to FIG. 3's channel bullet, the rinse path from the inlet end to the rinse openings and the flush bypass is then continuous.
- **[minor] FIG. 3 draws the flush bypass leading from the dose chamber, not opening downstream of it** (figures/FIG-3.md, Geometry bullet 3) - The brief describes the bypass passage as leading 'from the bore', and the same brief identifies the space between the sleeve bands as the bore, which FIG. 2 labels the dose chamber. The source, the description and claims 1 and 13 all require the flush bypass to open downstream of the dose chamber, not out of it. As written the figure brief contradicts the claim language it must support.
  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-3.md, change the bullet to begin: "Toward the right, downstream of the dose chamber and of the outlet-valve passage, a passage leads from the sleeve bore up through the upper sleeve band toward the outlet: the flush bypass."
- **[minor] FIG. 4 does not identify which end of the index collar carries the stepped stop faces** (figures/FIG-4.md, Geometry bullet 4; Targets entry for 46) - The brief states the function of the three faces - that the presented face limits the travel of an approaching part - but leaves the end of the collar unspecified, while the same brief fixes the piston rod as entering from the left. A rendered view that steps the far end would show the stop faces facing away from the piston whose travel they are said to limit, contradicting the function stated in the same bullet and in claim 7. Naming the end nearest the rod adds no undisclosed relationship, since the source ties the faces to limiting piston travel.
  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-4.md, change the opening of that bullet to: "The left end of the collar, the end from which the piston rod enters, is stepped: its end face is divided into three faces at three different axial positions, shown schematically, so that the face presented limits the travel of the approaching part."
- **[minor] FIG. 1's rectangular transparent-window panel is an unmarked generic outline** (figures/FIG-1.md, Geometry bullet 7) - The window's outline is a generic shape chosen by the drafter; the source discloses the window's existence and function but not its shape. Every other generic outline in this brief (the inlet and outlet stubs, the body in the sleeve bore) is expressly marked 'shown schematically', so the unmarked rectangle reads as a shape assertion rather than a depiction convention. The fix is confined to the figure brief; no shape or optional embodiment should be added to the application text.
  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-1.md, change the bullet to: "An unhatched panel of simple outline, shown schematically, is set into the upper housing wall band above the ring, the hatching stopping at its outline; it is the transparent window."

Fix every listed item before returning. If an advisory is a false positive, make
the wording or figure specification unambiguous enough that the check passes.

In the following description, the terms upstream and downstream refer to the direction of travel of the carrier liquid from the inlet toward the outlet, and the terms axial and radial refer to the axis along which the piston slides.

FIG. 1 shows an inline liquid metering valve 10 having a cylindrical housing 12 with an inlet 14 at one axial end and an outlet 16 at the opposite axial end, a metering sleeve 18 fixed within the housing 12, a cartridge 64 retained in the housing 12 by a threaded end cap 66, and a transparent window 52 in the housing 12.

The inline liquid metering valve 10 is connected in a line that already carries a flowing carrier liquid. Carrier liquid enters at the inlet 14, passes along the housing 12, and leaves at the outlet 16. That flow is the main flow into which each dose of concentrate is delivered, and it is also the flow that rinses the valve. The metering sleeve 18 is spaced radially inward from the inner surface of the housing 12.

FIG. 2 shows the metering sleeve 18 defining a dose chamber 20, a concentrate port 22 opening into the dose chamber 20 and a carrier-liquid admission port 24 opening into the dose chamber 20. FIG. 2 further shows an upstream sealing land 30 and a downstream sealing land 32 joined by a reduced-diameter waist 34 in the fill position, and a one-way outlet valve 38.

The dose chamber 20 is cylindrical. The concentrate port 22 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and is connected in use to a concentrate source. The carrier-liquid admission port 24 passes through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 at an axial position downstream of the concentrate port 22, and admits carrier liquid to the dose chamber 20. The metering sleeve 18 further defines a flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20.

A piston 28 is axially slidable in the dose chamber 20 between a fill position and a discharge position. The upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 are axially spaced from one another on the piston 28 and are joined by the reduced-diameter waist 34. Each sealing land bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20, while the waist 34 stands clear of that wall. A piston rod 36 extends from the piston 28 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 and is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke. The one-way outlet valve 38 is arranged to pass liquid from the dose chamber 20 toward the outlet 16 and to prevent flow in the opposite direction.

In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume of concentrate, the extent of which is fixed by the travel then permitted to the piston 28. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 while the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.

Movement of the piston 28 toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port 22 before the downstream sealing land 32 uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port 24. The upstream sealing land 30 arrives at the concentrate port 22 and shuts it while the downstream sealing land 32 is still overlying the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Only after that has happened does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.

The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every position of the piston 28 at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18. It does not depend on the order in which external commands are given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of a separately actuated shut-off element. A slow stroke, an interrupted stroke, or a stroke reversed part way through cannot open both ports at once, because the port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens.

FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, a follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62 of which one is directed across the concentrate port 22, and the flush bypass 26. The follower pin 44 is carried by the piston rod 36.

The flexible lip 56 is carried on the upstream sealing land 30 and bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20. As the return stroke begins, the flexible lip 56 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20.

The annular rinse channel 60 lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve 18 and an inner surface of the housing 12, and is supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet 14. The two radial rinse openings 62 pass through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and connect the annular rinse channel 60 to the dose chamber 20. One of the two radial rinse openings 62 is directed across the concentrate port 22 and the other is directed across the one-way outlet valve 38.

The flush poppet 58 is normally closed and is connected to the flush bypass 26. Near the end of the return stroke, the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows from the inlet 14 through the annular rinse channel 60, through the two radial rinse openings 62 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 to the outlet 16. The rinse liquid therefore reaches the outlet 16, as the dose does, and is carried away in the main flow.

The flush poppet 58 closes before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. The concentrate port 22 is closed throughout the interval in which the annular rinse channel 60 communicates with the flush bypass 26. Only when the flush poppet 58 has closed does the continuing return of the piston 28 bring the waist 34 back into register with the concentrate port 22, at which point the dose chamber 20 is charged again for the next dose.

Because the follower pin 44 that opens the flush poppet 58 is carried by the piston rod 36, the rinse occurs once for every dose and at the same point in every cycle. It is not a separate operation, it needs no command, and it cannot be omitted while the valve continues to be used. The rinse also occurs while the concentrate port 22 is shut and after the wall of the dose chamber 20 has been wiped.

FIG. 4 shows an index collar 40 having a helical cam groove 42 engaged by the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36, three selectable axial stop faces 46, a spring-biased detent 48 engaging one of three detent recesses 50, and three dose setting numerals 54.

The index collar 40 surrounds the metering sleeve 18. Each full stroke of the piston 28 draws the follower pin 44 along the helical cam groove 42 and turns the index collar 40 by one increment, so that the index collar 40 advances by itself as the valve is used and needs no separate indexing drive.

The three axial stop faces 46 are carried by the index collar 40 at different axial positions. The stop face presented by the current increment of rotation limits the travel of the piston 28 and thereby sets the dose volume, so that the three axial stop faces 46 correspond to three dose volumes. The spring-biased detent 48 engages one of the three detent recesses 50 to retain the selected setting until the index collar 40 is next indexed.

The transparent window 52 in the housing 12 shows one of the three dose setting numerals 54 carried by the index collar 40. The dose setting numeral presented at the transparent window 52 is the one associated with the axial stop face then limiting the travel of the piston 28, so that the dose setting is mechanically visible without electronics. What is seen at the transparent window 52 is the position of the index collar 40 itself.

The cartridge 64 contains the piston 28, the metering sleeve 18, the one-way outlet valve 38 and the flush poppet 58, and is removable from the housing 12 as a unit. Removing the threaded end cap 66 withdraws the cartridge 64 from the housing 12 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 without disturbing the connections at the inlet 14 and the outlet 16, so that the cartridge 64 is replaced as a unit while the housing 12 remains in the line.

In use, carrier liquid flows through the housing 12 from the inlet 14 to the outlet 16. With the piston 28 in the fill position, concentrate is admitted through the concentrate port 22 and past the waist 34 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume, the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolating the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. The piston 28 is then advanced toward the discharge position so as to close the concentrate port 22 and thereafter to uncover the carrier-liquid admission port 24 with the downstream sealing land 32. Carrier liquid is admitted through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16. The extent of the travel available to the piston 28, and therefore the measured volume, is fixed by the selected one of the three axial stop faces 46.

The piston 28 is then returned toward the fill position. During the return, the flexible lip 56 on the upstream sealing land 30 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20, and the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36 opens the normally closed flush poppet 58. Carrier liquid flows through the annular rinse channel 60 between the metering sleeve 18 and the housing 12, through the two radial rinse openings 62 in the metering sleeve 18 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20 to the outlet 16. The flush poppet 58 is closed before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. Over the same full stroke, the follower pin 44 travelling in the helical cam groove 42 turns the index collar 40 by one increment, the spring-biased detent 48 enters the next of the three detent recesses 50, and the dose setting numeral then presented at the transparent window 52 shows the setting that will govern the next dose. The valve is thereby left charged, rinsed and set, ready for the following cycle.

The foregoing description sets out embodiments of the invention. A skilled reader may make changes of detail to the described embodiments without departing from the scope of the claims that follow.

input.summary: All seven findings are fixed inside figures/, with one synchronizing edit to the description. The three critical FIG. 3 items: the invented poppet stem is gone, the flush poppet now being a plain closure element shown schematically adjacent the left end of the sleeve, at the position the follower pin reaches at the end of the return stroke, held open by that pin and connected to the flush bypass by a plain passage, with target 58 reading "the plain closure element held open by the follower pin"; the annular rinse channel is now the clear gap between the sleeve bands and the outer housing bands, supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet end at the left, with no closure of either end indicated, so no undisclosed flow boundary is asserted; and the two rinse openings are placed only at the axial station of the concentrate port and at that of the outlet-valve passage, with their relationship to the sealing lands and any direction of discharge expressly not indicated, which removes both the untraced station and the blocked jet. The major item: FIG. 1's clear gap now runs along the length of the sleeve and the unnumbered ring stands clear of the housing wall so the gap continues past it, so the collar no longer occupies the rinse annulus and the path from the inlet end to the rinse openings and the flush bypass is continuous. The three minor items: the flush bypass in FIG. 3 is now expressly downstream of the dose chamber and of the outlet-valve passage, matching claims 1 and 13; FIG. 4 names the left end, the end from which the piston rod enters, as the stepped end, with the shallow curved edge indicating the round section moved to the right end and target 46 reading "one of the three stepped faces at the left end of the collar"; and FIG. 1's window panel is now an unhatched panel of simple outline expressly shown schematically. The description edit is confined to the FIG. 3 recitation sentence, which now lists the two radial rinse openings 62 and the concentrate port 22 without stating that the figure shows a direction of discharge; the disclosed direction across the concentrate port and the one-way outlet valve remains in the following paragraph, in the summary and in claims 2 and 15. Every sheet's numeral list is unchanged, and the four briefs are 2763, 2777, 2789 and 2761 characters.
reasoning: The poppet fix was the one with real consequences for the drawing's coherence. A stem running from the bypass at the right to the pin outside the sleeve's left end would have to cross the sealed bore and the two-land piston, so the linkage could not exist in the depicted structure. Putting the closure element where the pin actually arrives at the end of the return stroke keeps the disclosed relationship, that the pin opens a normally closed poppet connected to the flush bypass, without inventing an actuating member or a route for it.

The rinse channel and the FIG. 1 ring had to be fixed together. Closing the channel's right end while the collar blocked the annulus at the left left the channel with neither a supply nor a discharge, which contradicts the description, the summary and claim 1. Leaving both ends unstated and standing the ring clear of the housing wall gives a continuous annulus from the inlet end through the rinse openings to the flush bypass, and it keeps both disclosed facts true at once: the collar surrounds the sleeve inside the housing, where a window can read it, and the rinse channel lies between the sleeve and the housing.

For the rinse openings I removed the axial station relative to the lands rather than moving it again. Two earlier passes moved that opening to cure a blocked path, and each new station was itself untraced. The source gives the number of openings and the surfaces they are directed across, nothing more, so stating only the two stations that are disclosed by reference to the port and the valve, and declining to fix any relationship to the lands or any jet direction, is the version that stays inside the disclosure.

The flush bypass wording mattered because the figure brief was contradicting the claim it has to support: claims 1 and 13 require the bypass to open downstream of the dose chamber, and the brief had it leading from the bore. Naming it downstream of the dose chamber and of the outlet-valve passage aligns the sheet with the claim without adding structure.

Naming the stepped end of the collar in FIG. 4 forced a second change in the same brief, since the first bullet had closed the left end with the curved edge that indicates the round section. I moved that edge to the right end rather than leave two incompatible statements about the left end, and updated target 46 to name the left end so the leader cannot land on the wrong end face.

The description edit was not requested, but the FIG. 3 recitation had asserted that the figure shows one rinse opening directed across the concentrate port, which is exactly what the brief now declines to indicate. Rather than reintroduce the direction into the drawing, I removed the claim about what the figure shows and left the disclosed direction where it belongs, in the body text and the dependent claims. Every numeral recited for the sheet is still recited, so the sheet list, the target list and the description paragraph still agree.

Length had to be managed again, since the poppet fix added a bullet. The space came from redundant phrasing in the same briefs, such as repeating 'shown schematically' twice in one sentence and naming the view twice in one target, not from geometry, relationships or the hedges that cure the untraced items.

The claimed combination is untouched this turn. Claim 1 still rests on the axial ordering of the land faces and the port edges, which closes the concentrate port before the downstream land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port so that separation is enforced by the moving geometry rather than by command sequencing, and on the flush poppet opened by the follower pin carried by the piston rod during the return stroke and closed before the waist reconnects the concentrate port. Two of this turn's fixes protect that ground: restoring an unbounded, inlet-fed rinse annulus keeps the claimed rinse flow traceable in the drawings, and moving the flush bypass expressly downstream of the dose chamber aligns the sheet with the words of claims 1 and 13 rather than with a passage leading out of the chamber. The dependent ladder that carries the fallbacks, the two directed rinse openings, the flexible lip, the closed-port rinse interval, the index collar with its three stop faces, detent and window, and the cartridge with threaded end cap, is unchanged.

structured_output.summary: All seven findings are fixed inside figures/, with one synchronizing edit to the description. The three critical FIG. 3 items: the invented poppet stem is gone, the flush poppet now being a plain closure element shown schematically adjacent the left end of the sleeve, at the position the follower pin reaches at the end of the return stroke, held open by that pin and connected to the flush bypass by a plain passage, with target 58 reading "the plain closure element held open by the follower pin"; the annular rinse channel is now the clear gap between the sleeve bands and the outer housing bands, supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet end at the left, with no closure of either end indicated, so no undisclosed flow boundary is asserted; and the two rinse openings are placed only at the axial station of the concentrate port and at that of the outlet-valve passage, with their relationship to the sealing lands and any direction of discharge expressly not indicated, which removes both the untraced station and the blocked jet. The major item: FIG. 1's clear gap now runs along the length of the sleeve and the unnumbered ring stands clear of the housing wall so the gap continues past it, so the collar no longer occupies the rinse annulus and the path from the inlet end to the rinse openings and the flush bypass is continuous. The three minor items: the flush bypass in FIG. 3 is now expressly downstream of the dose chamber and of the outlet-valve passage, matching claims 1 and 13; FIG. 4 names the left end, the end from which the piston rod enters, as the stepped end, with the shallow curved edge indicating the round section moved to the right end and target 46 reading "one of the three stepped faces at the left end of the collar"; and FIG. 1's window panel is now an unhatched panel of simple outline expressly shown schematically. The description edit is confined to the FIG. 3 recitation sentence, which now lists the two radial rinse openings 62 and the concentrate port 22 without stating that the figure shows a direction of discharge; the disclosed direction across the concentrate port and the one-way outlet valve remains in the following paragraph, in the summary and in claims 2 and 15. Every sheet's numeral list is unchanged, and the four briefs are 2763, 2777, 2789 and 2761 characters.
reasoning: The poppet fix was the one with real consequences for the drawing's coherence. A stem running from the bypass at the right to the pin outside the sleeve's left end would have to cross the sealed bore and the two-land piston, so the linkage could not exist in the depicted structure. Putting the closure element where the pin actually arrives at the end of the return stroke keeps the disclosed relationship, that the pin opens a normally closed poppet connected to the flush bypass, without inventing an actuating member or a route for it.

The rinse channel and the FIG. 1 ring had to be fixed together. Closing the channel's right end while the collar blocked the annulus at the left left the channel with neither a supply nor a discharge, which contradicts the description, the summary and claim 1. Leaving both ends unstated and standing the ring clear of the housing wall gives a continuous annulus from the inlet end through the rinse openings to the flush bypass, and it keeps both disclosed facts true at once: the collar surrounds the sleeve inside the housing, where a window can read it, and the rinse channel lies between the sleeve and the housing.

For the rinse openings I removed the axial station relative to the lands rather than moving it again. Two earlier passes moved that opening to cure a blocked path, and each new station was itself untraced. The source gives the number of openings and the surfaces they are directed across, nothing more, so stating only the two stations that are disclosed by reference to the port and the valve, and declining to fix any relationship to the lands or any jet direction, is the version that stays inside the disclosure.

The flush bypass wording mattered because the figure brief was contradicting the claim it has to support: claims 1 and 13 require the bypass to open downstream of the dose chamber, and the brief had it leading from the bore. Naming it downstream of the dose chamber and of the outlet-valve passage aligns the sheet with the claim without adding structure.

Naming the stepped end of the collar in FIG. 4 forced a second change in the same brief, since the first bullet had closed the left end with the curved edge that indicates the round section. I moved that edge to the right end rather than leave two incompatible statements about the left end, and updated target 46 to name the left end so the leader cannot land on the wrong end face.

The description edit was not requested, but the FIG. 3 recitation had asserted that the figure shows one rinse opening directed across the concentrate port, which is exactly what the brief now declines to indicate. Rather than reintroduce the direction into the drawing, I removed the claim about what the figure shows and left the disclosed direction where it belongs, in the body text and the dependent claims. Every numeral recited for the sheet is still recited, so the sheet list, the target list and the description paragraph still agree.

Length had to be managed again, since the poppet fix added a bullet. The space came from redundant phrasing in the same briefs, such as repeating 'shown schematically' twice in one sentence and naming the view twice in one target, not from geometry, relationships or the hedges that cure the untraced items.

input.summary: All three findings are fixed, and all three fixes are confined to the figure briefs; no application text needed to change. FIG. 4 no longer assigns the three axial stop faces to a named end of the collar and no longer states what abuts them: one end of the collar is stepped, its end face divided into three faces at three different axial positions shown schematically, with the arrangement order and the abutting part expressly not indicated. Target 46 follows, reading "one of the three stepped faces at the stepped end of the collar", and the shallow curved edge that indicates the round section is now placed at the end opposite the stepped end, so the brief names no absolute end for the stop faces while still describing a single coherent body. FIG. 3's rinse openings are now placed one adjacent the concentrate port and one adjacent the outlet-valve passage, each opening into the bore at a station clear of the sealing lands in the position shown, with any direction of discharge not indicated; that removes both the blocked path, since no opening now sits at the station the upstream sealing land covers, and the self-contradiction between a fixed station and a disclaimer about the lands. FIG. 1's inlet is now a short tubular stub projecting from the left end of the housing and opening into the interior, shown schematically, with the radial offset and its relation to the end cap and the shaft deleted; the two stub targets were reworded to name the stub at the left end and the stub at the right end so they no longer describe the stubs as axial after that change. The outlet sentence, the numeral table, the drawing descriptions, the detailed description and the claims are untouched, every sheet's numeral list is unchanged, and all four briefs remain under the 2800 character cap at 2742, 2777, 2788 and 2722 characters.
reasoning: All three findings were untraced statements rather than missing structure, so each was cured by deletion plus an express statement that the point is not indicated.
