1	# Previous review - verdict: fail
2	
3	Ledger result: the disclosure and the single USER passage in conversation.md are identical in content, and the application text traces cleanly. Every limitation of claims 1-20, every one of the 29 numerals (10-66), and every structure, relationship, sequence, result and variant in 06-summary and 08-detailed-description maps to an affirmative source passage: cylindrical housing with inlet/outlet at opposite axial ends; fixed metering sleeve defining a cylindrical dose chamber, radial concentrate port, carrier-liquid admission port and flush bypass opening downstream of the dose chamber; piston with two axially spaced sealing lands joined by a reduced-diameter waist; fill-position waist connection and land isolation; closure of the concentrate port before the downstream land uncovers the admission port; carrier liquid entering behind the measured volume and expulsion through the one-way outlet valve into the main flow; geometric (non-command) separation from the ordering of port edges and lands; flexible lip on the upstream land wiping the dose-chamber wall first; follower pin on the piston rod opening the normally closed flush poppet near the end of the return stroke; annular rinse channel between sleeve and housing; two radial rinse openings directed across the concentrate port and the one-way outlet valve; flush bypass to the outlet; poppet closing before the waist reconnects the concentrate port; index collar with helical cam groove indexed one increment per full stroke; three selectable axial stop faces setting three dose volumes by limiting travel; spring-biased detent in one of three recesses; transparent window showing one of three collar numerals without electronics; cartridge containing piston, sleeve, outlet valve and poppet, retained by a threaded end cap and withdrawable without disturbing the line connections; apparatus and method claims over the ordered isolation-metering-discharge-rinse sequence. Derived statements I accepted as inferences compelled by the source rather than additions: the admission port lying axially downstream of the concentrate port, the upstream land being the land that shuts the concentrate port on the discharge stroke, axial withdrawal of the cartridge, and the rinse channel drawing its carrier liquid from the inlet (the only carrier source recited). Claim 1's broadening of "two radial rinse openings" to "at least one rinse opening" (species in claim 2) and claim 12's cylindrical-housing fallback are supported. Brief-mandated terminology (metering sleeve, dose chamber, flush bypass, index collar, flush poppet, annular rinse channel) is preserved; the renaming of the collar's "reference numerals" to "dose setting numerals 54" is the same feature under a non-conflicting label. Formalities match the brief: title verbatim, "Not applicable." in both cross-reference and government-support sections, no means-plus-function language, apparatus plus method classes, single-paragraph abstract of about 143 words. Internal-text checks: each numeral denotes exactly one part and appears in numerals.md and on at least one figure; the per-figure numeral lists in 08-detailed-description (FIG. 1: 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 52, 64, 66; FIG. 2: 18, 20, 22, 24, 30, 32, 34, 38; FIG. 3: 22, 26, 28, 44, 56, 58, 60, 62; FIG. 4: 36, 40, 42, 44, 46, 48, 50, 54) match the briefs exactly; the four captions in 07-drawings match the four briefs; no named section-line designation is used anywhere, so none can mismatch; no drafting note, placeholder, open question, instruction, unresolved alternative or internal comment remains in any draft or figure file; the Background contains only prior-art/field characterisation and no reference citations, which a later review traces. Shape-neutral depiction conventions are correctly confined to the figure briefs (generic window panel, plain closure elements for the one-way valve and poppet, lip "without flare direction", cam groove with hand and pitch not indicated, stop faces with circumferential order and abutting part not indicated, rinse-opening discharge direction not indicated), and no draft text says "by way of example" or otherwise broadens an embodiment to justify a renderer's choice. Three defects remain, all in the figure briefs. First and most serious, FIG-2 verbalizes, for the fill position, an open flow path from the carrier-liquid gap outside the sleeve into the dose chamber at the very station where the concentrate port is shown open to that chamber; the source never describes the rinse openings' state in the fill position and affirmatively states the opposite relationship, and the description and Summary recite that no piston position places the concentrate source in communication with the carrier-liquid path. Second, FIG-4 treats two parts lying inside the collar inconsistently, drawing the tube as a hidden broken outline but the piston rod as a plain solid shaft over the collar. Third, FIG-3 declares the entire annular gap clear in a region where FIG-1 and FIG-4 place the index collar, without saying the collar is omitted. Each fix below is minimal and confined to the figure brief; none adds a speculative shape or optional embodiment to the application text. I did not inspect rendered images, prior_art contents, or patentability, and the art supplied may be incomplete.
4	
5	## Mechanical checks that did not pass
6	
7	- **Source fidelity is clean before rendering** (fail): Ledger result: the disclosure and the single USER passage in conversation.md are identical in content, and the application text traces cleanly. Every limitation of claims 1-20, every one of the 29 numerals (10-66), and every structure, relationship, sequence, result and variant in 06-summary and 08-detailed-description maps to an affirmative source passage: cylindrical housing with inlet/outlet at opposite axial ends; fixed metering sleeve defining a cylindrical dose chamber, radial concentrate port, carrier-liquid admission port and flush bypass opening downstream of the dose chamber; piston with two axially spaced sealing lands joined by a reduced-diameter waist; fill-position waist connection and land isolation; closure of the concentrate port before the downstream land uncovers the admission port; carrier liquid entering behind the measured volume and expulsion through the one-way outlet valve into the main flow; geometric (non-command) separation from the ordering of port edges and lands; flexible lip on the upstream land wiping the dose-chamber wall first; follower pin on the piston rod opening the normally closed flush poppet near the end of the return stroke; annular rinse channel between sleeve and housing; two radial rinse openings directed across the concentrate port and the one-way outlet valve; flush bypass to the outlet; poppet closing before the waist reconnects the concentrate port; index collar with helical cam groove indexed one increment per full stroke; three selectable axial stop faces setting three dose volumes by limiting travel; spring-biased detent in one of three recesses; transparent window showing one of three collar numerals without electronics; cartridge containing piston, sleeve, outlet valve and poppet, retained by a threaded end cap and withdrawable without disturbing the line connections; apparatus and method claims over the ordered isolation-metering-discharge-rinse sequence. Derived statements I accepted as inferences compelled by
8	  - FIG. 2 verbalizes an open fill-position flow path from the carrier-liquid gap into the dose chamber at the open concentrate port
9	  - FIG. 4 draws two parts lying inside the index collar under conflicting line conventions
10	  - FIG. 3 shows the annular gap clear in the region where FIG. 1 and FIG. 4 place the index collar, without stating that the collar is omitted
11	
12	## Reviewer findings
13	
14	- **[critical] FIG. 2 verbalizes an open fill-position flow path from the carrier-liquid gap into the dose chamber at the open concentrate port** (figures/FIG-2.md, Geometry bullet 8 (line 14), read with Geometry bullet 5 (line 11) and bullet 2 (line 8); cf. figures/) - FIG. 2 is the fill-position view. Its bullet 8 states affirmatively that unnumbered lower-band openings connect the gap outside the sleeve to the dose chamber, and locates the first of them "immediately right of the upstream sealing land", i.e. within the waist span, directly beneath the concentrate port that the same brief shows open into the space above the waist. FIG-3 and the description identify that same gap as the annular rinse channel supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet. Taken together the briefs therefore depict, at the fill position, a continuous open path from the carrier-liquid supply through the sleeve wall into the dose chamber, past the waist and out through the open concentrate port to the concentrate source. That is exactly the communication the description and Summary say never exists, and the source states the opposite relationship. The source describes the rinse openings only as part of the flush path taken during the return stroke while the flush poppet is held open; it never says the rinse openings stand open to the dose chamber in the fill position, and it never describes their station relative to the sealing lands in that position. The untraced element is the fill-position open-connection statement (a flow-path and relative-location assertion), not the existence of the rinse openings, which is disclosed.
15	  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-2.md, replace the bullet at line 14 with the break-off convention the same brief already uses for the carrier-liquid admission port, so the fill-position view makes no assertion about that path: "- Further openings pass through the lower sleeve band immediately right of the upstream sealing land and beneath the outlet-valve passage, each with its outer mouth broken off at a conventional break line within the lower sleeve band, so that what they open into is not indicated, and a further passage leads up through the upper sleeve band right of the outlet-valve passage; these are unnumbered." Make no change to draft/06-summary.md, draft/08-detailed-description.md, draft/09-claims.md or figures/FIG-3.md.
16	- **[minor] FIG. 4 draws two parts lying inside the index collar under conflicting line conventions** (figures/FIG-4.md, Geometry bullets 1 and 3 (lines 7 and 9) and Targets for 36 and 44 (lines 19 and 22)) - FIG. 4 is a side view, not a section. The brief expressly treats the tube (the metering sleeve) that lies inside the collar as a hidden feature drawn in broken line, but specifies the piston rod, which lies inside the same collar over the length drawn, as a plain solid shaft ending on the collar surface, with the follower pin projecting radially from its end. Two hidden items in the same view are therefore given opposite line treatments, so the specification of the view is internally inconsistent and, as written, shows a solid shaft crossing an unbroken collar surface.
17	  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-4.md, replace the bullet at line 9 with: "- A piston rod is drawn as a plain horizontal shaft entering the view from the left on the collar axis, its length lying within the collar drawn as a hidden outline in broken line in the same manner as the tube, and ending within the left part of the collar. A short follower pin projects radially from the end of the shaft, its hidden length drawn in broken line and its outer end sitting within the narrow band of the groove." Leave the Targets and all draft text unchanged.
18	- **[minor] FIG. 3 shows the annular gap clear in the region where FIG. 1 and FIG. 4 place the index collar, without stating that the collar is omitted** (figures/FIG-3.md, View line (line 3) and Geometry bullets 2 and 3 (lines 8 and 9); cf. figures/FIG-1.md Geometry bullet ) - FIG. 1 places a ring, identified as the index collar, surrounding the sleeve over the left portion of its length inside the gap between the sleeve and the housing, and FIG. 4 shows the follower pin engaged in that collar's cam groove where the rod passes beyond the sleeve's left end. FIG. 3 is an enlarged section of the same metering portion that includes the sleeve's left end and the projecting pin, yet it declares the whole gap between the sleeve bands and the outer bands to be clear and says no closure of either end is indicated, showing no collar in the region the other two views occupy. The same part is thus present in one view of a region and absent in another with no statement of omission, which a reader would take as a structural difference.
19	  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-3.md, extend the View line to read: "View: enlarged longitudinal section of the metering portion of FIG. 1 during the return stroke, axis horizontal, with the flush poppet held open. The index collar and the parts it carries are omitted from this view for clarity. All line work lies well inside the drawing area." Add no numerals and change no draft text.
20	
21	Fix every listed item before returning. If an advisory is a false positive, make
22	the wording or figure specification unambiguous enough that the check passes.

content.text: All three findings are fixed; the four briefs are 2742, 2753, 2794 and 2788 characters, under the cap.

input.summary: All three findings are fixed, and all three fixes stay inside figures/; no application text changed. In FIG. 2 the fill-position view no longer asserts an open path from the carrier-liquid gap into the dose chamber: the two lower openings now have their outer mouths broken off at a conventional break line within the band, so what they open into is not indicated, which is the same convention the brief already uses for the carrier-liquid admission port. In FIG. 4 the piston rod and the follower pin are now treated like the tube they lie inside, the rod's length within the collar and the pin's hidden length being drawn as hidden outlines in broken line, so one side view no longer mixes two line conventions for parts behind the same surface. In FIG. 3 the view line now states that the index collar and the parts it carries are omitted from that view for clarity, so the clear annulus in FIG. 3 no longer reads as a structural difference from the ring shown in FIG. 1 and the collar shown in FIG. 4. Adding those passages pushed all three briefs over the 2800 character cap, so I recovered the space from redundant phrasing in the same files: repeated "sleeve band" and "shown schematically" qualifiers, a restated reference to the recess broken into the outline, "This is the ..." constructions folded into colons, and two targets that named a band the sheet has only one of. Every sheet's numeral list, the four captions in the Brief Description, the numeral table, the detailed description and the claims are unchanged, and the four briefs now measure 2742, 2753, 2794 and 2788 characters.
reasoning: The FIG. 2 item was the one that mattered to the invention. As written the fill-position sheet showed carrier liquid able to reach the dose chamber at the same station where the concentrate port stood open to it, which is exactly the communication the description, the summary and claim 1 say the land and port geometry prevents. Breaking off the outer mouths leaves the openings on the sheet, since they are disclosed, while the figure stops asserting anything about the path they belong to in a position the source never describes them in.

I used the break-off convention rather than moving the openings again. Their axial station has already been moved twice in earlier passes to cure a blocked or open path, and each new station was itself untraced; withdrawing the flow-boundary assertion is the fix that does not invent a third position.

The FIG. 4 fix is a line-convention correction, not a geometry change. A side view has to treat everything behind the collar surface the same way, so the rod and the pin now follow the tube into broken line. No affirmative USER passage identifies the closing land or the axial direction of the discharge stroke. The source names the downstream land only in connection with uncovering the carrier-liquid admission port. Both directions are geometrically arrangeable while still satisfying the disclosed close-before-uncover ordering (with the concentrate port lying at the waist between the lands, either land can be the one that arrives at it, depending on the travel direction the source never states), so this is a drafted choice rather than a necessary consequence. This is substantive: it is a contact/seal topology statement about a functional port and it fixes the direction of the metering stroke.

For a flow boundary and check-valve seat this relative axial location is substantive, not a depiction convention: it determines whether the admitted carrier liquid can reach the valve at all (see the related internal-logic finding).

The brief places one rinse opening immediately right of the upstream sealing land, i.e. inside the waist region, and the other beneath the outlet-valve passage, in each case not covered by a land. The description states that the annular rinse channel is supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet. Background prior-art characterizations were not traced to the inventor, as instructed.

tool_use_result.originalFile:
In the following description, the terms upstream and downstream refer to the direction of travel of the carrier liquid from the inlet toward the outlet, and the terms axial and radial refer to the axis along which the piston slides.

FIG. 1 shows an inline liquid metering valve 10 having a cylindrical housing 12 with an inlet 14 at one axial end and an outlet 16 at the opposite axial end, a metering sleeve 18 fixed within the housing 12, a cartridge 64 retained in the housing 12 by a threaded end cap 66, and a transparent window 52 in the housing 12.

The inline liquid metering valve 10 is connected in a line that already carries a flowing carrier liquid. Carrier liquid enters at the inlet 14, passes along the housing 12, and leaves at the outlet 16. That flow is the main flow into which each dose of concentrate is delivered, and it is also the flow that rinses the valve. The metering sleeve 18 is spaced radially inward from the inner surface of the housing 12.

FIG. 2 shows the metering sleeve 18 defining a dose chamber 20, a concentrate port 22 opening into the dose chamber 20 and a carrier-liquid admission port 24 opening into the dose chamber 20. FIG. 2 further shows an upstream sealing land 30 and a downstream sealing land 32 joined by a reduced-diameter waist 34 in the fill position, and a one-way outlet valve 38.

The dose chamber 20 is cylindrical. The concentrate port 22 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and is connected in use to a concentrate source. The carrier-liquid admission port 24 passes through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 at an axial position downstream of the concentrate port 22, and admits carrier liquid to the dose chamber 20. The metering sleeve 18 further defines a flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20.

A piston 28 is axially slidable in the dose chamber 20 between a fill position and a discharge position. The upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 are axially spaced from one another on the piston 28 and are joined by the reduced-diameter waist 34. Each sealing land bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20, while the waist 34 stands clear of that wall. A piston rod 36 extends from the piston 28 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 and is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke. The one-way outlet valve 38 is arranged to pass liquid from the dose chamber 20 toward the outlet 16 and to prevent flow in the opposite direction.

In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume of concentrate, the extent of which is fixed by the travel then permitted to the piston 28. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 while the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.

Movement of the piston 28 toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port 22 before the downstream sealing land 32 uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port 24. The upstream sealing land 30 arrives at the concentrate port 22 and shuts it while the downstream sealing land 32 is still overlying the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Only after that has happened does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.

The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every position of the piston 28 at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18. It does not depend on the order in which external commands are given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of a separately actuated shut-off element. A slow stroke, an interrupted stroke, or a stroke reversed part way through cannot open both ports at once, because the port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens.

FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, a follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62, the concentrate port 22, and the flush bypass 26. The follower pin 44 is carried by the piston rod 36.

The flexible lip 56 is carried on the upstream sealing land 30 and bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20. As the return stroke begins, the flexible lip 56 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20.

The annular rinse channel 60 lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve 18 and an inner surface of the housing 12, and is supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet 14. The two radial rinse openings 62 pass through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and connect the annular rinse channel 60 to the dose chamber 20. One of the two radial rinse openings 62 is directed across the concentrate port 22 and the other is directed across the one-way outlet valve 38.

The flush poppet 58 is normally closed and is connected to the flush bypass 26. Near the end of the return stroke, the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows from the inlet 14 through the annular rinse channel 60, through the two radial rinse openings 62 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 to the outlet 16. The rinse liquid therefore reaches the outlet 16, as the dose does, and is carried away in the main flow.

The flush poppet 58 closes before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. The concentrate port 22 is closed throughout the interval in which the annular rinse channel 60 communicates with the flush bypass 26. Only when the flush poppet 58 has closed does the continuing return of the piston 28 bring the waist 34 back into register with the concentrate port 22, at which point the dose chamber 20 is charged again for the next dose.

Because the follower pin 44 that opens the flush poppet 58 is carried by the piston rod 36, the rinse occurs once for every dose and at the same point in every cycle. It is not a separate operation, it needs no command, and it cannot be omitted while the valve continues to be used. The rinse also occurs while the concentrate port 22 is shut and after the wall of the dose chamber 20 has been wiped.

FIG. 4 shows an index collar 40 having a helical cam groove 42 engaged by the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36, three selectable axial stop faces 46, a spring-biased detent 48 engaging one of three detent recesses 50, and three dose setting numerals 54.

The index collar 40 surrounds the metering sleeve 18. Each full stroke of the piston 28 draws the follower pin 44 along the helical cam groove 42 and turns the index collar 40 by one increment, so that the index collar 40 advances by itself as the valve is used and needs no separate indexing drive.

The three axial stop faces 46 are carried by the index collar 40 at different axial positions. The stop face presented by the current increment of rotation limits the travel of the piston 28 and thereby sets the dose volume, so that the three axial stop faces 46 correspond to three dose volumes. The spring-biased detent 48 engages one of the three detent recesses 50 to retain the selected setting until the index collar 40 is next indexed.

The transparent window 52 in the housing 12 shows one of the three dose setting numerals 54 carried by the index collar 40. The dose setting numeral presented at the transparent window 52 is the one associated with the axial stop face then limiting the travel of the piston 28, so that the dose setting is mechanically visible without electronics. What is seen at the transparent window 52 is the position of the index collar 40 itself.

The cartridge 64 contains the piston 28, the metering sleeve 18, the one-way outlet valve 38 and the flush poppet 58, and is removable from the housing 12 as a unit. Removing the threaded end cap 66 withdraws the cartridge 64 from the housing 12 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 without disturbing the connections at the inlet 14 and the outlet 16, so that the cartridge 64 is replaced as a unit while the housing 12 remains in the line.

In use, carrier liquid flows through the housing 12 from the inlet 14 to the outlet 16. With the piston 28 in the fill position, concentrate is admitted through the concentrate port 22 and past the waist 34 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume, the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolating the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. The piston 28 is then advanced toward the discharge position so as to close the concentrate port 22 and thereafter to uncover the carrier-liquid admission port 24 with the downstream sealing land 32. Carrier liquid is admitted through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16. The extent of the travel available to the piston 28, and therefore the measured volume, is fixed by the selected one of the three axial stop faces 46.

The piston 28 is then returned toward the fill position. During the return, the flexible lip 56 on the upstream sealing land 30 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20, and the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36 opens the normally closed flush poppet 58. In the following description, the terms upstream and downstream refer to the direction of travel of the carrier liquid from the inlet toward the outlet, and the terms axial and radial refer to the axis along which the piston slides.

FIG. 1 shows an inline liquid metering valve 10 having a cylindrical housing 12 with an inlet 14 at one axial end and an outlet 16 at the opposite axial end, a metering sleeve 18 fixed within the housing 12, a cartridge 64 retained in the housing 12 by a threaded end cap 66, and a transparent window 52 in the housing 12.

The inline liquid metering valve 10 is connected in a line that already carries a flowing carrier liquid. Carrier liquid enters at the inlet 14, passes along the housing 12, and leaves at the outlet 16. That flow is the main flow into which each dose of concentrate is delivered, and it is also the flow that rinses the valve. The metering sleeve 18 is spaced radially inward from the inner surface of the housing 12.

FIG. 2 shows the metering sleeve 18 defining a dose chamber 20, a concentrate port 22 opening into the dose chamber 20 and a carrier-liquid admission port 24 opening into the dose chamber 20. FIG. 2 further shows an upstream sealing land 30 and a downstream sealing land 32 joined by a reduced-diameter waist 34 in the fill position, and a one-way outlet valve 38.

The dose chamber 20 is cylindrical. The concentrate port 22 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and is connected in use to a concentrate source. The carrier-liquid admission port 24 passes through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 at an axial position downstream of the concentrate port 22, and admits carrier liquid to the dose chamber 20. The metering sleeve 18 further defines a flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20.

A piston 28 is axially slidable in the dose chamber 20 between a fill position and a discharge position. The upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 are axially spaced from one another on the piston 28 and are joined by the reduced-diameter waist 34. Each sealing land bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20, while the waist 34 stands clear of that wall. A piston rod 36 extends from the piston 28 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 and is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke. The one-way outlet valve 38 is arranged to pass liquid from the dose chamber 20 toward the outlet 16 and to prevent flow in the opposite direction.

In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume of concentrate, the extent of which is fixed by the travel then permitted to the piston 28. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 while the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.

Movement of the piston 28 toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port 22 before the downstream sealing land 32 uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Only after the concentrate port 22 has been closed does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.

The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every position of the piston 28 at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18. It does not depend on the order in which external commands are given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of a separately actuated shut-off element. A slow stroke, an interrupted stroke, or a stroke reversed part way through cannot open both ports at once, because the port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens.

FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, a follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62, the concentrate port 22, and the flush bypass 26. The follower pin 44 is carried by the piston rod 36.

The flexible lip 56 is carried on the upstream sealing land 30 and bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20. As the return stroke begins, the flexible lip 56 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20.

The annular rinse channel 60 lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve 18 and an inner surface of the housing 12, and is supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet 14. The two radial rinse openings 62 pass through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and connect the annular rinse channel 60 to the dose chamber 20. One of the two radial rinse openings 62 is directed across the concentrate port 22 and the other is directed across the one-way outlet valve 38.

The flush poppet 58 is normally closed and is connected to the flush bypass 26. Near the end of the return stroke, the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows from the inlet 14 through the annular rinse channel 60, through the two radial rinse openings 62 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 to the outlet 16. The rinse liquid therefore reaches the outlet 16, as the dose does, and is carried away in the main flow.

The flush poppet 58 closes before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. The concentrate port 22 is closed throughout the interval in which the annular rinse channel 60 communicates with the flush bypass 26. Only when the flush poppet 58 has closed does the continuing return of the piston 28 bring the waist 34 back into register with the concentrate port 22, at which point the dose chamber 20 is charged again for the next dose.

Because the follower pin 44 that opens the flush poppet 58 is carried by the piston rod 36, the rinse occurs once for every dose and at the same point in every cycle. It is not a separate operation, it needs no command, and it cannot be omitted while the valve continues to be used. The rinse also occurs while the concentrate port 22 is shut and after the wall of the dose chamber 20 has been wiped.

FIG. 4 shows an index collar 40 having a helical cam groove 42 engaged by the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36, three selectable axial stop faces 46, a spring-biased detent 48 engaging one of three detent recesses 50, and three dose setting numerals 54.

The index collar 40 surrounds the metering sleeve 18. Each full stroke of the piston 28 draws the follower pin 44 along the helical cam groove 42 and turns the index collar 40 by one increment, so that the index collar 40 advances by itself as the valve is used and needs no separate indexing drive.

The three axial stop faces 46 are carried by the index collar 40 at different axial positions. The stop face presented by the current increment of rotation limits the travel of the piston 28 and thereby sets the dose volume, so that the three axial stop faces 46 correspond to three dose volumes. The spring-biased detent 48 engages one of the three detent recesses 50 to retain the selected setting until the index collar 40 is next indexed.

The transparent window 52 in the housing 12 shows one of the three dose setting numerals 54 carried by the index collar 40. The dose setting numeral presented at the transparent window 52 is the one associated with the axial stop face then limiting the travel of the piston 28, so that the dose setting is mechanically visible without electronics. What is seen at the transparent window 52 is the position of the index collar 40 itself.

The cartridge 64 contains the piston 28, the metering sleeve 18, the one-way outlet valve 38 and the flush poppet 58, and is removable from the housing 12 as a unit. Removing the threaded end cap 66 withdraws the cartridge 64 from the housing 12 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 without disturbing the connections at the inlet 14 and the outlet 16, so that the cartridge 64 is replaced as a unit while the housing 12 remains in the line.

In use, carrier liquid flows through the housing 12 from the inlet 14 to the outlet 16. With the piston 28 in the fill position, concentrate is admitted through the concentrate port 22 and past the waist 34 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume, the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolating the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. The piston 28 is then advanced toward the discharge position so as to close the concentrate port 22 and thereafter to uncover the carrier-liquid admission port 24 with the downstream sealing land 32. Carrier liquid is admitted through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16. The extent of the travel available to the piston 28, and therefore the measured volume, is fixed by the selected one of the three axial stop faces 46.

The piston 28 is then returned toward the fill position. During the return, the flexible lip 56 on the upstream sealing land 30 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20, and the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36 opens the normally closed flush poppet 58. Carrier liquid flows through the annular rinse channel 60 between the metering sleeve 18 and the housing 12, through the two radial rinse openings 62 in the metering sleeve 18 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20 to the outlet 16. The flush poppet 58 is closed before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. Over the same full stroke, the follower pin 44 travelling in the helical cam groove 42 turns the index collar 40 by one increment, the spring-biased detent 48 enters the next of the three detent recesses 50, and the dose setting numeral then presented at the transparent window 52 shows the setting that will govern the next dose. The valve is thereby left charged, rinsed and set, ready for the following cycle.

The foregoing description sets out embodiments of the invention. A skilled reader may make changes of detail to the described embodiments without departing from the scope of the claims that follow.

In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume of concentrate, the extent of which is fixed by the travel then permitted to the piston 28. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 while the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.

Movement of the piston 28 toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port 22 before the downstream sealing land 32 uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Only after the concentrate port 22 has been closed does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.

The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every position of the piston 28 at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18. It does not depend on the order in which external commands are given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of a separately actuated shut-off element. The port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens.

FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, a follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62, the concentrate port 22, and the flush bypass 26. The follower pin 44 is carried by the piston rod 36.

input.summary: All nine findings are fixed. In the detailed description, the sentence assigning closure of the concentrate port to the upstream sealing land is gone, the passage now reading that only after the concentrate port has been closed does continued travel carry the downstream sealing land clear of the carrier-liquid admission port, and the enumerated slow, interrupted and part-way-reversed stroke conditions are gone, leaving the general statement that the port which must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens. In FIG. 3 the concentrate port is covered by the piston rather than by the left portion, the one-way outlet valve passage no longer carries a position relative to the piston, and the flush bypass is located only downstream of the dose chamber. In FIG. 2 the outlet valve passage no longer carries a position relative to the downstream sealing land, the rinse openings are removed from the fill-position view in favour of a single further opening whose outer mouth is broken off so that what it opens into is not indicated, and the clause placing a further passage right of the outlet-valve passage is deleted; the two rinse openings remain shown and numbered 62 in FIG. 3, at the return-stroke position where the source requires them to be open. Both FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 now close their geometry with a statement that the band in which each port, opening and passage is drawn is a section-plane convention only and that no circumferential relationship between them is intended. In FIG. 1 the inlet stub is offset from the axis and clear of the end cap ring and of the shaft, so the three features at that end no longer read as occupying the same place. In FIG. 4 the right end of the collar, through which the unnumbered tube enters, carries the shallow curved edge and the left end is stepped, with target 46 naming the left end, while the sentence declining to indicate the circumferential arrangement and the abutting part is retained. Space for the added sentences came from redundant phrasing in the same briefs; the numeral table, the per-sheet numeral lists, the Brief Description captions and the claims are unchanged, and the four briefs measure 2793, 2683, 2785 and 2787 characters.
reasoning: The two description edits were deletions of drafted inference. Removing the sentence that named the upstream land as the one shutting the concentrate port also removes the implied direction of the metering stroke, and with it the chain that made the axial ordering read as putting the downstream land between the admission port and the outlet valve. The remaining text recites only the disclosed sequence: concentrate port closed before the admission port is uncovered, then carrier liquid entering behind the measured volume and expelling it through the one-way outlet valve.

The same deletion resolves the expulsion-path contradiction without touching claim 1 or claim 5. Claim 5 recites the axial positioning of the land faces relative to the port edges in functional terms and never names which land arrives at which port, so nothing in the claims had to move once the description stopped fixing the choice.

Dropping the relative axial position of the outlet valve from both briefs was the fix that mattered most for coherence, because that position, not the disclosure, was what put a sealing land between the admitted carrier liquid and the valve it must reach. Stating only that the passage leads from the dose chamber up through the band toward the outlet keeps the disclosed function and leaves the ordering unasserted.

For the fill-position sheet I removed the rinse openings rather than moving them yet again. Their station has been relocated in three earlier passes, and each new station either blocked the flush path or opened the carrier side to the concentrate port. FIG. 3 is the view the source ties them to, since that is the position at which the poppet is held open, so the openings stay numbered there and FIG. 2 makes no assertion about them at all.

The circumferential convention sentence goes in the briefs only. A longitudinal section has to draw each port in one wall band, so the choice is forced by the view rather than disclosed, and the application text contains no orientation language at all. Saying so inside the brief keeps the forced choice from reading as an assertion that the ports are opposed, without putting any orientation into the specification.

On FIG. 1 I restored the inlet stub's offset, which an earlier pass had removed as untraced, because the end cap and the rod exit are both at that end and a renderer reading the bullet without the offset would stack all three in one place. The offset is a placement convention inside the brief; the description continues to recite only an inlet at one axial end.

On FIG. 4 the stepped end had to be named absolutely for numeral 46 to have a determinate target, and naming the right end as the one the tube enters supplies the other end at the same time. What stays unstated is the part the stop faces abut and their circumferential order, which is where the source is silent.

Every added sentence cost characters against the 2800 cap, so I trimmed wording that repeats what the brief already establishes: duplicated band names, a second 'shown schematically' in the same bullet, and two leader descriptions that specified more of the endpoint than was needed to identify the part.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so the Background carries no citations and none may be invented; the brief records that no prior-art search was run, so the art behind this draft may be incomplete and the independent claims should be re-tested against any later search. The claimed combination is unchanged. Claim 1 still rests on the axial ordering of the land faces and the port edges, which closes the concentrate port before the downstream land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port so that separation is enforced by the moving geometry rather than by command sequencing, and on the flush poppet opened by the follower pin carried by the piston rod during the return stroke and closed before the waist reconnects the concentrate port. The description still explains why that ordering solves the stated problem, that separation does not depend on the order in which external commands arrive, on any control signal, or on a separately actuated shut-off element, and that the port which must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other opens. What went was the drafted choice of which land arrives first and the enumerated stroke conditions, neither of which the claims rely on. Removing the rinse openings from the fill-position sheet also keeps the drawings from depicting the very communication the specification says the geometry prevents, which is the ground a later argument on that feature would stand on.

structured_output.summary: All nine findings are fixed. In the detailed description, the sentence assigning closure of the concentrate port to the upstream sealing land is gone, the passage now reading that only after the concentrate port has been closed does continued travel carry the downstream sealing land clear of the carrier-liquid admission port, and the enumerated slow, interrupted and part-way-reversed stroke conditions are gone, leaving the general statement that the port which must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens. In FIG. 3 the concentrate port is covered by the piston rather than by the left portion, the one-way outlet valve passage no longer carries a position relative to the piston, and the flush bypass is located only downstream of the dose chamber. In FIG. 2 the outlet valve passage no longer carries a position relative to the downstream sealing land, the rinse openings are removed from the fill-position view in favour of a single further opening whose outer mouth is broken off so that what it opens into is not indicated, and the clause placing a further passage right of the outlet-valve passage is deleted; the two rinse openings remain shown and numbered 62 in FIG. 3, at the return-stroke position where the source requires them to be open. Both FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 now close their geometry with a statement that the band in which each port, opening and passage is drawn is a section-plane convention only and that no circumferential relationship between them is intended. In FIG. 1 the inlet stub is offset from the axis and clear of the end cap ring and of the shaft, so the three features at that end no longer read as occupying the same place. In FIG. 4 the right end of the collar, through which the unnumbered tube enters, carries the shallow curved edge and the left end is stepped, with target 46 naming the left end, while the sentence declining to indicate the circumferential arrangement and the abutting part is retained. Space for the added sentences came from redundant phrasing in the same briefs; the numeral table, the per-sheet numeral lists, the Brief Description captions and the claims are unchanged, and the four briefs measure 2793, 2683, 2785 and 2787 characters.
reasoning: The two description edits were deletions of drafted inference. Removing the sentence that named the upstream land as the one shutting the concentrate port also removes the implied direction of the metering stroke, and with it the chain that made the axial ordering read as putting the downstream land between the admission port and the outlet valve. The remaining text recites only the disclosed sequence: concentrate port closed before the admission port is uncovered, then carrier liquid entering behind the measured volume and expelling it through the one-way outlet valve.

The same deletion resolves the expulsion-path contradiction without touching claim 1 or claim 5. Claim 5 recites the axial positioning of the land faces relative to the port edges in functional terms and never names which land arrives at which port, so nothing in the claims had to move once the description stopped fixing the choice.

Dropping the relative axial position of the outlet valve from both briefs was the fix that mattered most for coherence, because that position, not the disclosure, was what put a sealing land between the admitted carrier liquid and the valve it must reach. Stating only that the passage leads from the dose chamber up through the band toward the outlet keeps the disclosed function and leaves the ordering unasserted.

For the fill-position sheet I removed the rinse openings rather than moving them yet again. Their station has been relocated in three earlier passes, and each new station either blocked the flush path or opened the carrier side to the concentrate port. FIG. 3 is the view the source ties them to, since that is the position at which the poppet is held open, so the openings stay numbered there and FIG. 2 makes no assertion about them at all.

The circumferential convention sentence goes in the briefs only. A longitudinal section has to draw each port in one wall band, so the choice is forced by the view rather than disclosed, and the application text contains no orientation language at all. Saying so inside the brief keeps the forced choice from reading as an assertion that the ports are opposed, without putting any orientation into the specification.

On FIG. 1 I restored the inlet stub's offset, which an earlier pass had removed as untraced, because the end cap and the rod exit are both at that end and a renderer reading the bullet without the offset would stack all three in one place. The offset is a placement convention inside the brief; the description continues to recite only an inlet at one axial end.

On FIG. 4 the stepped end had to be named absolutely for numeral 46 to have a determinate target, and naming the right end as the one the tube enters supplies the other end at the same time. What stays unstated is the part the stop faces abut and their circumferential order, which is where the source is silent.

Every added sentence cost characters against the 2800 cap, so I trimmed wording that repeats what the brief already establishes: duplicated band names, a second 'shown schematically' in the same bullet, and two leader descriptions that specified more of the endpoint than was needed to identify the part.

input.summary: All five findings are fixed, all inside figures/; no application text needed to change. FIG. 1 now has the cartridge's sleeve end standing in the left mouth of the housing and meeting the inner face of the end cap ring that retains it, so the retention joint is a contact rather than a gap, and the piston rod bullet no longer says the shaft is broken off short of the end cap, which would have squeezed the rod into a zero-length space at that joint. The FIG. 1 ring bullet now states only that the unnumbered ring surrounds the sleeve over the left portion of its length with its left part standing beyond the sleeve's left end, and the inlet bullet is back to a generic stub projecting leftward from the housing at its left end; a single closing sentence records that the radial clearance drawn between the ring and the housing wall, and the position of the inlet stub within the left end, are drawing conventions only, with no flow path past the ring and no radial position of or relationship between the inlet, the end cap ring and the shaft intended. FIG. 4's cam groove is now a narrow band wrapping the collar body with its outline in broken line in the same manner as the hidden tube and rod, and the brief states that the surface of the collar on which the groove is formed, and its hand and pitch, are not indicated; the follower pin still has its outer end within that band. The extra unidentified opening is deleted from FIG. 2, leaving the concentrate port, the carrier-liquid admission port and the outlet-valve passage on that sheet, with the two radial rinse openings shown and numbered 62 in FIG. 3 at the return-stroke position. Because three of the fixes add text, I trimmed redundant phrasing in FIG. 1 and FIG. 4, including a duplicated statement about the interior of the housing, two leader descriptions that named the housing twice, and repeated broken-line qualifiers, so the four briefs measure 2787, 2490, 2785 and 2789 characters. The numeral table, the per-sheet numeral lists, the Brief Description captions, the detailed description and the claims are unchanged.
reasoning: The end cap joint was the fix that most affected the drawing's fidelity to the disclosure. A cap drawn short of the cartridge cannot retain it, which is the one relationship the source states about that joint, so closing the gap makes the sheet agree with the disclosed function rather than with a drafter's clearance.

That change forced a second edit in the same bullet: the rod had been broken off short of the end cap, which only made sense while a gap existed there. Dropping the phrase leaves the break line doing what a break line does, asserting nothing about where the rod goes, and avoids stating that the rod occupies a space the cartridge now fills.

For the cam groove I moved the whole feature into broken line and said in terms that the surface carrying it is not indicated. The earlier hedge covered only hand and pitch, which left the brief asserting an outer-surface or through-wall cam reached by a pin on an internal rod. Putting the groove in the same hidden-line treatment as the tube and the rod keeps the disclosed engagement between groove and pin visible without choosing a radial position for it.

The collar clearance and the inlet position both became labelled conventions rather than stated geometry, and I combined them into one closing sentence instead of two. The substance is that neither the flow past the collar nor the inlet's radial position is intended, which is exactly where the source is silent; a single sentence says both and costs fewer characters against the length cap.

Deleting the unidentified FIG. 2 opening was the cleanest resolution because every opening the source discloses is already drawn and numbered somewhere: the concentrate port and the admission port on FIG. 2, the flush bypass and the two rinse openings on FIG. 3. An opening that answers to no disclosed part cannot be traced, and its presence also left the two sections showing different counts through the same wall.

The rinse openings stay off the fill-position sheet, which is where earlier passes landed after their station proved untraceable in that position. FIG. 3 is the view the source ties them to, since that is the position at which the poppet is held open and the rinse flows.
Length was again the binding constraint, so the trims came from wording that repeats what a brief already establishes rather than from geometry or from the hedges that cure the untraced items.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no documents, so the Background carries no citations and none may be invented; the brief records that no prior-art search was run, so the art behind this draft may be incomplete and the independent claims should be re-tested against any later search. The claimed combination is unchanged. Claim 1 still rests on the axial ordering of the land faces and the port edges, which closes the concentrate port before the downstream land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port so that separation is enforced by the moving geometry rather than by command sequencing, and on the flush poppet opened by the follower pin carried by the piston rod during the return stroke and closed before the waist reconnects the concentrate port. This turn's changes protect two of the specification's own positions rather than altering scope: the end cap now retains the cartridge in the drawing as claim 11 and the description say it does, and the collar clearance is no longer drawn as a permanent route around the sleeve, which would have implied carrier liquid reaching the outlet independently of the flush poppet. The dependent ladder is untouched: the two directed rinse openings in claims 2 and 15, the flexible lip, the closed-port rinse interval, the express axial ordering of land faces and port edges, the index collar with its cam groove, three stop faces, detent and window, and the cartridge with threaded end cap.

- An unhatched panel of simple outline, shown schematically, is set into the upper housing wall band above that ring, the hatching stopping at its outline: the transparent window. On the ring beneath it a small patch shows.
- The radial clearance drawn between the unnumbered ring and the housing wall is a drawing convention only; no flow path past that ring is intended. input.summary: All five findings are fixed inside figures/; no application text needed to change. FIG. 4 no longer says which end of the collar carries the three axial stop faces or that the end face is stepped: one end is drawn with its end face divided into three faces at three different axial positions, shown schematically, and the brief states that which end carries the faces, the order in which they are arranged about the collar, and the part that abuts them are not indicated; target 46 follows, reading "one of the three faces at the divided end of the collar". FIG. 3 now names the further opening through the lower band at the right portion of the piston as the carrier-liquid admission port, unnumbered in that view, with its outer mouth broken off at a break line within the band, so no opening on that sheet is left unidentified and numeral 24 stays on FIG. 2 alone. FIG. 2 now carries an express omission note that the two radial rinse openings shown in FIG. 3 are omitted from the fill-position view for clarity, which matches the omission note FIG. 3 already carries for the index collar and removes the impression that the two sections show different structures. FIG. 1's sleeve bullet now says the clear gap is interrupted only where the unnumbered ring described below surrounds the sleeve, so the two bullets no longer give the renderer contradictory instructions for the same annulus. FIG. 1's closing convention bullet is split into two sentences, the first naming the unnumbered ring surrounding the sleeve for the radial clearance and the no-flow-path statement, the second naming the inlet stub position and stating that no radial position of or relationship between the inlet, the end cap ring and the shaft is intended, so the two rings on that sheet can no longer be confused and the no-flow-path statement cannot attach to the retention joint. Space for the added sentences came from redundant phrasing in the same briefs, chiefly repeated uses of "sleeve band", "housing wall band" and "plain" where the sheet has only one such band, and from three leader descriptions that named a part twice. The numeral table, the per-sheet numeral lists, the Brief Description captions, the detailed description and the claims are unchanged, and the four briefs measure 2795, 2569, 2790 and 2795 characters.
reasoning: The stop-face fix follows the pattern the same brief already uses twice, for the inlet stub position and for the surface carrying the cam groove: keep the depiction the renderer needs, and say in terms which part of it is convention. Naming the divided end in target 46 rather than the left end keeps the leader determinate without reintroducing the end designation the source does not support.

Naming the FIG. 3 opening was the right cure rather than deleting it, because FIG. 2 draws the same feature at the same station and names it the carrier-liquid admission port. Deleting it would have made the sections disagree about a disclosed port; naming it and marking it unnumbered here keeps numeral 24 meaning one thing on one sheet.

The FIG. 2 omission note and the FIG. 3 collar omission note now do the same work from opposite directions. Both sheets are longitudinal sections of the same metering portion, so where one view leaves out a part the other shows, the brief has to say so, otherwise the pair reads as two different structures rather than one structure drawn twice.

The FIG. 1 gap wording was a straight renderer conflict: a clear gap along the whole length cannot coexist with a ring occupying part of that annulus. Qualifying the gap resolves it without saying anything about flow, which is where the source is silent and where the existing convention label already speaks.

Splitting the closing convention sentence mattered more than it looks. With the end cap introduced as a short hatched ring and the collar as an unnumbered ring, an unqualified reference to the ring could have attached the no-flow-path disclaimer to the retention joint, which is the one relationship at that joint the source does affirm. Naming each ring puts the disclaimer where it belongs.

Every fix added text against the length cap, so the trims came from wording that repeats what the brief already establishes, band names the sheet has only one of and leader endpoints described in more words than the part needs, rather than from geometry, relationships or the hedges that cure the untraced items.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no documents, so the Background carries no citations and none may be invented; the brief records that no prior-art search was run, so the art behind this draft may be incomplete and the independent claims should be re-tested against any later search. The claimed combination is unchanged. - **[critical] FIG. 1 asserts an undisclosed flow boundary at the index collar that contradicts the disclosed rinse path** (figures/FIG-1.md, Geometry bullets 4 ("The metering sleeve lies inside the housing...") and 9 (final bullet); conflicts ) - The FIG. 1 brief verbalizes two untraced flow-boundary facts about the index collar: that the annular gap between the metering sleeve and the housing is "interrupted" where the collar ring surrounds the sleeve, and that "no flow path past that ring is intended." The inventor never described any sealing, blocking or clearance relationship between the index collar and the housing or the rinse channel; the only statement about the collar is that it "surrounds the metering sleeve and has a helical cam groove engaged by a follower pin." A statement about a flow boundary is substantive even under a schematic convention, so it must be removed. It is also internally inconsistent: FIG. 1 places the ring in the sleeve/housing annulus at the same (left) end as the inlet, while the description says "The annular rinse channel 60 lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve 18 and an inner surface of the housing 12, and is supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet 14", FIG. 3 says the channel is "supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet end", and claim 1 requires that "carrier liquid flows through the annular rinse channel." (delete "'s left end" and "and meeting the inner face of"), so that no contact face is asserted and the ring described in the later bullet does not overlap the end cap. View: longitudinal sectional view of the inline liquid metering valve, axis horizontal. All line work lies well inside the drawing area.

- The housing is an elongate cylinder cut lengthwise on its axis, appearing as upper and lower hatched bands joined at the right by a hatched end wall, the interior between them open.

- Within the sleeve bore, in the left half, is a body shown schematically as two hatched enlarged portions joined by a narrower middle portion, the shaft running leftward.

- An unhatched panel of simple outline, shown schematically, is set into the upper housing band above that ring, the hatching stopping at its outline: the transparent window. On the ring beneath it a small patch shows.
- The radial clearance drawn between the unnumbered ring and the housing wall is a drawing convention only; no flow path past that ring is intended. The undisclosed flow boundary at the index collar is gone: the sleeve bullet now ends at a clear gap visible above and below the sleeve, with no statement that the gap is interrupted, and the closing convention bullet no longer says that no flow path past the ring is intended, so it now covers only the inlet stub position and states that no radial position of, or relationship between, the inlet, the end cap ring and the shaft is intended. In its place the ring bullet carries the neutral statement that no relationship between that ring and the gap between the sleeve and the housing is indicated, which leaves the drawing silent where the disclosure is silent and no longer cuts off the rinse supply that the description, FIG. 3 and claim 1 require to reach the annular rinse channel from the inlet. The collision between the ring and the end cap is also resolved: the cartridge bullet now reads that the sleeve stands in the left mouth and is retained there by the end cap ring, asserting no contact face, and the ring bullet no longer places the ring's left part beyond the sleeve's left end, so nothing is drawn into the space the cap occupies. Removing the two disclaimed sentences left FIG. 1 well under the length cap, so no other trimming was needed. The numeral table, the per-sheet numeral lists, the Brief Description captions, the detailed description, the claims and the other three briefs are unchanged, and the four sheets measure 2573, 2569, 2790 and 2795 characters.
reasoning: The flow-boundary statement had to go rather than be reworded, because it was doing real damage in two directions: it asserted a sealing or blocking relationship the inventor never described, and it closed the only route by which carrier liquid can reach the annular rinse channel, which the description, FIG. 3 and claim 1 all depend on. Deleting the interruption and the no-flow-path sentence restores a continuous annulus without asserting anything about how the collar sits in it.

Replacing them with a statement that no relationship between the ring and the gap is indicated keeps the sheet honest in both directions. It neither claims clearance nor claims a seal, which matches a source that places the collar around the sleeve and the channel between the sleeve and the housing without reconciling them.

The cartridge and ring collision came from an earlier fix that closed the retention joint by naming a contact face. Retention is disclosed; contact at a particular face is not. Saying the sleeve stands in the left mouth and is retained there by the end cap ring keeps the disclosed function, drops the untraced contact, and removes the geometric impossibility of a cap bearing on the sleeve end face while a larger ring passes through the same space.

I also dropped the clause putting the ring's left part beyond the sleeve's left end. It had been added in an earlier round to keep the follower pin at one station across sheets, but FIG. 4 already places the collar extending leftward beyond the tube's left end, so the relationship survives where it is drawn and FIG. 1 no longer needs to assert a position that collides with the cap.
No compensating trims were required this turn: the two deleted sentences were longer than the one added, so FIG. 1 dropped to 2573 characters and the other three briefs were left untouched.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references and the Background cites none; the brief records that no prior-art search was run, so the art behind this draft may be incomplete and the independent claims should be re-tested against any later search. The claimed combination is unchanged. Claim 1 still rests on the axial ordering of the land faces and the port edges, which closes the concentrate port before the downstream land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port so that separation is enforced by the moving geometry rather than by command sequencing, and on the flush poppet opened by the follower pin carried by the piston rod during the return stroke and closed before the waist reconnects the concentrate port. This turn's edits protect the second of those directly: with the flow boundary at the collar removed, the drawings again show carrier liquid able to reach the annular rinse channel from the inlet, pass the rinse openings and leave through the flush bypass, which is the path claim 1 recites and the path the specification explains as making the rinse an unavoidable part of the same stroke. The dependent ladder is untouched: the two directed rinse openings in claims 2 and 15, the flexible lip, the closed-port rinse interval, the express axial ordering of land faces and port edges, the index collar with its cam groove, three stop faces, detent and window, and the cartridge with threaded end cap in claims 10, 11 and 20.

7	1. FIG. 3 draws the flush bypass as an unobstructed passage running from the bore up through the upper sleeve band to the outlet, and separately places the normally closed flush poppet in a side branch at the opposite (left) end "joined to the flush bypass by a plain passage". As drawn, closing the poppet leaves the bore-to-outlet bypass path open, so the poppet gates nothing. That contradicts the description ("The flush poppet 58 is normally closed and is connected to the flush bypass 26... the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows...") and claim 1's whereby clause, which make flow through the flush bypass conditional on the follower pin opening the poppet.
8	
9	2. FIG. 4 verbalizes an axial relationship between the index collar and the metering sleeve that no source passage supplies: "The tube's left end lies within the collar, the collar extending leftward beyond that end." The inventor says only that "An index collar surrounds the metering sleeve and has a helical cam groove engaged by a follower pin carried by the piston rod." The overhang is load-bearing technical substance (it is what lets a pin on the rod end reach the groove without passing through the sleeve wall), and it is also in tension with FIG. 1, where the same ring is drawn "over the left portion of [the sleeve's] length" with the sleeve "standing in the left mouth and retained there by the end cap ring". Two numerals then land on one component, risking a reading of 64 as the sleeve's end face rather than the removable unit.
12	
13	Everything else in the figure briefs is either an affirmatively disclosed part or a properly disclaimed depiction convention: the section-plane note that no circumferential relationship among ports is intended, the omission of rinse openings from FIG. 2 and of the collar from FIG. 3, the flexible lip "shown without flare direction", the rinse openings with "any direction of discharge is not indicated", the schematic inlet/outlet stubs with the express note that their drawn position is a convention only, and the broken-off outer mouth of the carrier-liquid admission port so that what it opens into is not indicated. The relative axial location of the carrier-liquid admission port downstream of the concentrate port is an entailment of the disclosed geometry (the waist between the lands registers with the concentrate port, and the downstream land "uncovers" the admission port), so it is not reported.

As drawn, closing the poppet leaves the bore-to-outlet bypass path open, so the poppet gates nothing. That contradicts the description ("The flush poppet 58 is normally closed and is connected to the flush bypass 26... the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows...") and claim 1's whereby clause, which make flow through the flush bypass conditional on the follower pin opening the poppet.

2. FIG. 4 verbalizes an axial relationship between the index collar and the metering sleeve that no source passage supplies: "The tube's left end lies within the collar, the collar extending leftward beyond that end." The inventor says only that "An index collar surrounds the metering sleeve and has a helical cam groove engaged by a follower pin carried by the piston rod." 1	# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)
2	
3	This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.
4	
5	A reusable inline liquid metering valve delivers a repeatable dose of concentrate into a flowing carrier liquid and automatically rinses the surfaces that contacted the concentrate after each dose. The valve has a cylindrical housing with an inlet at one axial end and an outlet at the opposite axial end. A metering sleeve is fixed inside the housing. The sleeve defines a cylindrical dose chamber, a radial concentrate port, a carrier-liquid admission port, and a flush bypass that opens downstream of the dose chamber.
6	
7	A piston slides axially in the dose chamber between a fill position and a discharge position. The piston has two axially spaced sealing lands joined by a reduced-diameter waist. In the fill position, the waist connects the concentrate port to the dose chamber while both lands isolate the carrier-liquid path. Movement to the discharge position closes the concentrate port before the downstream land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port. Carrier liquid then enters behind the measured volume and expels that volume through a one-way outlet valve into the main flow. The ordering of the port edges and lands prevents the concentrate source from communicating directly with the carrier-liquid inlet.
8	
9	An index collar surrounds the metering sleeve and has a helical cam groove engaged by a follower pin carried by the piston rod. Each full piston stroke turns the index collar by one increment. Three selectable axial stop faces on the collar set three dose volumes by limiting piston travel. A spring-biased detent engages one of three recesses to retain the selected setting. A transparent window in the housing shows one of three reference numerals carried on the collar, so the dose setting is mechanically visible without electronics.
10	
11	When the piston returns toward the fill position, a flexible lip on the upstream sealing land first wipes the dose-chamber wall. Near the end of the return stroke, the follower pin opens a normally closed flush poppet connected to the flush bypass. Carrier liquid flows through an annular rinse channel between the sleeve and housing, through two radial rinse openings directed across the concentrate port and the one-way outlet valve, and then through the flush bypass to the outlet. The flush poppet closes before the waist reconnects the concentrate port. A replaceable cartridge contains the piston, metering sleeve, one-way outlet valve, and flush poppet and is retained by a threaded end cap. Removing the end cap withdraws the cartridge without disturbing the housing connections. An apparatus claim and a method claim should cover the ordered isolation, metering, discharge, and automatic rinse sequence.
