content.text:
All four findings are fixed, entirely within the figure briefs; no application text changed.

**Radial discharge into the rinse channel (critical).** In FIG. 2 the one-way outlet-valve passage now leads from the dose chamber into the upper band and is broken off at a break line within the band, so what it opens into is not indicated. FIG. 3 does the same for its outlet-valve passage, and the flush bypass now runs from the poppet into the upper band toward the outlet end and is likewise broken off within the band. Neither passage is drawn crossing the sleeve wall into the inlet-fed annular rinse channel, so the depicted topology no longer contradicts the flow paths recited in the detailed description and claims 1 and 13. This is the same neutral convention FIG. 2 already used for the carrier-liquid admission port.

**FIG. 1 end-cap location (major).** The disclaimer now covers the axial matter as well as the radial one: the axial end at which the end cap ring and the mouth receiving the removable unit are drawn is a convention only, and no relationship between the end cap and either line connection is intended.

**Negative flow boundary (minor).** The clause stating that the bypass passage has no other opening to the bore is deleted.

**FIG. 4 groove convention (minor).** The helical cam groove band is now drawn in broken line throughout, consistent with the wholly hidden follower pin that engages it and with the brief's own statement that the groove surface is not indicated. The follower-pin bullet is unchanged.

Each of the four briefs grew with these fixes, so I offset the additions by removing depiction constraints that had no source behind them and identified no part: a hatching-stop instruction and two page-position modifiers on lead lines in FIG. 1, a duplicated "in the position shown" and a redundant contact phrasing in FIG. 3, and several instances of "conventional" before "break line". All four briefs are now within the length limit at 2783, 2653, 2788 and 2756 characters. Numeral sets, the numeral table, the drawing descriptions, the detailed description and the claims are unchanged and still match one another.

input.summary: All four findings are fixed and every one of them was confined to the figure briefs; the application text, the numeral table and the claims are untouched. The critical flow-topology defect is gone: in FIG. 2 the one-way outlet-valve passage now leads from the dose chamber into the upper band and is broken off at a break line within the band so that what it opens into is not indicated, and FIG. 3 does the same for both its outlet-valve passage and the flush bypass, which now runs from the flush poppet into the upper band toward the outlet end and is broken off within the band. Neither passage is drawn crossing the sleeve wall into the inlet-fed annular rinse channel any longer, so the depicted topology matches the flow paths recited in the detailed description and in claims 1 and 13. The FIG. 1 disclaimer now reaches the axial matter as well as the radial one, stating that the axial end at which the end cap ring and the mouth receiving the removable unit are drawn is a convention only and that no relationship between the end cap and either line connection is intended. The untraced negative clause that the bypass passage has no other opening to the bore is deleted. In FIG. 4 the helical cam groove band is now in broken line throughout, which is consistent with the wholly hidden follower pin that engages it and with the brief's own statement that the groove surface is not indicated. Because each fix lengthened its brief, I offset the additions by removing depiction constraints that had no source behind them and identified no part: a hatching-stop instruction and two page-position modifiers on lead lines in FIG. 1, a duplicated position phrase and a redundant contact phrasing in FIG. 3, and several instances of conventional before break line. All four briefs are within the length limit at 2783, 2653, 2788 and 2756 characters, the per-sheet numeral sets are unchanged, and no note, placeholder or em dash appears anywhere in draft/ or figures/. prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so the application carries no citations and, as the drafting brief records, the art available to this draft may be incomplete.
reasoning: The critical finding was about where two passages were drawn discharging, and the honest fix was to stop the drawing from answering a question the inventor never answered. The disclosure says the flush bypass opens downstream of the dose chamber and that rinse liquid leaves through it to the outlet; it never says which way the passage runs out of the sleeve, and it never places the one-way outlet valve. Breaking each passage off inside the wall band leaves the disclosed function visible and the undisclosed destination unstated, which is the same convention FIG. 2 already used for the carrier-liquid admission port.

I fixed this in the drawing rather than by adding a routing sentence to the specification. Writing a path for either passage into the description would have imported structure the inventor never gave, and the claims already recite the flow from the rinse channel through the rinse opening and the flush bypass to the outlet, which is all the support the figures need to conform to.

On FIG. 1, the existing disclaimer disclaimed only radial position, so it did not reach the choice that put the end cap, the cartridge withdrawal mouth and the inlet at the same axial end. That choice decides which line connection the cartridge passes on removal, which is technical substance, and the inventor says only that removing the end cap withdraws the cartridge without disturbing the housing connections. Extending the disclaimer to the axial end keeps the drawing usable without asserting the relationship.

The negative clause about the bypass having no other opening to the bore came in earlier to force a renderer to gate the poppet properly. It was doing a job, but it stated a contact topology the source never characterises, and the positive description that the poppet stands between the bore and the passage now carries that job on its own.

On FIG. 4 the two bullets were describing mutually exclusive constructions: a groove outlined as an outer-surface feature and a pin hidden along its whole length. Making the groove band broken line throughout resolves it in the direction that asserts nothing, which is what the brief's own disclaimer of the groove surface requires. The pin bullet stayed as it was.

Every trim I made to fit the length limit came out of rendering control rather than physical geometry: where a lead line sits on the page, whether hatching stops at a panel outline, and repeated phrases. The bodies, contacts, openings, break lines and occlusions the sheets must show are all still stated positively.

Claim 1 is unchanged and still rests on the axial order in which the concentrate port closes before the downstream sealing land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port, and on the follower pin carried by the piston rod opening the normally closed flush poppet during the return stroke with the poppet closing before the waist reconnects the concentrate port.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is no document to cite and none is cited anywhere in the application. The Background states the technical problems the invention addresses without attributing any of them to a publication. Claim 1 is unchanged this turn and continues to rest on two concrete relationships expressed in the inventor's own terms rather than in generic dosing-valve vocabulary. The first is that the axial order of the sealing land faces and the port edges closes the concentrate port before the downstream sealing land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port, so that no position of the piston places the concentrate source in communication with the carrier-liquid path and the separation does not depend on the order in which external commands arrive. The second is that a follower pin carried by the piston rod opens a normally closed flush poppet during the return stroke and the poppet closes before the waist reconnects the concentrate port, so the rinse of the concentrate-wetted surfaces is compelled by the same stroke that delivers the dose rather than being a separately commanded operation. The specification explains the problem each solves before it is needed. The dependent ladder retreats first to the two directed rinse openings and the flexible-lip wipe, then to the waist-out-of-register interval and the express axial-ordering recitation, then to the self-indexing collar with cam groove, stop faces, detent and window, and finally to the cartridge and threaded end cap. None of this turn's edits touched claim scope, since every finding was a depiction matter. The drafting brief records that no prior-art search was run for this matter, so the art available here may be incomplete and the claims should be re-checked against any later search results.

reasoning: The critical finding was about where two passages were drawn discharging, and the honest fix was to stop the drawing from answering a question the inventor never answered. The disclosure says the flush bypass opens downstream of the dose chamber and that rinse liquid leaves through it to the outlet; it never says which way the passage runs out of the sleeve, and it never places the one-way outlet valve. Breaking each passage off inside the wall band leaves the disclosed function visible and the undisclosed destination unstated, which is the same convention FIG. 2 already used for the carrier-liquid admission port.

I fixed this in the drawing rather than by adding a routing sentence to the specification. Writing a path for either passage into the description would have imported structure the inventor never gave, and the claims already recite the flow from the rinse channel through the rinse opening and the flush bypass to the outlet, which is all the support the figures need to conform to.

On FIG. 1, the existing disclaimer disclaimed only radial position, so it did not reach the choice that put the end cap, the cartridge withdrawal mouth and the inlet at the same axial end. That choice decides which line connection the cartridge passes on removal, which is technical substance, and the inventor says only that removing the end cap withdraws the cartridge without disturbing the housing connections. Extending the disclaimer to the axial end keeps the drawing usable without asserting the relationship.

The negative clause about the bypass having no other opening to the bore came in earlier to force a renderer to gate the poppet properly. It was doing a job, but it stated a contact topology the source never characterises, and the positive description that the poppet stands between the bore and the passage now carries that job on its own.

On FIG. 4 the two bullets were describing mutually exclusive constructions: a groove outlined as an outer-surface feature and a pin hidden along its whole length. Making the groove band broken line throughout resolves it in the direction that asserts nothing, which is what the brief's own disclaimer of the groove surface requires. The pin bullet stayed as it was.

Every trim I made to fit the length limit came out of rendering control rather than physical geometry: where a lead line sits on the page, whether hatching stops at a panel outline, and repeated phrases. The bodies, contacts, openings, break lines and occlusions the sheets must show are all still stated positively.

In the following description, the terms upstream and downstream refer to the direction of travel of the carrier liquid from the inlet toward the outlet, and the terms axial and radial refer to the axis along which the piston slides.

FIG. 1 shows an inline liquid metering valve 10 having a cylindrical housing 12 with an inlet 14 at one axial end and an outlet 16 at the opposite axial end, a metering sleeve 18 fixed within the housing 12, a cartridge 64 retained in the housing 12 by a threaded end cap 66, and a transparent window 52 in the housing 12.

The inline liquid metering valve 10 is connected in a line that already carries a flowing carrier liquid. Carrier liquid enters at the inlet 14, passes along the housing 12, and leaves at the outlet 16. That flow is the main flow into which each dose of concentrate is delivered, and it is also the flow that rinses the valve. The metering sleeve 18 is spaced radially inward from the inner surface of the housing 12.

FIG. 2 shows the metering sleeve 18 defining a dose chamber 20, a concentrate port 22 opening into the dose chamber 20 and a carrier-liquid admission port 24 opening into the dose chamber 20. FIG. 2 further shows an upstream sealing land 30 and a downstream sealing land 32 joined by a reduced-diameter waist 34 in the fill position, and a one-way outlet valve 38.

The dose chamber 20 is cylindrical. The concentrate port 22 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and is connected in use to a concentrate source. The carrier-liquid admission port 24 passes through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 at an axial position downstream of the concentrate port 22, and admits carrier liquid to the dose chamber 20. The metering sleeve 18 further defines a flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20.

A piston 28 is axially slidable in the dose chamber 20 between a fill position and a discharge position. The upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 are axially spaced from one another on the piston 28 and are joined by the reduced-diameter waist 34. Each sealing land bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20, while the waist 34 stands clear of that wall. A piston rod 36 extends from the piston 28 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 and is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke. The one-way outlet valve 38 is arranged to pass liquid from the dose chamber 20 toward the outlet 16 and to prevent flow in the opposite direction.

In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume of concentrate, the extent of which is fixed by the travel then permitted to the piston 28. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 while the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.

Movement of the piston 28 toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port 22 before the downstream sealing land 32 uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Only after the concentrate port 22 has been closed does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.

The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every position of the piston 28 at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18. It does not depend on the order in which external commands are given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of a separately actuated shut-off element. The port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens.

FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, a follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62, the concentrate port 22, and the flush bypass 26. The follower pin 44 is carried by the piston rod 36.

The flexible lip 56 is carried on the upstream sealing land 30 and bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20. As the return stroke begins, the flexible lip 56 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20.

The annular rinse channel 60 lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve 18 and an inner surface of the housing 12, and is supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet 14. The two radial rinse openings 62 pass through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and connect the annular rinse channel 60 to the dose chamber 20. One of the two radial rinse openings 62 is directed across the concentrate port 22 and the other is directed across the one-way outlet valve 38.

The flush poppet 58 is normally closed and is connected to the flush bypass 26. Near the end of the return stroke, the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows from the inlet 14 through the annular rinse channel 60, through the two radial rinse openings 62 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 to the outlet 16. The rinse liquid therefore reaches the outlet 16, as the dose does, and is carried away in the main flow.

The flush poppet 58 closes before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. Throughout the interval in which the annular rinse channel 60 communicates with the flush bypass 26, the waist 34 is out of register with the concentrate port 22, so that the waist 34 does not connect the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. Only when the flush poppet 58 has closed does the continuing return of the piston 28 bring the waist 34 back into register with the concentrate port 22, at which point the dose chamber 20 is charged again for the next dose.

Because the follower pin 44 that opens the flush poppet 58 is carried by the piston rod 36, the rinse occurs once for every dose and at the same point in every cycle. It is not a separate operation, it needs no command, and it cannot be omitted while the valve continues to be used. The rinse also occurs before the waist 34 has reconnected the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20 and after the wall of the dose chamber 20 has been wiped.

FIG. 4 shows an index collar 40 having a helical cam groove 42 engaged by the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36, three selectable axial stop faces 46, a spring-biased detent 48 engaging one of three detent recesses 50, and three dose setting numerals 54.

The index collar 40 surrounds the metering sleeve 18. Each full stroke of the piston 28 draws the follower pin 44 along the helical cam groove 42 and turns the index collar 40 by one increment, so that the index collar 40 advances by itself as the valve is used and needs no separate indexing drive.

The three axial stop faces 46 are carried by the index collar 40 at different axial positions. The stop face presented by the current increment of rotation limits the travel of the piston 28 and thereby sets the dose volume, so that the three axial stop faces 46 correspond to three dose volumes. The spring-biased detent 48 engages one of the three detent recesses 50 to retain the selected setting until the index collar 40 is next indexed.

The transparent window 52 in the housing 12 shows one of the three dose setting numerals 54 carried by the index collar 40. The dose setting numeral presented at the transparent window 52 is the one associated with the axial stop face then limiting the travel of the piston 28, so that the dose setting is mechanically visible without electronics. What is seen at the transparent window 52 is the position of the index collar 40 itself.

The cartridge 64 contains the piston 28, the metering sleeve 18, the one-way outlet valve 38 and the flush poppet 58, and is removable from the housing 12 as a unit. Removing the threaded end cap 66 withdraws the cartridge 64 from the housing 12 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 without disturbing the connections at the inlet 14 and the outlet 16, so that the cartridge 64 is replaced as a unit while the housing 12 remains in the line.

In use, carrier liquid flows through the housing 12 from the inlet 14 to the outlet 16. With the piston 28 in the fill position, concentrate is admitted through the concentrate port 22 and past the waist 34 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume, the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolating the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. The piston 28 is then advanced toward the discharge position so as to close the concentrate port 22 and thereafter to uncover the carrier-liquid admission port 24 with the downstream sealing land 32. Carrier liquid is admitted through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16. The extent of the travel available to the piston 28, and therefore the measured volume, is fixed by the selected one of the three axial stop faces 46.

The piston 28 is then returned toward the fill position. During the return, the flexible lip 56 on the upstream sealing land 30 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20, and the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36 opens the normally closed flush poppet 58. Carrier liquid flows through the annular rinse channel 60 between the metering sleeve 18 and the housing 12, through the two radial rinse openings 62 in the metering sleeve 18 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20 to the outlet 16. The flush poppet 58 is closed before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. Over the same full stroke, the follower pin 44 traveling in the helical cam groove 42 turns the index collar 40 by one increment, the spring-biased detent 48 enters the next of the three detent recesses 50, and the dose setting numeral then presented at the transparent window 52 shows the setting that will govern the next dose. The valve is thereby left charged, rinsed and set, ready for the following cycle.

The foregoing description sets out embodiments of the invention. A skilled reader may make changes of detail to the described embodiments without departing from the scope of the claims that follow.

The single finding is fixed.

**FIG. 4 lead sentence in the detailed description.** The sentence no longer parses as making the index collar carry the spring-biased detent. It now reads: "FIG. 4 shows an index collar 40 having a helical cam groove 42 engaged by the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36, three selectable axial stop faces 46, and three dose setting numerals 54. FIG. 4 further shows a spring-biased detent 48 engaging one of three detent recesses 50."

That restores agreement with the three places the relationship was already stated correctly: claim 8, which recites the detent as a separate element of the valve; figures/FIG-4.md, which places it adjacent the collar as a plain detent element seated in a recess; and the later description paragraph, which says only that the detent engages one of the three detent recesses to retain the selected setting. The Summary was checked and is likewise neutral, so it was left alone.

Numerals 48 and 50 remain attributed to FIG. 4 in the description and remain on that sheet's numeral list, so the per-figure numeral sets still match the numeral table and the four briefs. No other file changed; all four briefs remain within the length limit at 2783, 2653, 2788 and 2756 characters, and no note, placeholder, question or em dash appears anywhere in draft/ or figures/.

It is now split so that the collar is said to have the helical cam groove engaged by the follower pin carried by the piston rod, the three selectable axial stop faces, and the three dose setting numerals, with a second sentence stating that FIG. 4 further shows a spring-biased detent engaging one of three detent recesses. That brings the sentence into line with the three places the relationship was already correct: claim 8, which recites the detent as a separate element of the valve; figures/FIG-4.md, which places it adjacent the collar as a plain detent element seated in a recess; and the later description paragraph, which says only that the detent engages one of the three detent recesses to retain the selected setting. The Summary was checked for the same construction and is neutral, so it was left as written. Numerals 48 and 50 are still attributed to FIG. 4 in the description and still appear on that sheet's numeral list, so the per-figure numeral sets continue to match the numeral table and the four briefs exactly. No other file changed. All four figure briefs remain within the length limit at 2783, 2653, 2788 and 2756 characters, and no note, placeholder, question or em dash appears anywhere in draft/ or figures/. prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so the application carries no citations and, as the drafting brief records, the art available to this draft may be incomplete.
reasoning: The defect was a parsing accident in a figure-introduction sentence rather than a considered statement, and it mattered because the same sentence names four things after the participle 'having'. Three of them are collar-carried in the disclosure and one is not. Splitting the sentence is the minimal repair: the collar keeps exactly the features the inventor put on it, and the detent is introduced as something the figure shows rather than something the collar has.

I fixed the description rather than the drawing or the claim because the description was the outlier. The inventor says only that a spring-biased detent engages one of three recesses to retain the selected setting, and never makes the detent part of the collar. Claim 8 and the FIG. 4 brief both already reflected that, so conforming those to the loose sentence would have propagated the error into two more places.

I checked the Summary for the same construction before touching anything. It reads that a spring-biased detent engaging one of three recesses retains the selected setting, which attaches the detent to nothing, so rewriting it would have been churn on text that was already right.

The split preserves the per-figure numeral accounting. Numerals 48 and 50 still appear in the FIG. 4 introduction, so the set the description attributes to FIG. 4 is unchanged and still matches the sheet's list and the numeral table. Had I moved the detent out of the FIG. 4 introduction entirely, two numerals would have lost their figure attribution.

Claim 1 is unchanged and still rests on the two features that do the technical work: the axial order in which the concentrate port closes before the downstream sealing land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port, which makes the separation of the two liquids a property of the piston and sleeve geometry rather than of command sequencing, and the follower pin carried by the piston rod opening the normally closed flush poppet during the return stroke with the poppet closing before the waist reconnects the concentrate port, which makes the rinse compelled by the same stroke that delivers the dose.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is no document to cite and none is cited anywhere in the application. The Background states the technical problems the invention addresses without attributing any of them to a publication. Claim 1 is unchanged this turn and continues to rest on two concrete relationships expressed in the inventor's own terms rather than in generic dosing-valve vocabulary. The first is that the axial order of the sealing land faces and the port edges closes the concentrate port before the downstream sealing land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port, so that no position of the piston places the concentrate source in communication with the carrier-liquid path and the separation does not depend on the order in which external commands arrive. The second is that a follower pin carried by the piston rod opens a normally closed flush poppet during the return stroke and the poppet closes before the waist reconnects the concentrate port, so the rinse of the concentrate-wetted surfaces is compelled by the same stroke that delivers the dose rather than being a separately commanded operation. The specification explains the problem each solves before it is needed. The dependent ladder retreats first to the two directed rinse openings and the flexible-lip wipe, then to the waist-out-of-register interval and the express axial-ordering recitation, then to the self-indexing collar with cam groove, stop faces, detent and window, and finally to the cartridge and threaded end cap. This turn's edit touched no claim and no scope; it removed an unintended carrier relationship from one description sentence. The drafting brief records that no prior-art search was run for this matter, so the art available here may be incomplete and the claims should be re-checked against any later search results.

content.text:
Both findings are fixed.

**FIG. 4 detent recesses (major).** The brief no longer says which collar surface carries the recesses or from which direction the detent element enters them. The recesses are now shown schematically as plain recesses at three angular positions at one station along the collar's length, with the surface on which they are formed, their depth and profile, and the entry direction expressly not indicated. The detent bullet now reads as a plain detent element engaging that recess, with no contact relationship beyond the engagement itself indicated. This matches how the same brief already treats the cam groove and the stop faces. Target 48 was reworded to "engaging" to stay in step. The application text needed no change: claim 8 recites the detent and the three recesses as separate elements, and the description says only that the detent engages one of the three recesses to retain the selected setting.

**Claim 7 (minor).** Claim 7 now recites "each of the three selectable axial stop faces, when selected, limiting travel of the piston to set a respective dose volume", so it no longer reads as all three limiting travel at once. That agrees with the description, with claim 9's "a selected one of the three selectable axial stop faces", and with claim 18. No other claim changed.

Adding the two disclaimers pushed FIG. 4 over the brief length limit, so I recovered the space from constraints that identify no part: two instances of "conventional" before "break line", the curved-edge rationale, the direction in which the outer numeral patches curve, a verbose restatement of the stop-face order disclaimer, and four over-specified lead-line targets, which are now broad interior targets on the intended parts. FIG. 4 is 2764 characters; the other three briefs are unchanged at 2783, 2653 and 2788. Numeral sets, the numeral table, the drawing descriptions and the detailed description remain synchronized.

input.summary: Both findings are fixed. In figures/FIG-4.md the detent-recess bullets no longer verbalize which surface of the index collar carries the three recesses or from which direction the detent element enters them. The recesses are now shown schematically as plain recesses at three angular positions at one station along the collar's length, with the surface on which they are formed, their depth and profile, and the entry direction expressly not indicated, and the detent is shown as a plain detent element engaging that recess with no contact relationship beyond the engagement itself indicated. That matches the treatment the same brief already gives the cam groove and the stop faces. Target 48 was reworded from seated in to engaging so the leader description stays in step. No application text needed changing for this finding, since claim 8 recites the detent and the three recesses as separate elements and the description says only that the detent engages one of the three recesses to retain the selected setting. Claim 7 now recites that each of the three selectable axial stop faces, when selected, limits travel of the piston to set a respective dose volume, so it no longer reads as all three limiting travel simultaneously, and it agrees with the description, with claim 9 and with claim 18. Adding the two disclaimers pushed FIG. 4 past the 2800-character brief limit, so I recovered the space from constraints that identify no part: two instances of conventional before break line, the rationale attached to the collar's curved end edge, the direction in which the outer numeral patches curve, a verbose restatement of the stop-face order disclaimer, and four over-specified lead-line targets, which are now broad interior targets on the intended parts. FIG. 4 is 2764 characters and the other three briefs are unchanged at 2783, 2653 and 2788. The numeral table, the per-sheet numeral sets, the drawing descriptions and the detailed description remain synchronized, and no note, placeholder or em dash appears anywhere in draft/ or figures/. prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so the application carries no citations and, as the drafting brief records, the art available to this draft may be incomplete.
reasoning: The FIG. 4 finding was about the brief being inconsistent with itself. It disclaimed the collar surface carrying the cam groove and the end carrying the stop faces, then turned around and put the detent recesses on the curved outer surface with the detent entering them radially from outside. The inventor gives the detent and the recesses as a function only, so the fix was to extend the same neutralization already used twice in that brief rather than to invent a construction.

I kept the three angular positions at one axial station, because that much is forced: a single fixed detent has to meet a different recess at each of three rotational increments. What I removed was only the surface and the entry direction, which nothing in the disclosure decides.

Claim 7 was a drafting slip rather than a support problem. Reading each of three stop faces as limiting travel at the same time is physically impossible, and the description, claim 9 and claim 18 all already said one selected face governs at a time. Adding when selected fixes the reading without narrowing anything, since the claim always meant the collar carries three faces of which the presented one sets the dose.

I made no change to the description for either finding. The description was already neutral about where the recesses sit and already said the stop face presented by the current increment of rotation limits travel, so editing it would have been churn on text that was correct.

The length trims all came out of rendering control rather than physical geometry. The four target rewrites also serve the endpoint guidance directly: pointing numeral 40 at the collar body clear of the groove and recesses, and numeral 42 at the interior of the groove band, are broad interior targets, where the previous wording added an away-from-the-pin modifier and a visible-surface modifier that no source decides.

Claim 1 is unchanged and still rests on the axial order in which the concentrate port closes before the downstream sealing land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port, and on the follower pin carried by the piston rod opening the normally closed flush poppet during the return stroke with the poppet closing before the waist reconnects the concentrate port.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is no document to cite and none is cited anywhere in the application. The Background states the technical problems the invention addresses without attributing any of them to a publication. Claim 1 is unchanged this turn and continues to rest on two concrete relationships expressed in the inventor's own terms rather than in generic dosing-valve vocabulary. The first is that the axial order of the sealing land faces and the port edges closes the concentrate port before the downstream sealing land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port, so that no position of the piston places the concentrate source in communication with the carrier-liquid path and the separation does not depend on the order in which external commands arrive. The second is that a follower pin carried by the piston rod opens a normally closed flush poppet during the return stroke and the poppet closes before the waist reconnects the concentrate port, so the rinse of the concentrate-wetted surfaces is compelled by the same stroke that delivers the dose rather than being a separately commanded operation. content.text:
The finding is fixed.

**Band naming in the section views (FIG. 3, with FIG. 2 for consistency).** FIG. 3 now names the two pairs of bands distinctly: the housing wall appears as upper and lower hatched housing bands, and the sleeve wall inside as upper and lower hatched sleeve bands. Every port and passage that the description locates in the metering sleeve wall now names that wall explicitly: the concentrate port and the one-way outlet-valve passage in the upper sleeve band, the flush-bypass passage running into the upper sleeve band, and the two rinse openings and the carrier-liquid admission port in the lower sleeve band. The break-off phrases read "within that band", tied to the sleeve band named in the same sentence. The rinse-channel bullet now reads as the clear gap between the sleeve and housing bands, target 60 as the clear gap between the lower housing and sleeve bands, and the section-plane sentence as which sleeve band each port and passage is drawn in. A renderer following the brief can no longer put any of those features through the housing wall.

FIG. 2 received the same treatment for the one bare reference the review noted plus the two others in the same file: the outlet-valve passage and its break line now name the upper sleeve band, the admission port's break line reads "within that band", the sleeve is introduced as upper and lower hatched sleeve bands, the housing as hatched housing bands, and target 22 names the upper sleeve band. FIG. 1 now calls the sleeve's bands sleeve bands and targets 18 on the hatched upper sleeve band, so the naming is uniform across all four sheets.

The added words pushed FIG. 3 over the brief length limit, so I recovered the space from wording that identifies no part: the view line's note that the index collar is omitted (the sheet carries no collar numerals), a redundant "in the position shown" and a "conventional" before "break line", and a shortened phrase for the piston portion covering the admission port. All four briefs are within the limit at 2783, 2662, 2796 and 2764 characters. No application text changed, as the review indicated none was required, and the numeral table, per-sheet numeral sets, drawing descriptions and detailed description remain synchronized.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is no document to cite and none is cited anywhere in the application. The Background states the technical problems the invention addresses without attributing any of them to a publication. Claim 1 is unchanged this turn and continues to rest on two concrete relationships expressed in the inventor's own terms rather than in generic dosing-valve vocabulary. The first is that the axial order of the sealing land faces and the port edges closes the concentrate port before the downstream sealing land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port, so that no position of the piston places the concentrate source in communication with the carrier-liquid path and the separation does not depend on the order in which external commands arrive. The second is that a follower pin carried by the piston rod opens a normally closed flush poppet during the return stroke and the poppet closes before the waist reconnects the concentrate port, so the rinse of the concentrate-wetted surfaces is compelled by the same stroke that delivers the dose rather than being a separately commanded operation. The specification explains the problem each solves before it is needed. The dependent ladder retreats first to the two directed rinse openings and the flexible-lip wipe, then to the waist-out-of-register interval and the express axial-ordering recitation, then to the self-indexing collar with cam groove, stop faces, detent and window, and finally to the cartridge and threaded end cap. This turn's edits were confined to naming in the figure briefs and touched no claim and no scope. The drafting brief records that no prior-art search was run for this matter, so the art available here may be incomplete and the claims should be re-checked against any later search results.

1	Many liquid handling installations add a small, accurately measured quantity of a concentrate to a much larger stream of a carrier liquid that is already flowing in a pipe. The concentrate may be aggressive, staining, strongly colored, biologically active, or simply expensive, and the quantity that must be added is small in comparison with the carrier flow. The addition therefore has to be made repeatably, without measuring the concentrate by eye, and without allowing the concentrate to reach any part of the installation other than the carrier stream itself.
2	
3	Two practical difficulties dominate this kind of dosing. The first is separation of the two liquids upstream of the point of addition. A dosing device sits between a concentrate source and a pressurized carrier line, and any path that momentarily connects the two allows carrier liquid to be forced back into the concentrate source or allows concentrate to migrate into the carrier line at a time when no dose is called for. Devices that rely on separately actuated shut-off elements to keep the two sides apart depend on those elements being commanded in the correct order, so a control fault, a lost signal, or a slow-acting element can open both sides at once.
4	
5	The second difficulty is residue. The surfaces that the concentrate touches, in particular the port through which it enters the metering volume and the seat of the check element through which the dose leaves, retain a film of concentrate after the dose has been delivered. That film drips into the carrier stream between doses, so the quantity actually added is not the quantity that was measured. It also dries, crystallizes, or reacts on the wetted surfaces, so that a valve which was accurate when new drifts, sticks, or seizes in service. The usual remedy is to break the valve out of the line and clean it by hand, which takes the installation out of service and exposes the person doing the work to the concentrate. Where a rinse is provided at all, it is commonly a separate operation that has to be commanded after the dose, and it therefore depends on an operator or a controller performing an extra step at the right moment.
6	
7	Dose selection presents a further difficulty. Adjustable dosing devices are often set by a screw or by an electronically stored value. A screw setting can be lost during cleaning and gives no indication of what was set. An electronic setting requires power, a sensor and a display at the valve, which is unwelcome in wet, washdown or hazardous locations, and it tells the operator only what the controller believes rather than what the mechanism will actually deliver.
8	
9	There remains a need for an inline metering valve in which the separation of the concentrate from the carrier liquid is enforced by the geometry of the moving parts rather than by the order in which external commands arrive, in which the surfaces wetted by the concentrate are rinsed by the carrier liquid as an unavoidable part of the return of the metering element, and in which the selected dose is both retained and displayed mechanically.

Many liquid handling installations add a small, accurately measured quantity of a concentrate to a much larger stream of a carrier liquid that is already flowing in a pipe. The concentrate may be aggressive, staining, strongly colored, biologically active, or simply expensive, and the quantity that must be added is small in comparison with the carrier flow. The addition therefore has to be made repeatably, without measuring the concentrate by eye, and without allowing the concentrate to reach any part of the installation other than the carrier stream itself.

Two practical difficulties dominate this kind of dosing. The first is separation of the two liquids upstream of the point of addition. A dosing device sits between a concentrate source and a pressurized carrier line, and any path that momentarily connects the two allows carrier liquid to be forced back into the concentrate source or allows concentrate to migrate into the carrier line at a time when no dose is called for. Devices that rely on separately actuated shut-off elements to keep the two sides apart depend on those elements being commanded in the correct order, so a control fault, a lost signal, or a slow-acting element can open both sides at once.

The second difficulty is residue. The surfaces that the concentrate touches, in particular the port through which it enters the metering volume and the seat of the check element through which the dose leaves, retain a film of concentrate after the dose has been delivered. That film drips into the carrier stream between doses, so the quantity actually added is not the quantity that was measured. It also dries, crystallizes, or reacts on the wetted surfaces, so that a valve which was accurate when new drifts, sticks, or seizes in service. The usual remedy is to break the valve out of the line and clean it by hand, which takes the installation out of service and exposes the person doing the work to the concentrate. Where a rinse is provided at all, it is commonly a separate operation that has to be commanded after the dose, and it therefore depends on an operator or a controller performing an extra step at the right moment.

Dose selection presents a further difficulty. Adjustable dosing devices are often set by a screw or by an electronically stored value. A screw setting can be lost during cleaning and gives no indication of what was set. An electronic setting requires power, a sensor and a display at the valve, which is unwelcome in wet, washdown or hazardous locations, and it tells the operator only what the controller believes rather than what the mechanism will actually deliver.

There remains a need for an inline metering valve in which the separation of the concentrate from the carrier liquid is enforced by the geometry of the moving parts rather than by the order in which external commands arrive, in which the surfaces wetted by the concentrate are rinsed by the carrier liquid as an unavoidable part of the return of the metering element, and in which the selected dose is both retained and displayed mechanically.

All three reviewer findings are fixed.

**Claim 9.** The claim now uses the description's own wording: "the one of the three dose setting numerals presented at the transparent window being associated with a selected one of the three selectable axial stop faces that then limits the travel of the piston." The coined participle "shown" is gone from the claims, and "presented at the transparent window" matches the description sentence verbatim, which cures both the antecedent-basis warning and the claim-term warning.

**Claim 11.** The nominalization is gone: "the threaded end cap being removable to withdraw the cartridge from the housing without disturbing connections at the inlet and at the outlet." The limitation is unchanged in substance and now tracks the description's "Removing the threaded end cap 66 withdraws the cartridge 64 ... without disturbing the connections at the inlet 14 and the outlet 16."

**Background.** The two sentences asserting concrete facts about third-party devices are removed. The paragraph now reads: "Dose selection presents a further difficulty. Adjustable dosing devices may be set by a screw or by an electronically stored value. There remains a need for a setting that is retained by the mechanism itself and that is visible at the valve without electronics." That keeps the motivation the disclosure supports and drops what nothing in the workspace supports. The rest of the Background and the closing need paragraph are untouched.

On the two failing mechanical checks: figures/ holds the four Markdown briefs, which is the only form these files take, and no rendered sheets exist yet for the checks to inspect. The briefs are complete and ready to render. Between them they assign all 29 numerals from the table, each with an explicit target and each appearing in exactly one part's list: FIG. 1 carries 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 52, 64, 66; FIG. 2 carries 18, 20, 22, 24, 30, 32, 34, 38; FIG. 3 carries 22, 26, 28, 44, 56, 58, 60, 62; FIG. 4 carries 36, 40, 42, 44, 46, 48, 50, 54. Those sets still match the per-figure recitations in the detailed description and the view lines in the brief description of the drawings, and each sheet stays at eight numerals or fewer. All four briefs are within the length limit at 2783, 2662, 2796 and 2764 characters.

tool_use_result.originalFile:
Many liquid handling installations add a small, accurately measured quantity of a concentrate to a much larger stream of a carrier liquid that is already flowing in a pipe. The concentrate may be aggressive, staining, strongly colored, biologically active, or simply expensive, and the quantity that must be added is small in comparison with the carrier flow. The addition therefore has to be made repeatably, without measuring the concentrate by eye, and without allowing the concentrate to reach any part of the installation other than the carrier stream itself.

Two practical difficulties dominate this kind of dosing. The first is separation of the two liquids upstream of the point of addition. A dosing device sits between a concentrate source and a pressurized carrier line, and any path that momentarily connects the two allows carrier liquid to be forced back into the concentrate source or allows concentrate to migrate into the carrier line at a time when no dose is called for. Devices that rely on separately actuated shut-off elements to keep the two sides apart depend on those elements being commanded in the correct order, so a control fault, a lost signal, or a slow-acting element can open both sides at once.

The second difficulty is residue. The surfaces that the concentrate touches, in particular the port through which it enters the metering volume and the seat of the check element through which the dose leaves, retain a film of concentrate after the dose has been delivered. That film drips into the carrier stream between doses, so the quantity actually added is not the quantity that was measured. It also dries, crystallizes, or reacts on the wetted surfaces, so that a valve which was accurate when new drifts, sticks, or seizes in service. The usual remedy is to break the valve out of the line and clean it by hand, which takes the installation out of service and exposes the person doing the work to the concentrate. Where a rinse is provided at all, it is commonly a separate operation that has to be commanded after the dose, and it therefore depends on an operator or a controller performing an extra step at the right moment.

Dose selection presents a further difficulty. Adjustable dosing devices may be set by a screw or by an electronically stored value. There remains a need for a setting that is retained by the mechanism itself and that is visible at the valve without electronics.

There remains a need for an inline metering valve in which the separation of the concentrate from the carrier liquid is enforced by the geometry of the moving parts rather than by the order in which external commands arrive, in which the surfaces wetted by the concentrate are rinsed by the carrier liquid as an unavoidable part of the return of the metering element, and in which the selected dose is both retained and displayed mechanically.

tool_use_result.originalFile:
In the following description, the terms upstream and downstream refer to the direction of travel of the carrier liquid from the inlet toward the outlet, and the terms axial and radial refer to the axis along which the piston slides.

FIG. 1 shows an inline liquid metering valve 10 having a cylindrical housing 12 with an inlet 14 at one axial end and an outlet 16 at the opposite axial end, a metering sleeve 18 fixed within the housing 12, a cartridge 64 retained in the housing 12 by a threaded end cap 66, and a transparent window 52 in the housing 12.

The inline liquid metering valve 10 is connected in a line that already carries a flowing carrier liquid. Carrier liquid enters at the inlet 14, passes along the housing 12, and leaves at the outlet 16. That flow is the main flow into which each dose of concentrate is delivered, and it is also the flow that rinses the valve. The metering sleeve 18 is spaced radially inward from the inner surface of the housing 12.

FIG. 2 shows the metering sleeve 18 defining a dose chamber 20, a concentrate port 22 opening into the dose chamber 20 and a carrier-liquid admission port 24 opening into the dose chamber 20. FIG. 2 further shows an upstream sealing land 30 and a downstream sealing land 32 joined by a reduced-diameter waist 34 in the fill position, and a one-way outlet valve 38.

The dose chamber 20 is cylindrical. The concentrate port 22 is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and is connected in use to a concentrate source. The carrier-liquid admission port 24 passes through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 at an axial position downstream of the concentrate port 22, and admits carrier liquid to the dose chamber 20. The metering sleeve 18 further defines a flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20.

A piston 28 is axially slidable in the dose chamber 20 between a fill position and a discharge position. The upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 are axially spaced from one another on the piston 28 and are joined by the reduced-diameter waist 34. Each sealing land bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20, while the waist 34 stands clear of that wall. A piston rod 36 extends from the piston 28 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 and is arranged to be driven through a stroke and a return stroke. The one-way outlet valve 38 is arranged to pass liquid from the dose chamber 20 toward the outlet 16 and to prevent flow in the opposite direction.

In the fill position the waist 34 connects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20, and the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolate the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. Concentrate accordingly passes from the concentrate source through the concentrate port 22 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume of concentrate, the extent of which is fixed by the travel then permitted to the piston 28. Throughout the fill position the carrier-liquid path is closed to the concentrate, because the downstream sealing land 32 overlies the carrier-liquid admission port 24 while the upstream sealing land 30 closes the dose chamber 20 on the other side of the waist 34.

Movement of the piston 28 toward the discharge position closes the concentrate port 22 before the downstream sealing land 32 uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Only after the concentrate port 22 has been closed does continued travel of the piston 28 carry the downstream sealing land 32 clear of the carrier-liquid admission port 24. Carrier liquid then enters through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume of concentrate in the dose chamber 20 and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16, where it joins the main flow.

The axial ordering of the faces of the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 relative to the edges of the concentrate port 22 and the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is chosen so that the concentrate port 22 is closed at every position of the piston 28 at which the carrier-liquid admission port 24 is open. There is accordingly no position of the piston 28 at which the concentrate source communicates directly with the carrier-liquid path. The separation of the two liquids is a property of the geometry of the piston 28 and the metering sleeve 18. It does not depend on the order in which external commands are given, on any control signal, or on the correct operation of a separately actuated shut-off element. The port that must close does so at an earlier point on the same continuous path of travel than the point at which the other port opens.

FIG. 3 shows the piston 28 during the return stroke toward the fill position, with a flexible lip 56, a follower pin 44 holding a flush poppet 58 open, an annular rinse channel 60, two radial rinse openings 62, the concentrate port 22, and the flush bypass 26. The follower pin 44 is carried by the piston rod 36.

The flexible lip 56 is carried on the upstream sealing land 30 and bears on the wall of the dose chamber 20. As the return stroke begins, the flexible lip 56 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20.

The annular rinse channel 60 lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve 18 and an inner surface of the housing 12, and is supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet 14. The two radial rinse openings 62 pass through the wall of the metering sleeve 18 and connect the annular rinse channel 60 to the dose chamber 20. One of the two radial rinse openings 62 is directed across the concentrate port 22 and the other is directed across the one-way outlet valve 38.

The flush poppet 58 is normally closed and is connected to the flush bypass 26. Near the end of the return stroke, the follower pin 44 reaches the flush poppet 58 and opens it. Carrier liquid then flows from the inlet 14 through the annular rinse channel 60, through the two radial rinse openings 62 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 to the outlet 16. The rinse liquid therefore reaches the outlet 16, as the dose does, and is carried away in the main flow.

The flush poppet 58 closes before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. Throughout the interval in which the annular rinse channel 60 communicates with the flush bypass 26, the waist 34 is out of register with the concentrate port 22, so that the waist 34 does not connect the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. Only when the flush poppet 58 has closed does the continuing return of the piston 28 bring the waist 34 back into register with the concentrate port 22, at which point the dose chamber 20 is charged again for the next dose.

Because the follower pin 44 that opens the flush poppet 58 is carried by the piston rod 36, the rinse occurs once for every dose and at the same point in every cycle. It is not a separate operation, it needs no command, and it cannot be omitted while the valve continues to be used. The rinse also occurs before the waist 34 has reconnected the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20 and after the wall of the dose chamber 20 has been wiped.

FIG. 4 shows an index collar 40 having a helical cam groove 42 engaged by the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36, three selectable axial stop faces 46, and three dose setting numerals 54. FIG. 4 further shows a spring-biased detent 48 engaging one of three detent recesses 50.

The index collar 40 surrounds the metering sleeve 18. Each full stroke of the piston 28 draws the follower pin 44 along the helical cam groove 42 and turns the index collar 40 by one increment, so that the index collar 40 advances by itself as the valve is used and needs no separate indexing drive.

The three axial stop faces 46 are carried by the index collar 40 at different axial positions. The stop face presented by the current increment of rotation limits the travel of the piston 28 and thereby sets the dose volume, so that the three axial stop faces 46 correspond to three dose volumes. The spring-biased detent 48 engages one of the three detent recesses 50 to retain the selected setting until the index collar 40 is next indexed.

The transparent window 52 in the housing 12 shows one of the three dose setting numerals 54 carried by the index collar 40. The dose setting numeral presented at the transparent window 52 is the one associated with the axial stop face then limiting the travel of the piston 28, so that the dose setting is mechanically visible without electronics. What is seen at the transparent window 52 is the position of the index collar 40 itself.

The cartridge 64 contains the piston 28, the metering sleeve 18, the one-way outlet valve 38 and the flush poppet 58, and is removable from the housing 12 as a unit. Removing the threaded end cap 66 withdraws the cartridge 64 from the housing 12 along the axis of the dose chamber 20 without disturbing the connections at the inlet 14 and the outlet 16, so that the cartridge 64 is replaced as a unit while the housing 12 remains in the line.

In use, carrier liquid flows through the housing 12 from the inlet 14 to the outlet 16. With the piston 28 in the fill position, concentrate is admitted through the concentrate port 22 and past the waist 34 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume, the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolating the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. The piston 28 is then advanced toward the discharge position so as to close the concentrate port 22 and thereafter to uncover the carrier-liquid admission port 24 with the downstream sealing land 32. Carrier liquid is admitted through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16. The extent of the travel available to the piston 28, and therefore the measured volume, is fixed by the selected one of the three axial stop faces 46.

The piston 28 is then returned toward the fill position. During the return, the flexible lip 56 on the upstream sealing land 30 wipes the wall of the dose chamber 20, and the follower pin 44 carried by the piston rod 36 opens the normally closed flush poppet 58. Carrier liquid flows through the annular rinse channel 60 between the metering sleeve 18 and the housing 12, through the two radial rinse openings 62 in the metering sleeve 18 across the concentrate port 22 and the one-way outlet valve 38, and through the flush bypass 26 that opens downstream of the dose chamber 20 to the outlet 16. The flush poppet 58 is closed before the waist 34 reconnects the concentrate port 22 to the dose chamber 20. Over the same full stroke, the follower pin 44 traveling in the helical cam groove 42 turns the index collar 40 by one increment, the spring-biased detent 48 enters the next of the three detent recesses 50, and the dose setting numeral then presented at the transparent window 52 shows the setting that will govern the next dose. The valve is thereby left charged, rinsed and set, ready for the following cycle.

The foregoing description sets out embodiments of the invention. A skilled reader may make changes of detail to the described embodiments without departing from the scope of the claims that follow.

content.content:
1	Many liquid handling installations add a small, accurately measured quantity of a concentrate to a much larger stream of a carrier liquid that is already flowing in a pipe. The concentrate may be aggressive, staining, strongly colored, biologically active, or simply expensive, and the quantity that must be added is small in comparison with the carrier flow. The addition therefore has to be made repeatably, without measuring the concentrate by eye, and without allowing the concentrate to reach any part of the installation other than the carrier stream itself.
2	
3	Two practical difficulties dominate this kind of dosing. The first is separation of the two liquids upstream of the point of addition. A dosing device sits between a concentrate source and a pressurized carrier line, and any path that momentarily connects the two allows carrier liquid to be forced back into the concentrate source or allows concentrate to migrate into the carrier line at a time when no dose is called for. Where the two sides are kept apart by separately actuated shut-off elements, the separation depends on those elements being commanded in the correct order.
4	
5	The second difficulty is residue. The surfaces that the concentrate touches, in particular the port through which it enters the metering volume and the seat of the check element through which the dose leaves, retain a film of concentrate after the dose has been delivered. That film drips into the carrier stream between doses, so the quantity actually added is not the quantity that was measured. It also dries, crystallizes, or reacts on the wetted surfaces, so that a valve which was accurate when new drifts, sticks, or seizes in service. Where the valve must be broken out of the line and cleaned by hand, the installation is taken out of service; and where a rinse is a separate operation commanded after the dose, it depends on that operation being performed at the right moment.
6	
7	Dose selection presents a further difficulty. Adjustable dosing devices may be set by a screw or by an electronically stored value. There remains a need for a setting that is retained by the mechanism itself and that is visible at the valve without electronics.
8	
9	There remains a need for an inline metering valve in which the separation of the concentrate from the carrier liquid is enforced by the geometry of the moving parts rather than by the order in which external commands arrive, in which the surfaces wetted by the concentrate are rinsed by the carrier liquid as an unavoidable part of the return of the metering element, and in which the selected dose is both retained and displayed mechanically.
10

A dosing device sits between a concentrate source and a pressurized carrier line, and any path that momentarily connects the two allows carrier liquid to be forced back into the concentrate source or allows concentrate to migrate into the carrier line at a time when no dose is called for. Where the two sides are kept apart by separately actuated shut-off elements, the separation depends on those elements being commanded in the correct order.

The second difficulty is residue. The surfaces that the concentrate touches, in particular the port through which it enters the metering volume and the seat of the check element through which the dose leaves, retain a film of concentrate after the dose has been delivered. tool_use_result.originalFile:
Many liquid handling installations add a small, accurately measured quantity of a concentrate to a much larger stream of a carrier liquid that is already flowing in a pipe. The concentrate may be aggressive, staining, strongly colored, biologically active, or simply expensive, and the quantity that must be added is small in comparison with the carrier flow. The addition therefore has to be made repeatably, without measuring the concentrate by eye, and without allowing the concentrate to reach any part of the installation other than the carrier stream itself.

Two practical difficulties dominate this kind of dosing. The first is separation of the two liquids upstream of the point of addition. A dosing device sits between a concentrate source and a pressurized carrier line, and any path that momentarily connects the two allows carrier liquid to be forced back into the concentrate source or allows concentrate to migrate into the carrier line at a time when no dose is called for. Where the two sides are kept apart by separately actuated shut-off elements, the separation depends on those elements being commanded in the correct order.

The second difficulty is residue. The surfaces that the concentrate touches, in particular the port through which it enters the metering volume and the seat of the check element through which the dose leaves, retain a film of concentrate after the dose has been delivered. That film drips into the carrier stream between doses, so the quantity actually added is not the quantity that was measured. It also dries, crystallizes, or reacts on the wetted surfaces, so that a valve which was accurate when new drifts, sticks, or seizes in service. Where the valve must be broken out of the line and cleaned by hand, the installation is taken out of service; and where a rinse is a separate operation commanded after the dose, it depends on that operation being performed at the right moment.

Dose selection presents a further difficulty. Adjustable dosing devices may be set by a screw or by an electronically stored value. There remains a need for a setting that is retained by the mechanism itself and that is visible at the valve without electronics.

There remains a need for an inline metering valve in which the separation of the concentrate from the carrier liquid is enforced by the geometry of the moving parts rather than by the order in which external commands arrive, in which the surfaces wetted by the concentrate are rinsed by the carrier liquid as an unavoidable part of the return of the metering element, and in which the selected dose is both retained and displayed mechanically.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is no document to cite and none is cited anywhere in the application. With this turn the whole Background is conditional or need-framed: it names the separation problem, the residue problem and the dose-setting problem as technical situations the invention addresses, without asserting facts about third-party devices that nothing in the workspace supports and that could be read as admissions. Claim 1 is unchanged and continues to rest on two concrete relationships expressed in the inventor's own terms rather than in generic dosing-valve vocabulary. The first is that the axial order of the sealing land faces and the port edges closes the concentrate port before the downstream sealing land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port, so that no position of the piston places the concentrate source in communication with the carrier-liquid path and the separation does not depend on the order in which external commands arrive. The second is that a follower pin carried by the piston rod opens a normally closed flush poppet during the return stroke and the poppet closes before the waist reconnects the concentrate port, so the rinse of the concentrate-wetted surfaces is compelled by the same stroke that delivers the dose rather than being a separately commanded operation. The dependent ladder retreats first to the two directed rinse openings and the flexible-lip wipe, then to the waist-out-of-register interval and the express axial-ordering recitation, then to the self-indexing collar with cam groove, stop faces, detent and window, and finally to the cartridge and threaded end cap. The drafting brief records that no prior-art search was run for this matter, so the art available here may be incomplete and the claims should be re-checked against any later search results.

tool_use_result.originalFile:
Many liquid handling installations add a small, accurately measured quantity of a concentrate to a much larger stream of a carrier liquid that is already flowing in a pipe. The concentrate may be aggressive, staining, strongly colored, biologically active, or simply expensive, and the quantity that must be added is small in comparison with the carrier flow. The addition therefore has to be made repeatably, without measuring the concentrate by eye, and without allowing the concentrate to reach any part of the installation other than the carrier stream itself.

Two practical difficulties dominate this kind of dosing. The first is separation of the two liquids upstream of the point of addition. A dosing device sits between a concentrate source and a pressurized carrier line, and any path that momentarily connects the two allows carrier liquid to be forced back into the concentrate source or allows concentrate to migrate into the carrier line at a time when no dose is called for. Where the two sides are kept apart by separately actuated shut-off elements, the separation depends on those elements being commanded in the correct order.

The second difficulty is residue. The surfaces that the concentrate touches, in particular the port through which it enters the metering volume and the seat of the check element through which the dose leaves, may retain a film of concentrate after the dose has been delivered. Where such a film passes into the carrier stream between doses, the quantity actually added is not the quantity that was measured; and where it dries or reacts on the wetted surfaces, the accuracy of the valve changes in service. Where the valve must be broken out of the line and cleaned by hand, the installation is taken out of service; and where a rinse is a separate operation commanded after the dose, it depends on that operation being performed at the right moment.

Dose selection presents a further difficulty. Adjustable dosing devices may be set by a screw or by an electronically stored value. There remains a need for a setting that is retained by the mechanism itself and that is visible at the valve without electronics.

There remains a need for an inline metering valve in which the separation of the concentrate from the carrier liquid is enforced by the geometry of the moving parts rather than by the order in which external commands arrive, in which the surfaces wetted by the concentrate are rinsed by the carrier liquid as an unavoidable part of the return of the metering element, and in which the selected dose is both retained and displayed mechanically.
